the smaller the difference between the incomes of the low-income group and the high-income group.
the lower the degree of income inequality.

questions.explanation: A higher Gini coefficient indicates greater inequality, but it alone does not determine the absolute income of the low-income group or the size of every income gap.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (II)
questions.keyPoint: Equalising income
questions.stem: Which of the following government policies can reduce income inequality?

choices.text: changing the salaries tax system from progressive to proportional
reducing subsidies for primary and secondary education
raising the property tax on luxury flats

questions.explanation: A higher tax on luxury flats is progressive in effect and can reduce post-tax income inequality. The other policies tend to be regressive or reduce equalising opportunities.

questions.keyPoint: Relationship between scarcity and choice
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about scarcity is CORRECT?

choices.text: Scarcity exists if the supply of a resource is limited.
Only people in the developing countries have to face the problem of scarcity.
The existence of scarcity implies that people have to make choices.

questions.explanation: Scarcity means resources are insufficient relative to wants, so choices are unavoidable. A resource can be limited without being scarce, and scarcity is not the same as shortage.

questions.keyPoint: Identify and calculate the cost (explicit cost and implicit cost) involved in choosing an option
questions.stem: The digital version of the Riverside Scene at Qingming Festival will be shown at the Asia-World Expo. The ticket price is $10. Joe queued up for the ticket for 2 hours, which made him miss his tennis lesson. Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

choices.text: Joe's opportunity cost of obtaining the ticket is $10.
Joe's opportunity cost of obtaining the ticket is higher than $10.
Joe's opportunity cost of obtaining the ticket will be zero if his mother pays for the ticket.
Joe's opportunity cost of obtaining the ticket is the 2 hours spent on queuing for the ticket.

questions.explanation: The ticket price is an explicit cost and missing the tennis lesson is an implicit cost, so Joe's opportunity cost is higher than $10.

questions.keyPoint: Distinguishing between free goods and economic goods
questions.stem: In Hong Kong, some organisations provide food for street sleepers and emergency food supplies for the poor. The food provided is said to be economic goods because

choices.text: only the street sleepers and people referred by the community centers can get the food.
there are transportation costs for the needy to travel to the organisations.
more than one person prefer the food.

questions.explanation: A good is economic when it is scarce relative to wants. The fact that more food is preferred shows that it is scarce, even if provided free of charge.

questions.chapterTitle: The Three Basic Economic Problems and Private Property Rights
questions.keyPoint: The meaning of private property rights and its importance in a market economy
questions.stem:
Miss Chan is a personal assistant. Her boss provides a smartphone for her so that jobs can be done more conveniently. What is/are the private property rights Miss Chan may have over the smartphone?

(1) exclusive rights to use the smartphone
(2) exclusive rights to lease out the smartphone
(3) exclusive rights to sell the smartphone
questions.explanation: As an employee using her employer's phone, Miss Chan may be given the right to use it, but not the rights to lease or transfer it.

questions.keyPoint: Comparison of features, advantages and disadvantages of different forms of ownership
questions.stem: Mr. Cheung and Mr. Tang jointly own a firm and they enjoy limited liability. Which of the following must be TRUE?

choices.text: The firm is listed on the stock exchange.
Mr. Cheung can transfer his shares to others without the consent of Mr. Tang.
They do not have to disclose the financial statements to the public.
Mr. Tang can continue the business even if Mr. Cheung dies.

questions.explanation: Limited liability means the firm is a limited company with lasting continuity, so the business can continue after an owner's death. It need not be listed or have freely transferable shares.

questions.topicGroup: Types of goods and services produced
questions.keyPoint: Private goods and public goods
questions.stem: The card games provided in cafes are classified as
questions.explanation: The games are used by the cafe to provide its service, so they are producer goods. They are rival and excludable, hence private goods.

questions.keyPoint: Different methods of wage payment
questions.stem:
A publishing company prefers to pay a translator at piece rate rather than at time rate. This may be because

(1) it is easier to control the production cost.
(2) the cost of ensuring the translator not to shirk is lower.
(3) the cost of monitoring output quality is lower.
questions.explanation: Piece rate links pay to output, helping control costs and reduce shirking. It may increase the need to monitor quality.

questions.topicGroup: Input-output relationship in the short run
questions.keyPoint: Law of diminishing marginal returns
questions.stem: The following table shows the information of factory X.
questions.explanation: Total products for 5, 6 and 7 workers are 100, 150 and 210. Marginal product rises to 60 for the seventh worker, so the eighth worker's marginal product must be below 60; 265 is possible.
questions.postVisualStem: If diminishing marginal returns set in after the 7th worker is employed, the total product of 8 units of worker can be

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.topicGroup: The basic objective of firms: profit maximisation
questions.keyPoint: Profit-maximising choice of output for a competitive firm
questions.stem: Read the following information of a competitive firm.
questions.explanation: Marginal costs are $16, $18, $20 and $22. A competitive firm produces 3 units where MC equals price, and marginal revenue equals the market price of $20.
questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the market price is $20. The profit-maximising output level is ________ units and the marginal revenue is ________.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.keyPoint: Understand the meaning and give examples of each type of integration
questions.stem: Mrs. Ma runs a farm growing organic vegetables. Recently, she has acquired a shop selling organic products. This is an example of ____________ and this enables Mrs. Ma to ____________.

choices.text: backward expansion ... ensure a stable supply of organic vegetables for her shop
backward expansion ... diversify the sources of income
forward expansion ... build up a network for selling her organic products
forward expansion ... increase the market share of her shop selling organic products

questions.explanation: Acquiring a retailer is forward integration because it moves toward consumers and builds a distribution network for the farm's vegetables.

questions.topicGroup: Determination of equilibrium price and output
questions.keyPoint: Market disequilibrium: excess demand and excess supply
questions.stem: The table below shows the market supply schedule of good X.

choices.text: At $10, the quantity demanded of good X is smaller than 500 units.
At $40, the quantity transacted is smaller than 800 units.
At $50, the quantity demanded is 900 units.

questions.explanation: At a price above equilibrium, quantity demanded is below equilibrium quantity and below quantity supplied. Thus at $40, quantity transacted is less than 800 units.
questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the equilibrium price of good X is $20. Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the herbal tea market in Hong Kong. E0 is the original equilibrium point.
questions.explanation: Lower demand shifts the demand curve left while higher herb prices reduce supply. The intersection of the new curves is E1.

visuals.alt: Herbal tea market with equilibrium points E0-E4.

movements: Compare the market shifts represented by the five labelled equilibria.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Select the herbal-tea market outcome that follows from the stated change.

questions.postVisualStem:
Some Chinese medicine experts warn that herbal tea may not be suitable for everyone and some people may suffer from the side effects.

Suppose some people reduce drinking herbal tea and there is an increase in the price of most herbs. The new equilibrium point would be at _______.

questions.keyPoint: Supply of labour
questions.stem: The economic development of Country X has been growing rapidly in recent years. The growth of the construction sector attracts many fresh graduates to join the sector. Moreover, more and more new hotels are under construction. Which of the following must be TRUE?

choices.text: The number of construction workers employed increases.
The wage rate of construction workers increases.
The total income of construction workers increases.
The total expenditure on employing construction workers increases.

questions.explanation: More graduates raise labour supply and more hotel construction raises labour demand. Both changes increase the equilibrium number of construction workers employed; the wage effect is uncertain.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Types of price elasticity of demand
questions.stem: In Country Y, the market of ball pens is dominated by two producers. Producer A goes bankrupt and closes down. After the closing of producer A, the price of ball pens of producer B increases from $6 to $8 while the quantity transacted increases by 50%. We can conclude that

choices.text: the price elasticity of demand of ball pens of producer B is greater than 1.
the price elasticity of demand of ball pens of producer B is smaller than 1.
the price elasticity of supply of ball pens of producer B is greater than 1.
the price elasticity of supply of ball pens of producer B is smaller than 1.

questions.explanation: Producer A's exit raises demand for B's pens. Quantity rises by 50% while B's price rises by about 33%, so B's supply is elastic.

questions.topicGroup: Tax on goods and services (Sales tax)
questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of a unit tax on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc., and show the share of the tax burden between producers and consumers
questions.stem: The table below shows the market demand and supply of good X.
questions.explanation: The tax creates a $3 wedge: consumers pay $10, producers receive $7 and 110 units are traded, so tax revenue is $330. Demand is more elastic than supply around the new equilibrium.
questions.postVisualStem: Suppose a per-unit tax of $3 is imposed on good X. The total tax revenue received by the government is _______. The demand for good X is _______ elastic than the supply of good X.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) price floor on (money) price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc.
questions.stem:
Imposing an effective price floor on a good will result in

(1) a shortage of the good.
(2) a decrease in total expenditure on the good if the demand for the good is elastic.
(3) a decrease in the quantity transacted of the good.
questions.explanation: An effective floor causes excess supply, not shortage. The higher price lowers quantity traded and, with elastic demand, lowers total expenditure.

questions.keyPoint: State the general features of different market structures
questions.stem: In Hong Kong, the market structure of pay TV is said to be an oligopoly because

choices.text: the television programs broadcasted by different pay TV providers are similar.
the pay TV providers know the marketing strategies of each other well.
the pay TV providers share the market equally.
when one pay TV provider offers a promotion discount, others will most likely follow.

questions.explanation: Oligopolists are interdependent, so a promotion by one major provider is likely to prompt a response from others.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) quota on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, product quality, etc.
questions.stem: Suppose the government of Country X imposed a quota on the supply of a good. Which of the following is CORRECT?

choices.text: Producer surplus increases because the unit price of the good increases.
Consumer surplus decreases and the entire loss in consumer surplus is transferred to the producers.
Total social surplus decreases because there is a deadweight loss.

questions.explanation: An effective quota restricts trade below the efficient quantity and creates deadweight loss. The other effects are not guaranteed.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.keyPoint: Negative externality and economic inefficiency; internalising external costs
questions.stem: The building of a new landfill creates a bad smell and seriously affects residents living in a nearby private housing estate. Assume the residents have the right to live in an environment with fresh air. Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

choices.text: There is no divergence between private and social costs because the bad smell is not created within the area of the private housing estate.
There is no divergence between private and social costs if the cost involved in eliminating the external cost are higher than the benefits gained.
The divergence between private and social costs can only be solved by closing the landfill.
The divergence between private and social costs can be eliminated by paying compensation to the residents.

questions.explanation: The smell imposes external cost on residents. Compensation equal to the external cost can internalise the divergence between private and social costs.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (II)
questions.keyPoint: Interpret the information delivered from the Lorenz curve
questions.stem: The diagrams below show the Lorenz curves of two countries.
questions.explanation: Country B's Lorenz curve is further from the line of equality, so its high-income group has a higher income share and its Gini coefficient is higher. The curves do not show absolute incomes of the low-income groups.

visuals.alt: Lorenz curves of Country A and Country B.

movements: Compare the distance of each Lorenz curve from the line of equality.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Use the curves to compare income inequality between the two countries.

questions.postVisualStem:
According to the above diagrams, which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?

(1) The low-income group in Country B earns a lower income than that in Country A.
(2) The high-income group in County B has a higher percentage of total income than that in Country A.
(3) The Gini coefficient of Country A is greater than zero and smaller than that of Country B.

questions.keyPoint: Expenditure approach
questions.stem: The table below shows the gross domestic product data of Country X in a certain year.
questions.explanation: GDP at market price is GDP at factor cost plus indirect taxes minus subsidies, or $330 million. Using C + I + G + net exports gives X = $120 million.
questions.postVisualStem: If the GDP at factor cost is $333 million, the value of X is ________.

questions.keyPoint: Production/value added approach
questions.stem: The diagram below shows the production chain of electronic readers in an economy.
questions.explanation: GDP counts final output: $350,000 of local consumption including $5,000 sales tax plus $280,000 exports, less $150,000 imported parts, giving $480,000.

visuals.alt: Electronic-reader production chain with local and imported inputs, sales and exports.

movements: Follow the value flows through production, retailing, exports and inventory.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Identify which flows count as domestic value added and GDP.

questions.postVisualStem: What is the contribution of the above production chain to the economy's GDP at market prices?

questions.keyPoint: Growth rate of GDP
questions.stem:
The growth rates of nominal GDP, real GDP and population of Country X in a certain year are 7%, -2% and 5% respectively. Which of the following about Country X is TRUE?

(1) The general price level has increased.
(2) The per capita real GDP has increased.
(3) The per capita nominal GDP has increased.
questions.explanation: Nominal GDP grows faster than real GDP, so the price level rises. Per-capita real GDP falls, while per-capita nominal GDP rises.

questions.keyPoint: Gross national income (Gross national product)
questions.stem: Which of the following should be included in the calculation of Hong Kong's GNP but not GDP?

choices.text: income earned by a Hong Kong resident from working at a company owned by a Japanese in Hong Kong for 6 months
income earned by an American from working at a company in Hong Kong for six months
income earned by a Hong Kong resident from selling a diamond ring to a Mainland tourist
income earned by a Hong Kong resident from working at a company in New York for six months

questions.explanation: GNP includes income earned by Hong Kong residents abroad, while GDP includes production within Hong Kong regardless of the producer's residency.

questions.keyPoint: Expenditure approach
questions.stem: In an open economy, Y = $300, C = $140, I = $100, G = $80 and SP = $100 where Y, C, I, G and SP are national income, private consumption expenditure, gross investment, government consumption expenditure and private saving respectively. This means that the government has a __________________ and there is a __________________.
questions.explanation: Taxes equal Y - C - private saving = $60, so government saving is -$20: a budget deficit. National saving is $80 versus investment of $100, requiring $20 net capital inflow.

questions.keyPoint: Uses and limitations of national income statistics
questions.stem: Compared to the per capita nominal GDP, the per capita real GDP is a better indicator in reflecting the average living standard of an economy because

choices.text: the change in the size of population is taken into account.
the distribution of income is taken into account.
the composition of output is taken into account.
the change in the price level is taken into account.

questions.explanation: Both indicators are per capita, but real GDP removes price-level changes and hence better reflects changes in output and average living standard.

questions.keyPoint: Factors that cause a shift of an AD curve
questions.stem: Suppose the government of an economy raises the profits tax rate. This will result in

choices.text: a decrease in short-run aggregate supply.
a decrease in long-run aggregate supply.
a decrease in short-run and long-run aggregate supply.

questions.explanation: A higher profits tax reduces firms' retained profit and investment spending, shifting aggregate demand left.

questions.topicGroup: Factors affecting long run aggregate supply
questions.keyPoint: Factors affecting long run aggregate supply
questions.stem: An economy's long-run aggregate supply will decrease if

choices.text: the government passes the minimum wage law.
a drought destroys most of the crops.
many people choose to migrate overseas.

questions.explanation: Emigration reduces the labour force and productive capacity, shifting LRAS left. A drought is normally a short-run supply shock.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: Explain how a given event leads to changes in AD, SRAS and/or LRAS by specifying the component(s) of AD affected and/or factor(s) affecting SRAS and/or LRAS, leading to a shift of the AD curve, the SRAS curve and/or the LRAS curve
questions.explanation: The diagram shows a deflationary gap. Lowering sales tax shifts SRAS right, restoring full-employment output without raising price level.

visuals.alt: AS-AD diagram with SRAS, LRAS, AD and output Y*.

movements: Compare aggregate-demand and short-run aggregate-supply positions around full-employment output.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Identify the stated macroeconomic condition from the AS-AD diagram.

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the output level of an economy is currently at Y*. Which of the following helps restore the economy to the long-run equilibrium without raising the price level?

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: Explain how a given event leads to changes in AD, SRAS and/or LRAS by specifying the component(s) of AD affected and/or factor(s) affecting SRAS and/or LRAS, leading to a shift of the AD curve, the SRAS curve and/or the LRAS curve
questions.stem: Suppose an economy is initially operating at the long-run equilibrium. When there is an appreciation of the domestic currency, the price level will ____________ and the equilibrium output level will ____________ in the long run.
questions.explanation: Currency appreciation lowers import prices and reduces aggregate demand through exports, lowering price level. Long-run output remains at productive capacity.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: Explain how a given event leads to changes in AD, SRAS and/or LRAS by specifying the component(s) of AD affected and/or factor(s) affecting SRAS and/or LRAS, leading to a shift of the AD curve, the SRAS curve and/or the LRAS curve
questions.stem: Suppose an economy is initially operating at the long-run equilibrium. When ___________________________, the equilibrium level of output will increase while the change in the price level will be uncertain in the long run.

choices.text: the government spends more on elderly services
the government decides to build a new highway

questions.explanation: A new highway increases productive capacity, shifting LRAS right. It may also affect demand, leaving the long-run price-level effect uncertain while output rises.

questions.topicGroup: Factors affecting long run aggregate supply
questions.keyPoint: Factors affecting long run aggregate supply
questions.stem: Suppose an economy is initially operating at the long-run equilibrium. If a new energy which is more efficient and environmentally friendly is introduced into the economy,

choices.text: the aggregate demand curve will shift to the right.
the long-run aggregate supply curve will shift to the right.
both the short-run and long-run aggregate supply curves will shift to the right.
the aggregate demand, short-run aggregate supply and long-run aggregate supply curves will shift to the right.

questions.explanation: More efficient energy lowers production costs and increases productive capacity, shifting both SRAS and LRAS to the right.

questions.keyPoint: Barter and its limitations
questions.stem:
Which of the following is/are likely to happen when a barter economy changes to an economy that uses money?

(1) The transactions of goods and services drop to zero.
(2) It is easier to determine the exchange ratio.
(3) Transactions of small amounts can be made more easily.
questions.explanation: Money provides a common unit of account and divisibility, making prices and small transactions easier. It facilitates rather than eliminates transactions.

questions.keyPoint: Qualities of good money
questions.stem: Compared to 9999 gold, banknotes are a better form of money for transactions of large amounts because banknotes are more
questions.explanation: Banknotes are lighter and easier to carry and transfer for large-value transactions than gold.

questions.keyPoint: How central bank functions are carried out in
questions.stem: Which of the following functions is NOT performed by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority?

choices.text: to manage Hong Kong's foreign exchange reserves
to supervise and monitor the monetary sector
to issue all coins and banknotes

questions.explanation: The HKMA manages reserves, supervises banks and conducts monetary policy, but banknotes are issued by note-issuing banks and coins by the Government.

questions.topicGroup: Licensed banks, restricted licence banks and deposit-taking companies in
questions.keyPoint: Features of the three types of deposit-taking institutions
questions.stem: Which of the following time deposits can be accepted by both licensed banks and deposit-taking companies but not by restricted licence banks?
questions.explanation: Restricted licence banks accept deposits of at least $500,000 with maturity of at least three months. Deposit-taking companies require at least $100,000 and three months; $200,000 for six months meets the latter but not the former.

questions.keyPoint: Effects of asset transfers on money supply
questions.stem: Herman withdraws $10,000 from his savings deposit with a licensed bank in Hong Kong. He puts $4,000 as time deposit with a restricted licence bank and deposits the remaining $6,000 as demand deposits with a licensed bank. Which of the following is the immediate effect of the above actions on the money supply of Hong Kong?

choices.text: Both money supply M1 and money supply M3 remain unchanged.
Money supply M1 increases while money supply M2 remains unchanged.
Money supply M1 increases while money supply M2 decreases.
Money supply M2 increases while money supply M3 remains unchanged.

questions.explanation: Moving $6,000 from savings to demand deposits raises M1, while moving $4,000 to a restricted-licence bank removes it from M2. The net M3 position is unchanged.

questions.keyPoint: Understand and calculate maximum and actual banking multipliers
questions.stem: The table below shows the balance sheet of a banking system.
questions.explanation: Required reserves are $2,500, so the reserve ratio is 25% and maximum banking multiplier is 4. Money supply is $11,000 and monetary base is $4,000, so actual money multiplier is 2.75.
questions.postVisualStem:
Suppose the public holds $1,000 cash and the amount of excess reserves is $500. Which of the following about the banking system is/are CORRECT?

(1) The maximum banking multiplier is 3.33.
(2) The money supply is $11,000.
(3) The money multiplier is 2.75.

questions.keyPoint: Understand and calculate maximum and actual changes in deposits, loans, money supply, etc. after deposit creation/contraction
questions.stem: The table below shows the balance sheet of a banking system.
questions.explanation: Required reserves are $4,000, leaving $1,000 excess reserves. A $2,000 withdrawal reduces reserves to $3,000, supporting maximum deposits of $3,000 / 0.2 = $15,000.
questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the required reserve ratio is 20%. Someone withdraws $2,000 from the banking system. The maximum possible amount of bank deposits will be

questions.keyPoint: Analyse changes in money demand, money supply and nominal interest rate
questions.stem: Which of the following will lead to an increase in the nominal interest rate?

choices.text: The required reserve ratio is lowered.
The central bank issues more money.
People prefer to use electronic money more.

questions.explanation: Higher nominal income raises transaction demand for money. With money supply unchanged, the nominal interest rate rises.

questions.keyPoint: Relationship between scarcity, competition and discrimination
questions.stem:
The admission price of Ocean Park is fixed at $250 per adult. During Lunar New Year holidays, some people waited for hours at the ticket office but all tickets were sold out at their turns. Which of the following descriptions is/are CORRECT?

(1) There is an excess demand for the tickets.
(2) There is price competition for the tickets.
(3) There is non-price competition for the tickets.
questions.explanation: Sold-out tickets at a fixed price show excess demand. Queuing is non-price competition; price competition is absent because the admission price is fixed.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the eggs market in Hong Kong. E0 is the original equilibrium point.
questions.explanation: Both supply and demand fall. The resulting intersection is E1 in the source diagram.

visuals.alt: Eggs market with supply and demand shifts and equilibrium points E0-E4.

movements: Compare the labelled demand and supply shifts in the egg market.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Select the outcome that matches the stated eggs-market condition.

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose Germany stopped exporting eggs to Hong Kong after the feed in their farms had been found contaminated. Meanwhile, Hong Kong people buy fewer eggs as they feel uncertain about the hygienic condition of eggs in general. The new equilibrium point would be at

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Relationship between price elasticity of demand and total revenue
questions.stem: Due to an increase in the cost of production, the equilibrium price of chocolate increases by 35% and the seller's total revenue increases by 10%. We can conclude that

choices.text: the demand for chocolate is inelastic.
the supply of chocolate is elastic.
the demand for chocolate is more elastic than the supply of chocolate.
the price elasticity of demand of chocolate is 3.5.

questions.explanation: The higher price and higher total revenue imply that the percentage fall in quantity is smaller than the price increase, so demand is inelastic.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Measuring price elasticity of demand
questions.stem: Due to a decrease in transportation cost, the price of Australia's red wine decreases from $70 to $50 and the quantity demanded increases by 20%. What is the arc elasticity of demand of Australia's red wine?
questions.explanation: Arc price elasticity is (20%)/(20/60) = 0.6 when the midpoint price is used.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) price floor on (money) price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc.

choices.text: there will be an excess demand for good X.
the total revenue may increase, decrease or remain unchanged, depending on the elasticity of demand and supply.
the quantity transacted will be smaller than 50 units.

questions.explanation: The stated floor of $8 is below the equilibrium price of $10 and is ineffective. It does not change the market, so no black market arises.

visuals.alt: Supply and demand for good X with equilibrium price $10 and quantity 50.

movements: Compare the regulated price with the equilibrium price and quantity.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Determine the shortage or surplus implied by the price control.

questions.postVisualStem: Initially, the market of good X is at equilibrium. If the government imposes a price floor at $8,

questions.topicGroup: Tax on goods and services (Sales tax)
questions.keyPoint: Understand how price elasticities of demand and supply affect the share of the tax burden
questions.stem: Suppose the government levies a per-unit sales tax on a good. If demand is elastic and supply is inelastic, the total revenue received by sellers will ______________ and the consumers' tax burden will be ______________ than the producers' burden.
questions.explanation: A tax reduces producers' net price and quantity sold, lowering sellers' revenue. The more elastic demand side bears the smaller share of tax.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the provision of a unit subsidy on price, quantity transacted, total revenue etc., and show the share of the subsidy between producers and consumers
questions.stem: The following table shows the market demand and market supply of a good.
questions.explanation: At 20 units, consumers pay $2 and producers receive $5, yielding a $3 subsidy per unit. Total subsidy is $60, while consumer expenditure is $40, so only (1) and (3) are correct.
questions.postVisualStem:
If the quantity transacted of the good is 20 units after the government provides a per-unit subsidy to the producers, we can conclude that

(1) the amount of the per-unit subsidy is $3.
(2) the total expenditure of consumers is $100.
(3) the total amount of subsidy paid by the government is $60.

questions.keyPoint: Give examples of monopolistic competition, oligopoly and monopoly
questions.stem: Which of the following is LEAST likely to be an example of oligopoly in Hong Kong?
questions.explanation: Chinese restaurants are numerous with relatively small individual market shares, which is closer to monopolistic competition than oligopoly.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.keyPoint: Negative externality and economic inefficiency; internalising external costs
questions.stem: The existence of detrimental externality implies that

choices.text: the marginal private benefit must be higher than the marginal social benefit.
there must be under-production in the market.
there is a divergence between private and social costs.
government intervention is needed so as to restore the output to the socially optimal level.

questions.explanation: A detrimental externality creates a divergence between private and social costs. It causes overproduction, and government action is not the only possible correction.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (II)
questions.keyPoint: Interpret the information delivered from the Lorenz curve
questions.explanation: Country A's curve lies closer to equality, so its Gini coefficient is smaller and its distribution more even. Gini coefficients lie between zero and one.

visuals.alt: Lorenz curves for Country A and Country B.

movements: Compare the bows of the Lorenz curves from the equality line.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Use the curves to compare income inequality.

questions.postVisualStem:
Refer to the above diagram. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

(1) The Gini coefficient of Country A is smaller than Country B.
(2) The Gini coefficients of both countries are smaller than 1.
(3) The income distribution in Country A is less even than in Country B.

questions.keyPoint: Relationship between scarcity, competition and discrimination
questions.stem:
Which of the following statements about scarcity is/are CORRECT?

(1) Scarcity must exist when resources are limited.
(2) The existence of scarcity implies that people need to compete with each other for resources.
(3) The problem of scarcity is solved when a choice has been made.
questions.explanation: Scarcity requires resources to be insufficient relative to wants, not merely limited. It creates competition and remains after any particular choice.

questions.keyPoint: Explain whether and how cost changes under different circumstances
questions.stem: Suppose Miss Lee is considering one of the following options.

choices.text: The smartphone costs Miss Lee more than she expects.
Miss Lee finds that the smartphone is difficult to use.
There is a strike in France that affects most of the local traffic.
All tickets for the concert have been sold out.

questions.explanation: The opportunity cost is the best alternative forgone, the study tour to France. A transport strike lowers the value of that alternative.

visuals.caption: Miss Lee's options
rows: Joining a study tour to France

questions.postVisualStem: Which of the following will change Miss Lee's opportunity cost of buying a smartphone?

questions.keyPoint: Distinguishing between free goods and economic goods
questions.stem: During peak hours in summer, the air conditioning on buses can be classified as

choices.text: economic goods, because people prefer to have more air conditioning.
economic goods, because the price of electricity is included in the bus fare.
free goods, because people can enjoy the air conditioning as much as they want.
free goods, because the air conditioning has no alternative uses.

questions.explanation: Bus air conditioning uses scarce electricity and passengers prefer more of it, so it is an economic good. Its ticket price is not the criterion.

questions.chapterTitle: The Three Basic Economic Problems and Private Property Rights
questions.keyPoint: Ways of tackling the three basic economic problems by different societies
questions.stem: In a market-oriented economy,

choices.text: resource allocation is guided by price signals.

questions.explanation: The price mechanism guides allocation in a market-oriented economy. It can also include public ownership and non-price competition.

questions.keyPoint: Comparison of features, advantages and disadvantages of different forms of ownership
questions.stem:
Compared to a partnership, a private limited company

(1) enjoys a lower profits tax rate.
(2) has more capital.
(3) is easier to practise division of labour.
questions.explanation: A private limited company has a higher, not lower, profits tax rate. It does not necessarily have more capital or find division of labour easier than a partnership.

questions.topicGroup: Types of goods and services produced
questions.keyPoint: Private goods and public goods
questions.stem: The free public Wi-Fi service provided by the government in public libraries can be classified as

choices.text: a consumer good and a private good.
an economic good and a private good.
a producer good and a public good.
a free good and a public good.

questions.explanation: Library Wi-Fi helps users produce information and study services, so it is a producer good. It is non-rival and non-excludable in the stated setting, hence public.

questions.keyPoint: Different methods of wage payment
questions.stem: Miss Cheung is considering profit-sharing, time rate and piece rate. If she aims at raising workers' incentive to work and lowering the cost of monitoring output quality, she can adopt

choices.text: profit-sharing, time rate and piece rate.

questions.explanation: Profit-sharing encourages workers to improve the firm's overall performance without giving them an incentive to sacrifice quality for piece output.

questions.keyPoint: Internal economies/diseconomies of scale
questions.stem: Under which of the following situations will diseconomies of scale exist?

choices.text: Total cost increases when output increases.
Marginal revenue is smaller than marginal cost.
Average cost increases when output increases.

questions.explanation: Diseconomies of scale occur when output increases and long-run average cost rises.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.keyPoint: Understand the meaning and give examples of each type of integration
questions.stem: Suppose a supermarket in Hong Kong took over a farm in New Zealand. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be the aim of the action?

choices.text: to reduce the number of competitors
to enjoy a lower average cost
to ensure a reliable supply of meat

questions.explanation: Taking over a supplier is backward integration, which can secure inputs, spread risk and lower average cost. It does not directly remove retail competitors.

questions.topicGroup: Determination of equilibrium price and output
questions.keyPoint: Difference between scarcity and shortage
questions.stem: Which of the following about scarcity and shortage is INCORRECT?

choices.text: Shortage can be eliminated by setting the price to the equilibrium level.
Scarcity exists at the market clearing price level.
Shortage exists when there is scarcity.
The problem of scarcity cannot be eliminated by adjusting the market price.

questions.explanation: Scarcity exists generally, but shortage is excess demand at a below-equilibrium price and need not exist whenever there is scarcity.

questions.keyPoint: Growth rate of GDP
questions.stem: Suppose the growth rate of population in Country A is 5% in a certain year. At the same time, the growth rates of nominal GDP and real GDP are 3% and 7% respectively. We can conclude that

choices.text: both per capita nominal GDP and per capita real GDP increased.
the implicit price deflator of GDP increased.

questions.explanation: Real GDP grows faster than nominal GDP, so the general price level falls. Per-capita nominal GDP also falls because its 3% growth is below population growth.

questions.topicGroup: Meanings of GDP and resident producing units; items included/excluded in calculating GDP
questions.keyPoint: Meanings of GDP and resident producing units; items included/excluded in calculating GDP
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT included in the gross domestic product of Hong Kong in 2008?

choices.text: the value of a vase produced but unsold in 2008
the dividends received by a Japanese from holding shares of a listed company in Hong Kong
the expenditure on holding a fund-raising activity
the money donated by Hong Kong citizens to India

questions.explanation: A donation is a transfer payment and does not represent current production. Unsold output is inventory investment, dividends reflect production income, and fund-raising expenditure pays for current services.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Current account (main components: goods, services, income and current transfers)
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of trade surplus and deficit
questions.stem: Suppose there is a trade deficit in an open economy. This implies that the amount of capital inflow is ______________ than that of capital outflow and the capital and financial account balance is ______________.
questions.explanation: A trade deficit is a current-account deficit. In the balance-of-payments accounts it is matched by a positive capital and financial account balance, so capital inflow exceeds capital outflow.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: Explain how a given event leads to changes in AD, SRAS and/or LRAS by specifying the component(s) of AD affected and/or factor(s) affecting SRAS and/or LRAS, leading to a shift of the AD curve, the SRAS curve and/or the LRAS curve

choices.text: a decrease in supply of labour and a decrease in the cost of production
an increase in the cost of production and a decrease in the cost of borrowing
an increase in the profits tax rate and an increase in the sales tax rate
an increase in government expenditure and a decrease in the interest rate

questions.explanation: Higher production cost shifts SRAS left from SRAS0 to SRAS1. Lower borrowing cost raises consumption and investment, shifting AD right from AD0 to AD1.

visuals.alt: AS-AD diagram: SRAS shifts left from SRAS0 to SRAS1 and AD shifts right from AD0 to AD1; axes are price level and quantity of output (real GDP).

movements: SRAS shifts left from SRAS0 to SRAS1 and AD shifts right from AD0 to AD1.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Identify the combined short-run effect on price level and output.

questions.postVisualStem: Which of the following will shift the AD curve and the SRAS curve as the diagram above?

questions.topicGroup: Deviations of short run equilibrium from long run equilibrium
questions.keyPoint: Deflationary gap
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about a deflationary gap is CORRECT?

choices.text: A deflationary gap can exist in both the short run and long run.
There is a deflationary gap when the full-employment output level is lower than the equilibrium output level.
The existence of a deflationary gap implies that the short-run equilibrium is not attained.
A deflationary gap can be eliminated by an increase in aggregate demand.

questions.explanation: A deflationary gap occurs at a short-run equilibrium below full-employment output. Increasing aggregate demand can restore output to the full-employment level.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: The mechanism of moving from a short run equilibrium to a long run equilibrium
questions.stem: Suppose an economy is operating at the short-run equilibrium. An improvement in technology level in production will lead to ______________ in the price level and ______________ in the output level in the long run.

choices.text: There is insufficient information to answer.

questions.explanation: Technology increases productive capacity, but an economy that begins only at a short-run equilibrium may have an inflationary or deflationary gap. Without its initial position, the long-run price and output changes cannot both be determined.

questions.keyPoint: Barter and its limitations
questions.stem: Which of the following about an economy that uses money in exchange and a barter economy is INCORRECT?

choices.text: The problem of double coincidence of wants exists in a barter economy but not in an economy that uses money in exchange.
Inflation exists in an economy that uses money in exchange but not in a barter economy.
The exchange ratio can be determined more easily in an economy that uses money in exchange than in a barter economy.
The purchasing power is more easily to be stored in an economy that uses money in exchange than in a barter economy.

questions.explanation: Money solves double coincidence of wants, gives a unit of account and stores purchasing power more conveniently. Inflation is a persistent rise in the general price level and is not defined by whether an economy uses money.

questions.keyPoint: Understand and calculate maximum and actual banking multipliers
questions.stem: The following table shows the balance sheet of a banking system.
questions.explanation: Required reserves are $500, so the required reserve ratio is 20% and the maximum banking multiplier is 5. With reserves of $750, maximum deposits are $750 / 0.2 = $3,750.

visuals.caption: Balance sheet of a banking system

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the banking system has excess reserves of $250 and the public holds $200 cash. The maximum banking multiplier is ______________ and the maximum possible amount of deposits is ______________.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse changes in money demand, money supply and nominal interest rate
questions.stem: The following will lead to an increase in transaction demand for money EXCEPT

choices.text: people prefer to use credit cards less often.
the growth rate of real GDP increases.

questions.explanation: A higher interest rate raises the opportunity cost of holding money and does not increase transaction demand. Less card use, higher prices and higher real output all raise the money needed for transactions.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Features of the four phases of a business cycle
questions.stem:
If an economy is in the recovery stage, which of the following phenomena can possibly be observed?

(1) The inflation rate increases.
(2) The employment situation improves.
(3) The money supply increases.
questions.explanation: During recovery, output and employment rise and inflation can accelerate. A change in the money supply is not a necessary feature of that phase.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Definitions of inflation and deflation
questions.stem: Deflation does not occur when

choices.text: the consumer price index decreases from 100 to 95.
the implicit price deflator of GDP decreases from 120 to 110.
the inflation rate decreases from 5% to 3%.
the prices of most goods and services decrease persistently.

questions.explanation: A fall in the inflation rate from 5% to 3% is disinflation: prices are still rising. The other cases describe a falling general price level.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Inflation and quantity theory of money
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of quantity theory of money
questions.stem: According to the Quantity Theory of Money (QTM), money is neutral in the long run. This implies that

choices.text: a change in money supply will not lead to a change in real output.
a change in money supply will not lead to a change in purchasing power of money.
a change in the general price level will not lead to a change in money supply.
a change in real output will not lead to a change in money supply.

questions.explanation: In the long run under QTM, a money-supply change affects nominal variables such as the price level, not real output.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Explain why debtors will gain (lose) and creditors will lose (gain) under unanticipated inflation (deflation)
questions.stem: Which of the following persons would lose when there is unanticipated deflation?

choices.text: Mr. Wong, who receives a fixed amount of interest from holding government bonds every month
Miss Chan, who hires a domestic helper by paying a fixed monthly wage
Mrs. Cheung, who receives a fixed amount of money from her husband every month
Mr. Luk, who deposits money into a time deposit account at a fixed interest rate

questions.explanation: Unexpected deflation increases the real value of fixed nominal payments. Miss Chan, as the payer of a fixed wage, loses; the recipients and fixed-interest creditor gain.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Relationship between nominal and real interest rates
questions.keyPoint: Understand the equation: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation rate
questions.stem: Suppose the expected real interest rate is 7%. If the actual inflation rate turns out to be 3% higher than the expected inflation rate, then the realised real interest rate will be

choices.text: higher than the realised inflation rate by 3%.
lower than the expected real interest rate by 3%.
equal to the nominal interest rate.

questions.explanation: With the nominal interest rate set using expected inflation, actual inflation 3 percentage points higher reduces the realised real interest rate by 3 percentage points.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Calculate the unemployment rate and identify the labour force
questions.stem: Refer to the following table.
questions.explanation: The labour force is employed plus unemployed people: 950,000 + 101,000 = 1,051,000. The unemployment rate is 101,000 / 1,051,000 = 9.6%. Underemployed people are already employed, so neither (2) nor (3) follows.
questions.postVisualStem:
According to the above information, which of the following is/are CORRECT?

(1) The unemployment rate is 9.6%.
(2) The labour force is 1,096,000.
(3) The employment rate is 90.8%.

questions.keyPoint: Surplus budget, deficit budget and balanced budget
questions.stem: Suppose the government's planned revenue is greater than its planned expenditure. If the actual revenue turns out to be smaller than the actual expenditure, we know that a ______________ ends up as a ______________.
questions.explanation: Planned revenue exceeding planned expenditure is a surplus budget. Actual revenue below actual expenditure makes the realised result a budget deficit.

questions.topicGroup: Effects of fiscal policy on price and output levels
questions.keyPoint: Effects of expansionary fiscal policy
questions.stem: Refer to the following diagram.
questions.explanation: E0 lies to the right of Yf, so the economy has an inflationary gap. Raising salaries tax is contractionary fiscal policy and reduces aggregate demand. The discount rate is a monetary-policy tool.

visuals.alt: AS-AD diagram with initial equilibrium E0 to the right of the vertical full-employment output level Yf.

movements: The initial equilibrium E0 lies to the right of full-employment output Yf.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Identify the fiscal-policy response appropriate to an inflationary gap.

questions.postVisualStem: The economy initially operates at E0. Suppose the government wants to use fiscal policies to restore the output to the full-employment output level (Yf), she can consider

questions.topicGroup: Understand the condition(s) under which mutually beneficial trade is possible
questions.keyPoint: Understand the condition(s) under which mutually beneficial trade is possible
questions.stem: Suppose there are two countries and they produce good X and good Y. In which of the following situations MUST the two countries not trade with each other?

choices.text: The gain from trade of importing 1 unit of good X is higher than the opportunity cost of production but lower than the transportation cost.
One of the countries has absolute advantages in producing both good X and good Y over another country.
Both countries have technological advancement in producing both goods.
The terms of trade lies between the opportunity costs of the two countries.

questions.explanation: Trade must not occur when the transportation cost exceeds the importing country's gain from trade. The other cases can still allow mutually beneficial trade.

questions.keyPoint: Comparison between tariff and quota
questions.stem: Compared to a tariff, imposing an effective import quota on a good

choices.text: leads to a greater increase in the producer surplus.
results a smaller amount of deadweight loss.
incurs a higher cost of administration.

questions.explanation: For an equivalent restriction, a tariff and quota can produce the same domestic price, output, consumption, producer-surplus change and deadweight loss. An effective quota need not cost more to administer.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on imports and exports
questions.keyPoint: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on import and export prices in terms of domestic and foreign currencies, import and export volumes, and values of imports and exports in terms of domestic and foreign currencies
questions.stem: Suppose there is a change in the exchange rate between the British Pound (GBP) and the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) as below.
questions.explanation: Fewer HKD are needed to buy one GBP, so the HKD has appreciated against the GBP. British goods become cheaper in HKD, increasing Hong Kong's quantity demanded of imports from Britain.

visuals.caption: GBP-HKD exchange rate in Year X

questions.postVisualStem: During the above period, the Hong Kong dollar has ______________ against the British Pound and the quantity of goods imported from Britain to Hong Kong would ______________.

questions.topicGroup: Tax on goods and services (Sales tax)
questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of a unit tax on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc., and show the share of the tax burden between producers and consumers
questions.stem: Suppose the government imposes a per-unit sales tax on cigarettes, which is collected from the producers. Which of the following is CORRECT?

choices.text: The after-tax revenue of cigarette producers must decrease.
The tax burden borne by consumers equals zero.
The demand for cigarettes will decrease due to an increase in the price of cigarettes.
There will be a surplus of cigarettes in the market.

questions.explanation: A per-unit tax reduces the net price received by producers and the quantity sold, so their after-tax revenue falls. It changes quantity demanded, not demand, and the market remains in equilibrium.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the provision of a unit subsidy on price, quantity transacted, total revenue etc., and show the share of the subsidy between producers and consumers
questions.stem:
Answer Questions 12 and 13 by referring to the following information.

The table below shows the market of good X.
questions.explanation: At a consumer price of $3, producers receive $5 including the subsidy, so quantity supplied and demanded are both 400. The price falls from $4 to $3 and quantity rises by 50.
questions.postVisualStem:
Suppose the government provides a per-unit subsidy of $2 to the producers of good X.

The new market price would be __________, and the quantity transacted would change by __________ units.

questions.keyPoint: Understand how price elasticities of demand and supply affect the share of the subsidy
questions.stem: Based on the proportion of tax burden to be shared by consumers and producers, the elasticity of supply of good X between the original and new market prices is implied to be

choices.text: smaller than its elasticity of demand.
greater than its elasticity of demand.
equal to its elasticity of demand.

questions.explanation: The $2 subsidy lowers the consumer price by $1 and raises the producer price by $1. Consumers and producers share the benefit equally, implying equal elasticities over this range.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Types of price elasticity of supply
questions.stem: During Lunar New Year, people like to buy chicken for celebrations. As a result, the price of chicken increases by 30% and the quantity transacted of it increases from 250,000 to 300,000 per month. Within the above price range, chicken has an
questions.explanation: The higher demand causes a movement along the supply curve. Quantity rises by 20% while price rises by 30%, so price elasticity of supply is below one.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the newspaper market in Hong Kong. Point E is the original equilibrium point.
questions.explanation: Fewer newspaper issuers reduce supply from S0 to S1, while preference for e-newspapers reduces demand from D0 to D1. Their new intersection is T.

visuals.alt: Newspaper market diagram with supply curves S0-S2, demand curves D0-D2, and equilibrium points T, U, V, W and E.

movements: Compare the demand and supply positions associated with the labelled equilibria.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Match the newspaper-market statement to the correct diagram outcome.

questions.postVisualStem: If several dominant newspaper issuers left the newspaper market and at the same time more people prefer reading e-newspaper to the printed version, the new equilibrium point in the diagram would be ______.

questions.topicGroup: Money Price (Nominal Price) and Relative Price
questions.keyPoint: Explain phenomena by applying the law of demand (using relative price or full price)
questions.stem: To attract customers, a bakery decides to lower the price of all items by 20% after 5:00pm everyday. Which of the following concepts can be used to explain the above behaviour?

choices.text: the law of diminishing marginal returns

questions.explanation: A lower price increases quantity demanded, ceteris paribus. The bakery uses the law of demand to attract more buyers.

questions.keyPoint: State the general features of different market structures
questions.stem: A market can be regarded as monopolistically competitive when

choices.text: there are many buyers and sellers in the market.

questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition has many sellers, differentiated products and price-searching sellers. Therefore all statements A-C are true, so the correct option is none of the above.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.keyPoint: Positive externality and economic inefficiency; correcting externality
questions.stem: There may be NO divergence between private and social costs/benefits if

choices.text: a quarry mine pollutes nearby farmland during production process without compensating the land owner.
a property developer builds a new subway connecting an auxiliary estate and an MTR station, where part of the capital comes from the government.
a student practises guitar at home and does not notice that he is annoying his neighbourhood.
someone smokes in the street without considering the effects on others.

questions.explanation: Government funding can internalise the external benefit from a subway connection. The other cases impose unpriced costs on third parties.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (II)
questions.keyPoint: Interpret the information delivered from the Lorenz curve
questions.stem: Study the following Lorenz curves of Country X and Country Y.

choices.text: The Gini coefficient of Country X is higher than that of Country Y.
The Gini coefficient of Country Y is higher than that of Country X.
The low-income group in Country X earns a higher income than that of Country Y.
The low-income group in Country Y earns a higher income than that of Country X.

questions.explanation: Country Y's Lorenz curve is farther from the line of equality, so Country Y has the higher Gini coefficient. Absolute incomes cannot be compared from the curves alone.

visuals.alt: Lorenz curves for Country X and Country Y, with cumulative percentages of income and households.

movements: Compare curve distance from the line of equality.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Use the Lorenz curves to infer the relative inequality.

questions.postVisualStem: Which of the following is a CORRECT description?

questions.topicGroup: Tax on goods and services (Sales tax)
questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of a unit tax on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc., and show the share of the tax burden between producers and consumers
questions.stem: Suppose the government imposes a per-unit tax on a good. This would lead to

choices.text: an increase in consumer surplus and a decrease in producer surplus, so the change in total social surplus is uncertain.
a decrease in consumer surplus and an increase in producer surplus, so the change in total social surplus is uncertain.
a decrease in total social surplus because both consumer surplus and producer surplus decrease.
a decrease in total social surplus because the sum of fall in consumer surplus and producer surplus is larger than the increase in government tax revenue.

questions.explanation: A tax lowers consumer and producer surplus and creates a deadweight loss. Government tax revenue partly offsets those losses, but the combined fall in private surplus is larger.

questions.keyPoint: Relationship between scarcity, competition and discrimination
questions.stem:
Scarcity is implied when there is

(1) excess demand.
(2) price competition.
(3) non-price competition.
questions.explanation: Excess demand shows resources are insufficient at the stated price. Price and non-price competition are both ways people compete for scarce resources.

questions.keyPoint: Explain whether and how cost changes under different circumstances
questions.stem:
Albert is choosing between two ways of spending his Easter holiday: to join a tour to Europe or to work as a helper in a comic fair.

Which of the following will increase Albert's opportunity cost of joining the tour to Europe?

choices.text: Albert is not interested in comic.
There are widespread riots in Europe.
The wage rate of working as a helper at the comic fair increases by $20 per hour.
The price of the Europe tour increases by 10%.

questions.explanation: The opportunity cost of joining the tour is the value of the best forgone option, working at the comic fair. A higher wage raises that forgone value.

questions.topicGroup: Distinction between positive statements and normative statements
questions.keyPoint: Distinction between positive statements and normative statements
questions.stem: A normative statement

choices.text: may not involve any value judgment.

questions.explanation: Normative statements contain value judgments, so facts alone cannot prove or disprove them.

questions.keyPoint: Comparison of features, advantages and disadvantages of different forms of ownership
questions.stem: Study the information below.

choices.text: Firm A pays a lower profits tax rate than firm B.
Firm A is a legal entity while firm B is not.
Firm B's continuity is more limited than that of firm A.
Both firm A and firm B can issue shares to the public.

questions.explanation: Firm A is a partnership and Firm B is a public limited company. Partnerships pay a lower profits tax rate; a public limited company is a legal entity with lasting continuity and can issue shares to the public.

visuals.caption: Information about Firm A and Firm B
rows: has to disclose its financial statements to its shareholders only
has to disclose its financial statements to the public regularly

questions.postVisualStem: According to the above information, which of the following statements is CORRECT?

questions.topicGroup: Types of goods and services produced
questions.keyPoint: Private goods and public goods
questions.stem: Which of the following comes closest to being a public good?
questions.explanation: A television programme is close to non-rival and non-excludable in consumption. The other examples are rival, excludable, or both.

questions.keyPoint: Productivity of labour
questions.stem: Which of the following would NOT affect the average labour productivity?

choices.text: a change in the wage payment system from piece rate to time rate
an improvement in working conditions resulting from stricter government regulation
a raise in government subsidies for continuing education

questions.explanation: Population size does not directly change output per worker. Wage incentives, working conditions and education can affect workers' productivity.

questions.keyPoint: Internal economies/diseconomies of scale
questions.stem: The following table shows the change in a firm's total cost after increasing all its inputs to double its output.
questions.explanation: Economies of scale mean long-run average cost falls as output rises. Total cost at two units must be below twice $4,000, so $7,500 is possible.
questions.postVisualStem: If the firm enjoys economies of scale, the possible value of X is

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.topicGroup: The basic objective of firms: profit maximisation
questions.keyPoint: The supply schedule of a competitive firm
questions.stem:
The marginal cost schedule of a firm can be interpreted as its supply schedule in the production of a good. Which of the following are the necessary conditions?

(1) The firm is a price taker.
(2) The marginal cost of production is increasing when output increases.
(3) The average cost of production is not higher than the marginal revenue of production at every output level.
questions.explanation: For a competitive firm, supply is the rising part of its marginal-cost curve above average cost. The firm must be a price taker and marginal cost must be rising; condition (3) is not required at every output level.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.keyPoint: Understand the meaning and give examples of each type of integration
questions.stem: A car manufacturer acquires a tyre manufacturer. Which of the following is NOT an advantage to the car manufacturer in the above acquisition?

choices.text: building up a network for selling its products
ensuring a steady supply of input
taking advantage of the tyre manufacturer's brand name

questions.explanation: This is backward vertical integration. It can secure tyre inputs and may use the supplier's brand, but acquiring an input supplier does not build a network for selling the car manufacturer's products.

questions.chapterTitle: The Three Basic Economic Problems and Private Property Rights
questions.keyPoint: Ways of tackling the three basic economic problems by different societies
questions.stem:
Which of the following are guided by price signals?

(1) Paul receives $2,500 for working in his uncle's restaurant for one week.
(2) Mary gives her son pocket money every month with its amount increases with his age.
(3) John buys a flat from his cousin.
questions.explanation: A wage and the price of a flat are determined through market price signals. Pocket money that varies with age is allocated by a family decision, not by the price mechanism.

questions.keyPoint: Meaning of per capita GDP
questions.stem: The following table shows the economic performance of two countries in a year.

choices.text: the general living standard of the high-income group in Country A is higher than that of Country B.
the per capita real GDP of Country A is lower than that of Country B.
the cost of living in Country A is higher than that in Country B.

questions.explanation: Per-capita real GDP is about $51,739 million/ million people in Country A and $58,000 in Country B. The data do not show inflation, income-group living standards or cost of living.
questions.postVisualStem: Based on the above information, we can conclude that

questions.keyPoint: Growth rate of GDP
questions.stem: Refer to the table below.

choices.text: The per capita real output increased in 2014.
The general price level remained unchanged in 2014.
The per capita nominal GDP increased in 2014.
The nominal GDP in 2013 is higher than that of 2014.

questions.explanation: In 2014 nominal and real GDP both grow by 1%, so the implicit price deflator is unchanged. Population grows by 2%, so both per-capita measures fall.

visuals.caption: Growth rate relative to previous year

questions.postVisualStem: Which of the following about the economy is CORRECT?

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Calculate the unemployment rate and identify the labour force
questions.stem: Suppose the employed population of an economy is 3,800,000 while the unemployment rate is 5%. The unemployed population is ____________.
questions.explanation: If unemployed people are 5% of the labour force, employed people are 95%. Thus unemployed population is 3,800,000 x 5 / 95 = 200,000.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: The mechanism of moving from a short run equilibrium to a long run equilibrium
questions.stem: The diagram below shows the aggregate demand (AD) curves, the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curves and the long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve of an economy.
questions.explanation: A leftward AD shift creates a deflationary gap and long-run adjustment returns output to LRAS at E'. A rightward SRAS shift lowers price but long-run output remains at LRAS, point E.

visuals.alt: AS-AD diagram with LRAS, AD1-AD2, SRAS1-SRAS2, and long-run equilibrium points E and E'.

movements: Trace the labelled AD and SRAS changes back to long-run equilibrium.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Identify the long-run AS-AD adjustment shown.

questions.postVisualStem:
Point E is the initial equilibrium point. Which of the following are CORRECT in the long run?

(1) If AD1 shifts to AD2, the long-run equilibrium point is at point E.
(2) If AD1 shifts to AD2, the long-run equilibrium point is at point E'.
(3) If SRAS1 shifts to SRAS2, the long-run equilibrium point is at point E.
(4) If SRAS1 shifts to SRAS2, the long-run equilibrium point is at point E'.

questions.topicGroup: Factors affecting long run aggregate supply
questions.keyPoint: Factors affecting long run aggregate supply
questions.stem: The long-run aggregate supply curve will shift to the right if

choices.text: the general price level is expected to fall.
a new renewable energy is discovered.
people are optimistic about the economic prospects.

questions.explanation: A new renewable energy raises productive capacity, shifting LRAS right. The other changes affect expectations, short-run costs or aggregate demand.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: Explain how a given event leads to changes in AD, SRAS and/or LRAS by specifying the component(s) of AD affected and/or factor(s) affecting SRAS and/or LRAS, leading to a shift of the AD curve, the SRAS curve and/or the LRAS curve
questions.stem: With a downward sloping aggregate demand curve, an increase in the price of oil would lead to ____________ in real national income and ____________ in the price level.
questions.explanation: Higher oil prices raise production costs and shift SRAS left, producing lower real output and a higher price level.

questions.keyPoint: Definition of money
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about money is CORRECT?

choices.text: Money helps solve the problem of double coincidence of wants by bringing parties into the market for exchange.
Inflation increases the purchasing of money.
Money still exists in a cashless society where all transactions are settled through electronic payment systems.

questions.explanation: Electronic balances can perform the functions of money. Money does not need intrinsic value, inflation lowers purchasing power, and money solves double coincidence by acting as a medium of exchange.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Relationship between nominal and real interest rates
questions.keyPoint: Understand the equation: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation rate
questions.stem: If the nominal interest rate on a one-year bond is 2% and the realised inflation rate is 6%, the real rate of return and the expected cost of holding cash are __________ and __________ respectively.
questions.explanation: The real rate of return on holding cash is 0% minus 6%, or -6%. The expected cost of holding cash is the nominal interest rate forgone, 2%.

questions.keyPoint: Effects of asset transfers on money supply
questions.stem: Miss Lee withdraws HK$300,000 from her savings account in a licensed bank in Hong Kong. She transfers HK$250,000 to her current account in another licensed bank in Hong Kong and remits the remaining HK$50,000 to her daughter in Australia. The immediate effect of the above events on the Hong Kong dollar money supply would be:

choices.text: M1 increases while M2 remains unchanged.
M1 increases while M3 remains unchanged.

questions.explanation: The $250,000 transfer from savings to current deposits raises M1 but leaves M2 unchanged. The $50,000 remittance removes a Hong Kong dollar deposit, reducing M2 and M3; overall M2 and M3 decrease.

questions.keyPoint: Expansionary and contractionary monetary policy, including changes in required reserve ratio and discount rate
questions.stem:
Which of the following may lead to a decrease in money supply?

(1) A commercial bank buys government bonds from the central bank.
(2) The discount rate increases.
(3) The central bank prints more money.
questions.explanation: A bank's purchase of bonds from the central bank withdraws monetary base, while a higher discount rate discourages bank borrowing. Printing money increases money supply.

questions.keyPoint: Understand and calculate maximum and actual banking multipliers
questions.stem: The table below shows the balance sheet of a banking system. Suppose the public do not hold any cash and there are excess reserves of $400.

choices.text: The maximum amount of deposits is $5,000.

questions.explanation: Required reserves are $600, so the required reserve ratio is 20% and the maximum banking multiplier is 5. With $1,000 reserves, maximum deposits equal $5,000.

visuals.caption: Balance sheet of a banking system

questions.postVisualStem: Which of the following statements about the banking system is CORRECT?

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Inflation and quantity theory of money
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of quantity theory of money
questions.stem: The Quantity Theory of Money predicts that

choices.text: the velocity of circulation of money is fixed in both the short run and the long run.
a change in money supply will not affect the level of real output in both the short run and the long run.
a growth in money supply will lead to a proportional growth in nominal national income in both the short run and the long run.

questions.explanation: QTM assumes a stable velocity and predicts a proportional change in nominal national income when money supply changes. In the short run, real output may change.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Inflation and quantity theory of money
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of quantity theory of money
questions.stem: In the short run, a change in money supply will NOT affect
questions.explanation: In the short run, a money-supply change can change aggregate demand, nominal output and the price level. Therefore none of A-C is unaffected.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Measurements of the general price level
questions.keyPoint: Calculate/Determine the rate of change in the general price level (inflation/ deflation rate) by using the CPI and the implicit price deflator of GDP
questions.stem: Refer to the diagram below.

choices.text: the general price level is first rising and then falling.
the cost of living is rising.
the purchasing power of money is rising.

questions.explanation: The implicit GDP deflator growth rate is positive in every year shown, so the general price level and cost of living are rising throughout. The rate changes, but does not become negative.

visuals.alt: Line chart of the growth rate of the implicit GDP deflator from 2008 to 2012; every plotted rate is positive.

labels: Growth rate of implicit GDP deflator
movements: Read the annual plotted deflator-growth values over time.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Distinguish a positive but changing inflation rate from a fall in the price level.
