questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Current account (main components: goods, services, income and current transfers)
questions.keyPoint: Whether and how a given transaction affects the current account
questions.stem: Which of the following should be recorded in the credit side of the current account of Hong Kong?

choices.text: A foreign student pays school fee to take a Putonghua course in Hong Kong.
A Hong Kong enterprise donates money to Africa for a child sponsorship programme.
A Hong Kong firm pays dividends to a foreign investor.
A Mainland resident buys a residential flat in Hong Kong.

questions.explanation: Tuition paid by a foreign student is an export of education services and a current-account credit. The other transactions are current-account debits or capital/financial-account entries.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: Refer to the following demand-supply diagram showing the market for gold in India. The initial equilibrium point is at E0.
questions.explanation: An import duty raises sellers' costs and shifts supply left from S0 to S1. More people liking gold shifts demand right from D0 to D1. The resulting intersection is E1.

visuals.alt: Gold-market demand and supply curves D0-D2 and S0-S2, with equilibrium points E0-E4.
visuals.caption: Gold market in India

curves: Demand curves D0-D2 slope downward.
Supply curves S0-S2 slope upward.
movements: Import duty shifts supply left from S0 to S1.
Greater preference for gold shifts demand right from D0 to D1.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The new intersection of S1 and D1 is E1.

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose India increases import duty on gold. At the same time, more Indians like buying gold. The new equilibrium point will be at ______.

questions.keyPoint: Understand the meanings of complements, substitutes, normal and inferior goods
questions.stem:
A rise in the price of good X will lead to a drop in the price of good Y if

(1) good X and good Y are in competitive demand.
(2) good X and good Y are in joint demand.
(3) good X and good Y are in joint supply.
(4) good X and good Y are in competitive supply.
questions.explanation: The mock's official answer key marks D, namely statements (2) and (4). There is a source issue to flag: under the standard definitions, joint demand makes Y's demand and price fall, while joint supply makes Y's supply rise and price fall; competitive supply would normally reduce Y's supply and raise its price. The answer key is retained exactly as published and this note keeps the conflict visible for teacher review.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Relationship between price elasticity of demand and total revenue
questions.stem: When the price of a good decreases by 30% due to an increase in its supply, consumers' expenditure on the good increases by 50%. This implies that

choices.text: the demand for the good is elastic.
the demand for the good is inelastic.
the supply of the good is elastic.
the supply of the good is inelastic.

questions.explanation: The price falls while total expenditure rises. A fall in price raises total revenue/expenditure only when demand is elastic, because the percentage increase in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage fall in price.

questions.topicGroup: Tax on goods and services (Sales tax)
questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of a unit tax on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc., and show the share of the tax burden between producers and consumers
questions.stem: The following table shows the demand and supply schedules of good X.
questions.explanation: The listed supply schedule is after the $2 tax. Removing the tax shifts supply down by $2. At a buyer price of $5, quantity demanded is 60 and the pre-tax quantity supplied is also 60, so new sales revenue is $5 x 60 = $300.

visuals.caption: Demand and supply schedules of good X
rows: Quantity supplied after tax is imposed (units)

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the government removes the per-unit sales tax of $2 imposed on good X. The new total sales revenue is _________.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) price ceiling on (money) price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc.
questions.stem: Refer to the following demand-supply diagram:

choices.text: may rise or fall, depending on the price elasticity of demand.

questions.explanation: Both P1 and P2 lie above the equilibrium price in the diagram, so the price ceiling remains ineffective. Neither ceiling changes the market price or quantity transacted, and sellers' total revenue remains unchanged.

visuals.alt: Price-ceiling diagram with downward demand curve D, vertical supply curve S, prices P1 and P2, and quantities Q1-Q3.
visuals.caption: Price ceiling

curves: D is a downward-sloping demand curve.
S is a vertical supply curve at Q3.
movements: The ceiling is lowered from P1 to P2.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Both marked ceilings are above the supply-demand intersection, so they are ineffective and revenue is unchanged.

questions.postVisualStem: If the government lowers the price ceiling for the good from P1 to P2, the total revenue received by the sellers

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) price ceiling on (money) price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc.
questions.stem:
Suppose the government introduces an effective maximum price control on infant milk formula. Which of the following statements are correct?

(1) More infant milk formula cannot be sold.
(2) There will be a shortage of infant milk formula.
(3) Black market in trading infant milk formula will exist.
questions.explanation: An effective maximum price is below equilibrium, creating excess demand and a shortage. It can encourage a black market. The quantity actually sold falls to the smaller quantity supplied, so statement (1) is false.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the provision of a unit subsidy on price, quantity transacted, total revenue etc., and show the share of the subsidy between producers and consumers
questions.stem: The following table shows the demand and supply schedules of good X.
questions.explanation: A $6 subsidy shifts supply down by $6 to buyers. At the new buyer price of $36, quantity demanded is 50 and suppliers receive $42, at which they supply 50 units. Total subsidy is $6 x 50 = $300.

visuals.caption: Demand and supply schedules of good X

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the government provides a per-unit subsidy of $6 to good X. The total amount of subsidy provided is _________.

questions.topicGroup: Money Price (Nominal Price) and Relative Price
questions.keyPoint: Explain phenomena by applying the law of demand (using relative price or full price)
questions.stem: Which of the following is INCONSITENT with the law of demand?

choices.text: When the government reduces the amount of import quota, the quality of imported toys improves.
When there is a depreciation of the HK dollar against the Renminbi, Hong Kong people consume less in the Mainland.
When people expect the property market to worsen, the price of residential flats rises.
When a levy on litter is imposed, more people recycle used items.

questions.explanation: If people expect the property market to worsen, their demand for residential flats should decrease and put downward pressure on the price. The claim that the price rises is inconsistent with the law of demand.

questions.keyPoint: State the general features of different market structures
questions.stem: The market structure of the fixed line services in Hong Kong is

choices.text: an oligopoly because there are several companies in the market in which their market shares are similar.
an oligopoly because the pricing strategies of the companies are interdependent.
a monopoly because there are no close substitutes for the services provided by each company.
a monopoly because there is only one company providing services in every district.

questions.explanation: Fixed-line services are supplied by several firms whose pricing decisions are interdependent, a defining feature of oligopoly. Similar market shares are not required, and there is not one sole supplier in every district.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.keyPoint: Negative externality and economic inefficiency; internalising external costs
questions.stem: Suppose the market equilibrium output level will be closer to the efficient output level if production is reduced. This implies that the marginal private benefit is _________ the marginal private cost while the marginal social benefit is _________ the marginal social cost.
questions.explanation: At the market equilibrium, marginal private benefit equals marginal private cost. If reducing output moves the economy closer to efficiency, the original output has marginal social benefit below marginal social cost, as with a negative external cost of production.

questions.chapterTitle: The Three Basic Economic Problems and Private Property Rights
questions.keyPoint: The meanings of the three basic economic problems and examples of the problems
questions.stem:
To address the shortage of Primary One places in the North District, the Education Bureau is asking primary schools in North District to increase class sizes, from the current 25 or 30 students to a maximum of 33 students for the school year 2013-14.

The case above is related to the _________ problem in economics.

(1) what to produce
(2) how to produce
(3) for whom to produce
questions.explanation: The policy responds to insufficient Primary One education places, which is a decision about the amount of education to provide (what to produce). It does not state an allocation rule for recipients or a choice between production techniques.

questions.keyPoint: Explain whether and how cost changes under different circumstances
questions.stem: Anna is going to have dinner with friends in Mong Kok. She can take either the bus or the MTR. The travelling time and cost are the same. Which of the following situations Anna's opportunity cost of taking the bus to Mong Kok will increase?

choices.text: Anna's bus arrived 5 minutes earlier due to smooth traffic.
The air conditioning of Anna's bus does not work well.
Anna met her idol in the MTR train compartment.
All MTR trains arrived 10 minutes late due to signal failure.

questions.explanation: The opportunity cost of taking the bus is the value of the best forgone alternative, the MTR. Meeting her idol on the MTR increases the benefit she gives up by taking the bus.

questions.keyPoint: Total cost, average cost and marginal cost
questions.stem: The following table shows the cost-output relationship of a firm.
questions.explanation: With fixed cost of $20, marginal cost is $15, $29, $26, $22 and $21 as output rises. It first increases and then decreases. Average variable cost is not continuously increasing, and this short-run table cannot establish economies of scale.
questions.postVisualStem:
Based on the above table, we can conclude that

(1) the marginal cost is first increasing but then decreasing.
(2) the average variable cost is increasing.
(3) the firm enjoys the benefits of economies of scale.

questions.topicGroup: Input-output relationship in the short run
questions.keyPoint: Law of diminishing marginal returns
questions.stem: The table below shows the production of a firm where the law of diminishing marginal returns applies.
questions.explanation: With machines fixed, the marginal products from the sixth and seventh units of labour are 30 and 35. X = 185 gives later marginal products of 20 and 15, which decline after the peak. Each other option would require the marginal product to rise again after X.

visuals.caption: Production where the law of diminishing marginal returns applies

questions.postVisualStem: Which of the following is a possible value of X?

questions.keyPoint: External economies/diseconomies of scale
questions.stem: To attract more people to constitute the industry, the government has increased the subsidy on the training of construction workers. In this case, private construction companies will _________.
questions.explanation: The training subsidy improves the supply of skilled labour available to construction firms across the industry. This industry-wide benefit is an external economy of scale, rather than one created solely inside an individual firm.

questions.topicGroup: Types of goods and services produced
questions.keyPoint: Producer goods and consumer goods
questions.stem:
Many DVD rental stores play DVDs to allow passers-by to view films on the spot. These films are _________.

(1) public goods
(2) free goods
(3) producer goods
(4) consumer goods
questions.explanation: Passers-by can view the films without being excluded and one viewer does not prevent others from viewing, so the display has public-good characteristics. The stores use the films to promote their rental business, so they are producer goods rather than consumer goods in this use.

questions.keyPoint: Different methods of wage payment
questions.stem: Property agents in Hong Kong are usually paid a basic salary plus commission because

choices.text: this can attract more people to join the industry.
this can improve agents' incentive to work.
agents prefer getting more pay for more work.
agents' output can be measured at no cost.

questions.explanation: Commission links part of an agent's income to completed business and therefore strengthens the incentive to work. Measuring output is not costless, and the other statements do not explain the usual mixed payment method.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.keyPoint: Understand the meaning and give examples of each type of integration
questions.stem: A restaurant chain acquires a local cake shop. It also takes over a farm in the Mainland. The former is a kind of _________ while the latter is a kind of _________.
questions.explanation: A restaurant chain and a cake shop operate at different stages/products without a direct supplier-customer relationship, so this is lateral integration. Taking over a farm acquires an earlier-stage supplier of inputs, which is backward integration.

questions.keyPoint: Comparison of features, advantages and disadvantages of different forms of ownership
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons for a partnership to turn into a private limited company?

choices.text: Personal assets of owners are safeguarded.
The firm has a wider source of capital.
The firm do not have to disclose the financial statements to the public.

questions.explanation: Limited liability, a wider source of capital and lasting continuity are advantages of converting to a private limited company. A partnership also does not need to disclose financial statements to the public, so this is not a reason for conversion.

questions.keyPoint: Explain how prices of related goods, income, price expectations, weather, number of consumers in the market, etc. affect individual demand and market demand
questions.stem:
Which of the following will lead to a shift of the market demand curve of a good?

(1) a change in the supply of the good
(2) more advertising
(3) a change in people's disposable income
(4) a change in the price of the good
questions.explanation: Advertising and consumers' disposable income are non-price determinants of demand, so they shift the demand curve. A change in the good's own price causes movement along the curve, while a change in supply does not shift demand.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) quota on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, product quality, etc.
questions.stem: Refer to the following demand-supply diagram of a good with the government setting a quota at Q1.
questions.explanation: The mock's official answer key marks D. The diagram itself gives a teacher-review issue: removing a binding quota moves output toward the competitive equilibrium, raises consumer surplus and total social surplus, while producer surplus would normally fall as price falls. The published answer is retained for this mock's answer key, with the conflict surfaced rather than silently teaching it as a standard result.

visuals.alt: Quota diagram with downward demand D0, normal supply S0, quota-restricted supply S1 and quota Q1.
visuals.caption: Quota market

curves: D0 slopes downward.
S0 slopes upward as the ordinary supply curve.
S1 is vertical at the binding quota Q1.
movements: Removing the quota removes the vertical restriction at Q1 and restores supply curve S0.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The official key marks all three; the standard surplus interpretation needs teacher review.

questions.postVisualStem:
Which of the following will increase by removing the quota on the good?

(1) consumer surplus
(2) producer surplus
(3) total social surplus

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.keyPoint: Negative externality and economic inefficiency; internalising external costs
questions.stem: During the renovation work carried out in Mr. Chan's flat, the constant noise created by electric drills intensively annoyed his neighbor Mr. Wong. Which of the following statements about this case is correct?

choices.text: Mr. Chan's private benefit is higher than Mr. Wong's private cost.
There will be a divergence between Mr. Chan's private and social costs.
There will be a divergence between Mr. Wong's private and social benefits.
Mr. Wong's external benefit is higher than Mr. Chan's external cost.

questions.explanation: The drilling imposes a negative external cost on Mr. Wong. That external cost makes Mr. Chan's social cost exceed his private cost, creating a divergence between the two.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (II)
questions.keyPoint: Understand the relationship between the size of the Gini coefficient and the shape of the Lorenz curve
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the Lorenz curve is incorrect?

choices.text: The closer the Lorenz curve to the line of perfect income inequality, the more uneven the income distribution.
The Lorenz curve cannot reflect the actual income of the households.
The Gini coefficient may not change when the Lorenz curve changes.
The closer the Lorenz curve to the line of perfect income equality, the higher the Gini coefficient.

questions.explanation: A Lorenz curve closer to the line of perfect equality indicates a more even distribution and a lower, not higher, Gini coefficient. A Lorenz curve describes relative income shares, not households' absolute incomes.

questions.topicGroup: Meanings of GDP and resident producing units; items included/excluded in calculating GDP
questions.keyPoint: Meanings of GDP and resident producing units; items included/excluded in calculating GDP
questions.stem: Which of the following items is NOT included in Hong Kong's GNP for the current year?

choices.text: the income received by a Macau resident who worked for a shopping mall in Hong Kong as a security guard for a year
the salary received by a Hong Kong resident for teaching in a Macau university for three months
the annual dividends received by a Hong Kong residents from holding shares of a shopping mall in Macau
the revenue earned by a Macau resident from renting artworks to an exhibition in Hong Kong

questions.explanation: GNP measures income generated by Hong Kong resident producing units. The revenue from renting artworks belongs to a Macau resident, so it is not Hong Kong GNP. The other items are counted through production by a resident unit or net factor income received by Hong Kong residents.

questions.topicGroup: Relationship between GDP at factor cost and GDP at market prices
questions.keyPoint: Relationship between GDP at factor cost and GDP at market prices
questions.stem: Consider the following Gross Domestic Product (GDP) data about a country.
questions.explanation: Gross domestic fixed capital formation is 70 + 30 depreciation = 100. GDP at market prices is 140 + 100 + 10 + 60 + 40 + 60 - 50 + 30 - 40 = $350 million. GDP at factor cost is therefore 350 - 40 indirect business tax + 10 subsidies = $320 million.
questions.postVisualStem: GDP at factor cost for that year is $ _________ million.

questions.keyPoint: Factors that cause a shift of an AD curve
questions.stem: The aggregate demand curve will shift to the right if

choices.text: civil servants get a pay rise that is lower than current inflation rate.
some foreign direct investment projects are approved by the government.
the public asks for opening up the free TV market.
more secondary students go abroad for further studies.

questions.explanation: Approved foreign direct investment projects raise investment expenditure, a component of aggregate demand, and shift the AD curve to the right. The other changes do not necessarily raise an AD component.

questions.topicGroup: Deviations of short run equilibrium from long run equilibrium
questions.keyPoint: Inflationary gap
questions.stem: The diagram below shows the aggregate demand (AD) curve, the short run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve and the long run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve of an economy.
questions.explanation: E0 lies to the right of LRAS, so the economy has an inflationary gap. Cutting government expenditure shifts AD left, reducing aggregate demand and the price level while output returns toward its long-run level.

visuals.alt: AS-AD diagram with upward SRAS, downward AD, vertical LRAS and initial equilibrium E0 to the right of LRAS.
visuals.caption: Inflationary-gap equilibrium

curves: AD slopes downward.
SRAS slopes upward.
LRAS is vertical at the long-run output level.
movements: Cutting government expenditure shifts AD left.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: E0 is an inflationary gap; lower government expenditure lowers the price level as equilibrium returns to LRAS.

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose initially the economy operates at E0. The government can help restore the long run equilibrium by _________ its expenditure, causing the price level to _________.

questions.topicGroup: Licensed banks, restricted licence banks and deposit-taking companies in
questions.keyPoint: Features of the three types of deposit-taking institutions
questions.stem:
Mr. Lee plans to deposit HK$500,000 in a financial institution in Hong Kong as a demand deposit. Which of the following institution(s) can accept his deposit?

(1) licensed banks
(2) restricted licence banks
(3) deposit-taking companies
questions.explanation: Only licensed banks may accept demand deposits. Restricted licence banks and deposit-taking companies can accept time deposits subject to their minimum requirements, but not demand deposits.

questions.keyPoint: Definitions of M1, M2 and M3 in
questions.stem:
Which of the following is NOT included in the money supply M2?

(1) legal tender held by the public
(2) deposits with deposit-taking companies
(3) demand deposits with licensed banks
(4) time deposits with restricted licence banks
questions.explanation: M2 includes legal tender held by the public and deposits with licensed banks. Deposits with deposit-taking companies and time deposits with restricted licence banks are not included in M2.

questions.keyPoint: Understand and calculate maximum and actual changes in deposits, loans, money supply, etc. after deposit creation/contraction
questions.stem: Initially, a banking system has an excess reserve of $100 million and the public holds $100 million cash. The balance sheet of the banking system is as follows:
questions.explanation: Required reserves are $300 million - $100 million = $200 million, so the required reserve ratio is 20%. After the $60 million deposit, reserves are $360 million and maximum deposits are $360 / 0.2 = $1,800 million. Adding the $100 million cash held by the public gives a money supply of $1,900 million.

visuals.caption: Balance sheet of the banking system

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose a remittance of $60 million from abroad is deposited into the banking system. What will the money supply be if the banks lend out all excess reserves?

questions.keyPoint: Analyse changes in money demand, money supply and nominal interest rate
questions.stem: Refer to the following diagram.

choices.text: an increase in the price level
an increase in the transaction demand for money
an increase in the use of electronic money
a decrease in the money supply

questions.explanation: The move from M to N is a leftward shift of money demand from Md0 to Md1 at unchanged money supply. Greater use of electronic money reduces transaction demand for money and lowers the nominal interest rate.

visuals.alt: Money-market diagram with vertical money supply MS, money-demand curves Md0 and Md1, and interest-rate points M and N.
visuals.caption: Money market

curves: MS is vertical.
Md0 and Md1 slope downward, with Md1 left of Md0.
movements: More electronic money reduces transaction demand and shifts Md0 left to Md1.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: At unchanged MS, the equilibrium moves from M to N and the nominal interest rate falls.

questions.postVisualStem: Which of the following will cause the nominal interest rate to move from point M to point N?

questions.keyPoint: Expansionary and contractionary monetary policy, including changes in required reserve ratio and discount rate
questions.stem:
Which of the following are contractionary monetary measures?

(1) raising the bank discount rate
(2) issuing bonds by the government in the market
(3) raising the required reserve ratio
questions.explanation: A higher discount rate restrains bank borrowing, bond sales withdraw money from the market, and a higher required reserve ratio limits deposit creation. All three reduce the money supply or credit and are contractionary.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: Explain how a given event leads to changes in AD, SRAS and/or LRAS by specifying the component(s) of AD affected and/or factor(s) affecting SRAS and/or LRAS, leading to a shift of the AD curve, the SRAS curve and/or the LRAS curve
questions.stem: The Hong Kong government is currently carrying out rail construction projects including Western Island Line, Sha Tin-Central Link and Kwun Tong Line Extension. Which of the following can best explain the effect of the above infrastructure projects on the price and output levels?
questions.explanation: The construction raises aggregate demand through investment/public expenditure. Better rail infrastructure also raises productive capacity, shifting LRAS right; the source's best diagram is D, which shows rightward shifts of AD, SRAS and LRAS.

visuals.alt: Four AS-AD diagrams A-D showing possible shifts of AD, SRAS and LRAS.
visuals.caption: Effects of rail infrastructure

curves: Option D contains AD, SRAS and LRAS curves.
movements: Rail construction raises aggregate demand.
Transport infrastructure improves productive capacity, shifting LRAS right.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Option D shows the source's combined rightward shifts.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on imports and exports
questions.keyPoint: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on import and export prices in terms of domestic and foreign currencies, import and export volumes, and values of imports and exports in terms of domestic and foreign currencies
questions.stem: Which of the following must lead to a fall in the net exports of an economy?

choices.text: There is an increase in the desire to consume in the economy and its major trading partners.
There is an increase in the desire to consume in the economy but a decrease in that of its major trading partners.
There is a decrease in the desire to consume in the economy but an increase in that of its major trading partners.
The currency of the economy appreciates against the currency of its major trading partners.

questions.explanation: A higher domestic desire to consume raises imports, while a lower desire to consume in trading partners lowers demand for this economy's exports. Both changes reduce net exports.

questions.keyPoint: Surplus budget, deficit budget and balanced budget
questions.stem: An economy initially operates at the full-employment equilibrium and the government expenditure equals its tax revenue. An increase in money supply will result in the coexistence of _________ and _________.

choices.text: a deflationary gap ... a budget surplus
a deflationary gap ... a budget deficit
an inflationary gap ... a budget surplus
an inflationary gap ... a budget deficit

questions.explanation: More money raises aggregate demand, creating an inflationary gap from an initial full-employment equilibrium. Higher output/income raises tax revenue while government expenditure is unchanged, producing a budget surplus.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Inflation and quantity theory of money
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of quantity theory of money
questions.stem: The real output of an economy rises at a higher rate than the money supply. According to the quantity theory of money, we can conclude that the price level of the economy is _________ while its nominal output is _________.
questions.explanation: With constant velocity, MV = PY. If real output grows faster than the money supply, the price level falls. Nominal output equals MV and still rises when the money supply is growing, though more slowly than real output.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Features of the four phases of a business cycle
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT observed in an economy in the peak phase of a business cycle?
questions.explanation: At the peak, output has expanded beyond the normal full-employment level rather than merely attaining it. Production, employment, consumption and the general price level are all high.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Effects of inflation and deflation on different aspects
questions.stem:
Which of the following people will benefit from unanticipated inflation?

(1) a person who pay the same amount of monthly fee for broadband services
(2) a person who make a purchase with cash coupons
(3) a person who hold inflation-linked bonds (ibonds)
(4) a person who collect a dozen of cakes with a cake coupon bought a year ago
questions.explanation: A person paying a fixed monthly broadband fee benefits because inflation reduces its real cost. A cake coupon bought earlier fixes the price of the cakes and also benefits its holder. A cash coupon loses real purchasing power, while an inflation-linked bond protects rather than increases the holder's real return.

questions.keyPoint: Four basic principles of taxation
questions.stem:
A government official in a city suggested that the government impose a food waste tax. A levy of $1 should be collected for each kilogram of food waste in order to lessen the burden of landfills.

The above method of collecting tax is LEAST in line with the ________ principle of taxation put forward by Adam Smith.
questions.explanation: A flat $1 charge per kilogram does not vary with taxpayers' ability to pay, so it is least consistent with Adam Smith's equality principle. Its fixed per-unit basis is comparatively clear and certain.

questions.keyPoint: Progressive tax, proportional tax and regressive tax
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the change in the salaries tax structure of an economy.
questions.explanation: The new tax schedule starts at a lower income, showing a smaller personal allowance, and has a higher flat segment, showing a higher standard rate. Starting at a lower income widens rather than narrows the tax base.

visuals.alt: Salaries-tax diagram with income on the horizontal axis, tax rate on the vertical axis, and old versus new tax structures.
visuals.caption: Salaries tax structure

curves: Each schedule rises from its allowance threshold to a horizontal standard-rate segment.
movements: The new schedule begins at a lower income and reaches a higher standard-rate segment.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The new structure has a smaller allowance and higher rate, but a wider tax base.

questions.postVisualStem:
Compared to the old salaries tax structure, the new tax structure

(1) has a smaller personal allowance.
(2) has a higher standard tax rate.
(3) will narrow the tax base.

questions.keyPoint: Explain which country has a comparative advantage in the production of a good in a given case
questions.stem:
Answer Questions 41 and 42 by referring to the following information.

Suppose Country A and Country B are endowed with same amount of resources for production. Country A allocates its resources in the proportion of 1:2 to produce good X and good Y while Country B allocates its resources in the proportion of 2:1 to produce good X and good Y. Their output is shown below:
questions.explanation: The mock's official answer key marks B. The figures create a teacher-review conflict: Country A's implied full-specialisation outputs are 15 X or 9 Y, while Country B's are 18 X or 24 Y. Thus A has comparative advantage in X, but B has absolute advantage rather than disadvantage in both goods; specialisation would give 15 X and 24 Y versus the current 17 X and 14 Y. Standard analysis therefore supports statement (1) only. The published key is retained exactly for mock-answer matching.

visuals.caption: Output with the stated allocation of equal resources

questions.postVisualStem:
Which of the following statements about the above case is correct?

(1) Country A has a comparative advantage in producing good X.
(2) Country B has an absolute disadvantage in producing both good X and good Y.
(3) With complete specialisation in the two countries, the total output of both good X and good Y will increase.

questions.keyPoint: Calculate the gains from trade
questions.stem: Suppose the terms of trade is 1 unit of good X = 1 unit of good Y and the transportation cost for exporting 1 unit of good X is 0.1 units of good Y. To export 10 units of good X, the net gain of the exporting country is ________.
questions.explanation: Country A's opportunity cost of one X is 9 / 15 = 0.6 Y. At the terms of trade, exporting 10 X gives 10 Y, while domestic production would cost 6 Y. Gross gain is 4 Y; transportation costs 1 Y, leaving a net gain of 3 Y.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on imports and exports
questions.keyPoint: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on import and export prices in terms of domestic and foreign currencies, import and export volumes, and values of imports and exports in terms of domestic and foreign currencies
questions.stem: If Hong Kong's demand for Japanese car imports is elastic, the depreciation of the Japanese yen will cause the total import value of Japanese cars (in terms of HK$) to ________.
questions.explanation: A depreciation of the yen lowers the HK-dollar price of Japanese cars. With elastic Hong Kong demand, the percentage rise in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage fall in price, so total import value in HK dollars rises.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Current account (main components: goods, services, income and current transfers)
questions.keyPoint: Whether and how a given transaction affects the current account
questions.stem: Mr. Chan is a Mainland resident who often visits Hong Kong for business. Which of the following should be included in Hong Kong's current account?

choices.text: Mr. Chan's payment for purchasing a residential flat in Hong Kong.
Mr. Chan's expenditure on renting an office in Hong Kong.
Mr. Chan's expenditure on the transport service he bought from a Mainland airline.
Mr. Chan's payment for purchasing on the shares of a Hong Kong's listed company.

questions.explanation: Renting an office in Hong Kong is payment for a Hong Kong service by a non-resident and is recorded in the current account. Purchasing property or shares is a financial/capital transaction, while a Mainland airline's service is not a Hong Kong service export.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Brief introduction to the linked exchange rate system in
questions.keyPoint: Brief introduction to the linked exchange rate system in
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the linked exchange rate system of Hong Kong is correct?

choices.text: Hong Kong dollar banknotes are fully backed by a basket of currencies.
The exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar to the Renminbi is fixed by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.
The exchange rate of the US dollar to the Hong Kong dollar is fixed between the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the note-issuing banks.
The exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar to the US dollar in the foreign exchange market is fixed at US$1 to HK$7.80.

questions.explanation: Under Hong Kong's linked exchange rate system, note-issuing banks obtain Certificates of Indebtedness from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority at the fixed US-dollar conversion rate. The market exchange rate is not simply fixed at one exact point, and the linked currency is the US dollar rather than the Renminbi or a basket.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.keyPoint: Understand the meaning and give examples of each type of integration
questions.stem: A Hong Kong chained store is famous for selling snacks and drinks imported from Japan. Recently, it expands its business by selling products like cosmetics, frozen food, kitchenware and personal care products. This is an example of ____________ with an advantage of ____________.

choices.text: lateral expansion ... increasing the firm's revenue
lateral expansion ... increasing its market share
conglomerate expansion ... ensuring a market outlet for its products

questions.explanation: The store expands into unrelated product lines, so it is conglomerate expansion. Selling different kinds of products diversifies the firm's business risk. Lateral expansion concerns expanding the same stage of production, while ensuring a market outlet is a motive for vertical integration.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Relationship between price elasticity of demand and total revenue
questions.stem:
Lawrence buys a bottle of tea drink at a convenience store every morning. Recently, the store lowers the selling price of the tea drink by $1, and Lawrence still buys a bottle of the tea drink every morning. Holding other things constant, we can conclude that

(1) Lawrence's demand for that brand of tea drink is perfectly inelastic for that price range.
(2) Lawrence's total expenditure on the tea drink will drop.
(3) The total sales volume of the tea drink of that convenience store will remain unchanged.
questions.explanation: Lawrence's quantity demanded is unchanged when the price falls, so his individual demand is perfectly inelastic over this price range. Because he still buys one bottle at a lower price, his expenditure falls. The information about one customer does not establish that the store's total sales volume is unchanged.

questions.keyPoint: Explain how prices of related goods, income, price expectations, weather, number of consumers in the market, etc. affect individual demand and market demand
questions.stem:
___________________ will lead to an increase in the demand for hotel rooms in Hong Kong.

(1) An increase in the number of tourists visiting Hong Kong
(2) An increase in the price of guesthouse (賓館) rooms in Hong Kong
(3) A decrease in the price of hotel rooms in Hong Kong
questions.explanation: More tourists raise market demand for hotel rooms. Guesthouse rooms are substitutes for hotel rooms, so an increase in their price also raises hotel-room demand. A lower hotel-room price causes an increase in quantity demanded, not an increase in demand.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: Suppose the Mainland experiences economic recession, leading to fewer Mainland tourists visiting Hong Kong, and the rent of premises in Hong Kong drops. In this situation, the total sales revenue of jewellery in Hong Kong

choices.text: might increase, decrease or remain unchanged.

questions.explanation: Fewer tourists reduce demand for jewellery, while lower rent reduces sellers' costs and increases supply. Equilibrium quantity rises, but the effect on equilibrium price is uncertain. Therefore the change in total sales revenue, which depends on both price and quantity, cannot be determined.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Relationship between price elasticity of demand and total revenue
questions.stem: A factory increases the price of its products by 10% and its revenue increases by 5%. We can conclude that

choices.text: the demand for the products is elastic.
the demand for the products is inelastic.
the supply of the products is elastic.
the supply of the products is inelastic.

questions.explanation: When price rises and total revenue also rises, the percentage fall in quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage price rise. Demand is therefore inelastic over the relevant price range.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the provision of a unit subsidy on price, quantity transacted, total revenue etc., and show the share of the subsidy between producers and consumers
questions.stem: Refer to the following demand and supply schedule of good X.
questions.explanation: Before the subsidy, equilibrium is at $10 and 80 units. A $2 subsidy creates a $2 wedge between the price paid by consumers and received by producers. At consumer price $9, quantity demanded is 100; producers receive $11 including subsidy, so quantity supplied is also 100. Sales revenue net of subsidy is the consumers' payment, $9 x 100 = $900, less the $2 x 100 subsidy, which equals $700.

visuals.caption: Demand and supply schedule of good X

questions.postVisualStem:
Suppose the government provides a per-unit subsidy of $2 to the producers of good X. The total sales revenue of

good X net of subsidy is

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Measuring price elasticity of demand
questions.stem: Refer to the following demand and supply schedule of good X.
questions.explanation: The consumer price falls from $10 to $9 and quantity demanded rises from 80 to 100. The quantity changes by 25%, which is greater than the 10% price change, so the price elasticity of demand over this range is greater than 1.

visuals.caption: Demand and supply schedule of good X

questions.postVisualStem: The price of good X changes after the subsidy is provided. For the range between the price before and the price after providing the subsidy, the elasticity of demand of good X is

questions.keyPoint: State the general features of different market structures
questions.stem:
In a monopolistically competitive market,

(1) once a seller raises the price, all customers will go to other sellers.
(2) products can be homogeneous or heterogeneous.
(3) neither buyers nor sellers have complete information about the market.
(4) there are no entry barriers for new sellers to enter the market.
questions.explanation: In monopolistic competition, products are differentiated, so a price rise does not make every customer leave and products are not homogeneous. Information is imperfect and firms can enter freely, so statements (3) and (4) are correct.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.topicGroup: With the aid of a demand-supply diagram, analyse the effects of market interventions on consumer surplus, producer surplus and efficiency
questions.keyPoint: Price ceiling
questions.stem: Below is the demand-supply diagram of a good. The government sets a price ceiling at P1.

choices.text: consumers' total expenditure on the good may increase or decrease.
the consumer surplus may increase or decrease.
the producer surplus may increase or decrease.
the quality of the good will be worsened.

questions.explanation: P1 is an effective price ceiling. Raising it raises the price paid but also increases the quantity transacted as the shortage narrows. For consumers, the higher price reduces surplus on units bought, while the larger quantity can increase surplus; the net effect is uncertain. Therefore consumer surplus may increase or decrease.

visuals.alt: Demand-supply diagram with a price ceiling P1 below equilibrium.
visuals.caption: Price ceiling at P1

curves: Upward-sloping supply curve S
Downward-sloping demand curve D
diagramDetails.intervention: Horizontal price ceiling P1 is below the market equilibrium.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: When the effective price ceiling is raised, the change in consumer surplus is indeterminate.

questions.postVisualStem: When the government raises the price ceiling,

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.keyPoint: Negative externality and economic inefficiency; internalising external costs
questions.stem: Suppose the Hong Kong government increases the duty on tobacco to encourage people to quit smoking. Which of the following descriptions is correct?

choices.text: From the viewpoint of society, there may still be an over-consumption of smoking.
It has the same effect as a strict enforcement of a no-smoking law on the divergence between private and social costs of public smoking.
Fewer people will smoke because the duty on tobacco reduces the private benefit of smoking.
The divergence between private costs and social costs of public smoking can be eliminated.

questions.explanation: A tobacco duty raises the private cost of smoking and may reduce consumption, but it need not equal the marginal external cost. Therefore smoking can still be over-consumed from society's viewpoint. The duty does not reduce private benefit, and it need not eliminate the divergence between private and social costs.

questions.keyPoint: Identify and calculate the cost (explicit cost and implicit cost) involved in choosing an option
questions.stem: Mr. Lee owns a taxi. He earns $40,000 per month as a taxi driver. Suppose Mr. Lee changes his job to be a courier with a monthly income of $15,000, and he leases the taxi out to receive $20,000 per month. His opportunity cost of changing occupation is
questions.explanation: Changing occupation means giving up the best alternative use of Mr. Lee's labour and taxi: continuing to drive the taxi for $40,000 per month. The income he earns after changing job is a benefit of the new choice, not a deduction from its opportunity cost.

questions.keyPoint: Distinguishing between free goods and economic goods
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about scarcity is correct?

choices.text: Anything which is produced with scarce resources is scarce.
There is no scarcity if people's wants are limited.
Anything which has a market value greater than zero is scarce.
There is no scarcity when there is no price competition.

questions.explanation: A positive market value indicates that a good is scarce relative to wants. A good made with scarce inputs can still be freely available in the relevant situation, while scarcity can exist without price competition and even when wants are limited.

questions.chapterTitle: The Three Basic Economic Problems and Private Property Rights
questions.keyPoint: Ways of tackling the three basic economic problems by different societies
questions.stem:
In a market economy,

(1) private property rights of all resources are well-protected.
(2) resources are allocated by price signals.
(3) resources are allocated in the most efficient way.
(4) most resources are owned privately.
questions.explanation: Market economies allocate resources through price signals and have most resources privately owned. Not all resources are privately owned, and market allocation does not guarantee the most efficient outcome in every case.

questions.keyPoint: Comparison of features, advantages and disadvantages of different forms of ownership
questions.stem: If a private limited company is turned into a listed company,

choices.text: its shares can be freely transferred.
the risk of being taken over is reduced.
the company will pay a higher profits tax rate.

questions.explanation: A listed company's shares can be traded freely. This makes a takeover more rather than less possible; listing does not create a different profits-tax rate or remove the firm's legal liability.

questions.keyPoint: Advantages and disadvantages of division of labour
questions.stem: By practising simple division of labour,

choices.text: workers' risk of unemployment is lower.
more goods can be produced with the same amount of resources.
different stages of production become more dependent.

questions.explanation: Simple division of labour raises productivity through specialisation, learning by doing and less time moving between tasks. It therefore allows more output from the same resources.

questions.keyPoint: Different methods of wage payment
questions.stem:
Tour guides are usually paid a low basic salary. A large portion of their income is the tips given by tourists. This is because

(1) this can improve the working incentive of tour guides.
(2) it is costly to monitor the performance of tour guides.
(3) part of the business risk can be transferred to the tour guides.
questions.explanation: Tips link income to service quality and give tour guides an incentive to work well. They reduce the need for costly direct monitoring and make part of income depend on tourist demand, transferring some business risk to guides.

questions.keyPoint: Describe the inter-relationship between the three types of production
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the inter-relationships between the three types of production.
questions.explanation: Primary production supplies raw materials to secondary production, so X is raw materials. Tertiary production supplies services to secondary production, so Y is services.

visuals.alt: Diagram of primary, secondary and tertiary production with arrows labelled X and Y.
visuals.caption: Relationships between the three types of production

flows: X is the flow of raw materials from primary to secondary production.
Y is the flow of services from tertiary to secondary production.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: X = raw materials; Y = services.

questions.postVisualStem: X and Y represent ___________ and ___________ respectively.

questions.keyPoint: Mobility of labour
questions.stem: Which of the following will increase the geographical mobility of labour of an economy?

choices.text: The government tightens the requirements to immigrate into the economy.
The government increases subsidy for continuing education.
The government decreases the unemployment benefit to the unemployed.

questions.explanation: Political instability can make workers move geographically away from the economy, increasing geographical mobility. Tighter immigration reduces mobility, continuing education mainly affects occupational mobility, and the stated benefit change does not directly remove a geographical barrier.

questions.keyPoint: Internal economies/diseconomies of scale
questions.stem: The table below shows the production of a firm. Machines and labour are the only inputs required for production.

choices.text: The firm enjoys economies of scale.
The firm suffers from diseconomies of scale.
The law of diminishing marginal returns applies to the firm.
The firm's optimal scale of production is 4 units.

questions.explanation: Both machines and labour rise together, so this is a long-run scale comparison. Average cost rises from $5 to $9 as scale increases, showing diseconomies of scale. It does not isolate one variable factor, so it cannot establish diminishing marginal returns.
questions.postVisualStem: Which of the following statements about the firm is correct?

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.topicGroup: The basic objective of firms: profit maximisation
questions.keyPoint: Profit-maximising choice of output for a competitive firm
questions.stem: The following table shows the production costs of a firm. The unit price of the good is $10.
questions.explanation: Profit is total revenue minus total cost. At 4 units it is $40 - $22 = $18 and at 5 units it is $50 - $32 = $18; the listed correct option gives a profit-maximising output of 5 units and maximum profit of $18.
questions.postVisualStem: The profit-maximising output level of the firm is ______ and the maximum profit is ______.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (II)
questions.keyPoint: Interpret the information delivered from the Gini coefficient
questions.stem: The table below shows the change in Gini coefficients of Country A and Country B in a certain period.

choices.text: The income gaps between the rich and the poor are enlarging in both countries.
Country A has a higher national income than Country B.
Country B provides more social transfers to people than Country A does.
The ratio of low-income people to high-income people in Country A is higher than that of Country B.

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient rises in both countries over the period, indicating that their income distributions become more uneven. A Gini coefficient does not reveal national income, the size of social transfers or the ratio of low-income people to high-income people.
questions.postVisualStem: We can conclude from the above information that

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) price floor on (money) price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc.
questions.stem:
Which of the following are the possible effects of implementing a minimum wage law?

(1) a higher unemployment rate
(2) more uneven distribution of income
(3) a decrease in the total wage earnings of workers in the economy
questions.explanation: An effective minimum wage can reduce employment, raising unemployment. Workers who lose their jobs can make income distribution more uneven. Total wage earnings can fall when the fall in employment is large enough to outweigh the higher wage rate, so all three are possible effects.

questions.keyPoint: Gross national income (Gross national product)
questions.stem: The income of a British accountant working at the Hong Kong branch of a Japanese accounting firm for two years is counted in

choices.text: both Hong Kong's GDP and GNP.
neither Hong Kong's GDP nor GNP.

questions.explanation: The Hong Kong branch is a resident producing unit and the accountant works in Hong Kong for two years. The income is generated by production within Hong Kong and is also national income under the resident producing-unit concept. The nationality of the accountant and firm does not decide the classification.

questions.keyPoint: Expenditure approach
questions.stem: Study the table below carefully.
questions.explanation: Using the expenditure approach: $250 + ($100 + $15) - $25 + $150 + $100 - $120 + $160 - $130 = $500 billion. Gross domestic fixed capital formation is net formation plus depreciation; indirect taxes, subsidies and net factor income from abroad are not used in GDP at market prices by this approach.
questions.postVisualStem: GDP at market prices for that year is $ ________ million.

questions.keyPoint: Production/value added approach
questions.stem: The following diagram shows a production chain of leather belts in an economy.
questions.explanation: Add the domestic value added in the production chain: local raw materials $800, manufacturers $2,500 - $500 - $800 = $1,200, and local retailers $1,500 + $2,200 - $2,500 = $1,200. The total is $3,200. Imported raw materials and a tariff charged by foreign countries are not domestic value added.

visuals.alt: Production chain of leather belts from imported and local raw materials through local manufacturers and retailers to customers and foreign importers.
visuals.caption: Leather belt production chain

diagramDetails.answerFocus: Domestic value added at factor cost is $800 + $1,200 + $1,200 = $3,200.

questions.postVisualStem: The contribution of the above production chain to the economy's GDP at factor cost is

questions.keyPoint: Meanings of nominal GDP and real GDP
questions.stem: Refer to the information below about an economy.
questions.explanation: When nominal GDP and the general price level both rise by 3%, real GDP remains unchanged. Since population rises by 3% while real GDP is unchanged, per-capita real GDP falls.
questions.postVisualStem: The economy's real GDP __________ and the per-capita real GDP __________.

questions.topicGroup: Factors affecting short run aggregate supply
questions.keyPoint: Factors affecting short run aggregate supply
questions.stem: The diagram below shows the aggregate demand (AD) curve and the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curves of an economy. Yf is the long-run full-employment output level.

choices.text: SRAS1 will shift to SRAS2 ... an inflationary gap
SRAS1 will shift to SRAS2 ... a deflationary gap
SRAS1 will shift to SRAS3 ... an inflationary gap
SRAS1 will shift to SRAS3 ... a deflationary gap

questions.explanation: Higher expected future prices make firms expect higher costs and reduce current short-run aggregate supply, shifting SRAS1 left to SRAS3. With AD unchanged, equilibrium output falls below Yf, so a deflationary gap results.

visuals.alt: AD-SRAS diagram with initial equilibrium E0 at full-employment output Yf and SRAS curves SRAS1, SRAS2 and SRAS3.
visuals.caption: Expected prices and short-run aggregate supply

curves: Downward-sloping AD
SRAS3 is left of SRAS1
SRAS2 is right of SRAS1
diagramDetails.movement: Rising expected future prices shift SRAS1 left to SRAS3.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The leftward SRAS shift moves output below Yf, creating a deflationary gap.

questions.postVisualStem: The economy initially operates at E0. When many firms expect the price level to rise in the future, ____________________ in the short run and there will be ____________.

questions.keyPoint: Factors that cause a shift of an AD curve
questions.stem:
Which of the following is assumed to be constant when the aggregate demand curve of an economy is derived?

(1) real output
(2) the working population of the economy
(3) general price level
(4) the productive capacity of the economy
questions.explanation: An aggregate demand curve shows the inverse relationship between the general price level and real output, so neither is held constant. The working population and productive capacity are held constant when the curve is derived; changes in them affect aggregate supply rather than movement along AD.

questions.keyPoint: Functions and services provided by commercial banks
questions.stem:
Which of the following is the function of Bank of China (Hong Kong) Limited?

(1) issuing letters of credits
(2) issuing banknotes of various face values
(3) acting as a government's bank
questions.explanation: Bank of China (Hong Kong) provides commercial banking services, including issuing letters of credit, and is one of Hong Kong's note-issuing banks. Acting as the government's bank is a central-bank function carried out by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.

questions.keyPoint: Definitions of M1, M2 and M3 in
questions.stem: Money supply M1 emphasises the function of money as a ____________, while money supply M3 emphasises the function of money as a ____________.

choices.text: medium of exchange ... store of value
medium of exchange ... unit of account
standard of deferred payment ... store of value
standard of deferred payment ... medium of exchange

questions.explanation: M1 contains the most liquid forms of money used directly to make payments, so it emphasises money as a medium of exchange. M3 includes broader deposits that can be held as financial assets, so it emphasises money as a store of value.

questions.keyPoint: Understand and calculate maximum and actual banking multipliers
questions.stem: Below is the balance sheet of a banking system. The banks in the system together have excess reserves of $1,100 million.

choices.text: The actual banking multiplier of the banking system is 4.
The money supply will be $12,400 if the banks lend out all the excess reserves.
The maximum amount of loans the banking system can make is $7,500.
The maximum amount of deposits in the banking system is $12,400.

questions.explanation: Initially, required reserves are $3,600 - $1,100 = $2,500 million, so the required reserve ratio is 25%. After the withdrawal, reserves are $3,100 million. Maximum deposits are therefore $3,100 x 4 = $12,400 million. Hence D is correct.

visuals.caption: Balance sheet of a banking system

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose someone withdraws $500 million from the banking system and remits the money overseas. Which of the following statements is correct?

questions.keyPoint: Analyse changes in money demand, money supply and nominal interest rate
questions.stem:
The use of the Octopus Card is becoming popular in Hong Kong. This will result in

(1) a decrease in transaction demand for money.
(2) a decrease in velocity of circulation of money.
(3) a decrease in the nominal interest rate.
questions.explanation: An electronic payment card reduces the need to hold money for transactions, so transaction demand for money falls. It allows money to be used more efficiently, so velocity rises rather than falls. With money supply unchanged, lower money demand lowers the nominal interest rate.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Features of the four phases of a business cycle
questions.explanation: At year 2, the implicit GDP deflator is increasing while unemployment is falling. These are features of economic recovery, when economic activity strengthens after a trough.

visuals.alt: Graph of the implicit GDP deflator growth rate rising and unemployment rate falling from year 1 to year 3.
visuals.caption: Business-cycle indicators

diagramDetails.answerFocus: The combination of rising price growth and falling unemployment indicates recovery in year 2.

questions.postVisualStem: According to the above information, the economy was in a stage of __________ in year 2.

questions.topicGroup: Effects of fiscal policy on price and output levels
questions.keyPoint: Effects of expansionary fiscal policy
questions.stem: Which of the following policies can be used to narrow a deflationary gap?
questions.explanation: Lowering salaries tax raises households' disposable income and consumption, shifting aggregate demand to the right and narrowing a deflationary gap. The other policies are contractionary or reduce net exports.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Calculate the unemployment rate and identify the labour force
questions.explanation: The labour force is 2,850,000 / (1 - 0.05) = 3,000,000. Underemployment is 3% of the labour force, so the underemployed population is 90,000. The total population cannot be found from labour-force data alone.
questions.postVisualStem: According to the above information of an economy,

questions.keyPoint: Surplus budget, deficit budget and balanced budget
questions.stem: ________________ can improve a budget deficit but worsen a visible trade deficit.

choices.text: An increase in people's pre-tax income
Providing cash subsidies to local producers

questions.explanation: Higher pre-tax income raises tax revenue and can improve a budget deficit. It also raises purchasing power and demand for imports, which can worsen the visible trade deficit.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Inflation and quantity theory of money
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of quantity theory of money
questions.stem: According to the quantity theory of money, an increase in money supply will result in

choices.text: an increase in the potential output level.

questions.explanation: The quantity theory relates money supply to nominal output through MV = PY. With velocity stable, a higher money supply raises nominal output. It does not by itself establish the separate changes in prices, real output or potential output.

questions.keyPoint: Measuring the size of the public sector

choices.text: the government adopts a contractionary monetary policy.
more resources are controlled by private sectors.

questions.explanation: GDP rises while public expenditure falls. Public expenditure therefore forms a smaller share of GDP, indicating a smaller public sector and relatively more resources controlled by the private sector. The diagram does not identify monetary policy, recurrent expenditure or tax revenue.

visuals.alt: Graph of GDP rising and public expenditure falling over time.
visuals.caption: GDP and public expenditure

diagramDetails.answerFocus: Public expenditure becomes a smaller share of GDP, so private-sector resource control increases.

questions.postVisualStem: We can conclude from the above diagram that

questions.keyPoint: Progressive tax, proportional tax and regressive tax
questions.stem: Which of the following tax structure will widen the income gap between the rich and the poor?
questions.explanation: Diagram C shows a tax payment with a positive intercept that rises less than proportionately with income. The average tax rate therefore falls as income rises, making it regressive and widening the post-tax income gap. Diagram A is progressive, while B and D are proportional.

visuals.alt: Four tax diagrams A to D relating tax rate or tax payment to income.
visuals.caption: Tax structures

movements: Compare how each tax-rate or tax-payment line changes as income rises.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Diagram C is regressive because tax payment rises less than proportionately from a positive intercept.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Relationship between nominal and real interest rates
questions.keyPoint: Understand the equation: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation rate
questions.stem: If people correctly foresee an increase in the general price level,

choices.text: their cost of living will not be affected.
the purchasing power of money can be maintained.
the real income of fixed income earners will not change.
the realised interest rate of a sum of loan is equal to the expected rate.

questions.explanation: When the price-level increase is correctly expected, the actual inflation rate equals the expected inflation rate. Therefore the realised real interest rate equals the expected real interest rate. Cost of living still rises, and fixed nominal income loses purchasing power unless adjusted.

questions.keyPoint: Calculate the gains from trade
questions.stem: The table below shows the amount of inputs required by Country X and Country Y to produce 1 unit of lemons or apples.

choices.text: Country X will gain 0.5 units of lemons per unit of exports.
Country X will gain 0.33 units of apples per unit of exports.
Country Y will gain 0.17 units of lemons per unit of imports.
Country Y will gain 0.2 units of apples per unit of exports.

questions.explanation: Country X's opportunity cost of one lemon is 4/6 = 0.67 apples, while one exported lemon trades for one apple. Country X therefore gains about 0.33 apples per unit of lemon exported. Country Y has the comparative advantage in apples.

visuals.caption: Inputs required to produce one unit

questions.postVisualStem: If the terms of trade is 1 unit of lemons = 1 unit of apples,

questions.keyPoint: Calculate the gains from trade
questions.stem:
Country X and Country Y trade with each other. Both of them produce two goods only. To determine the total gain from trade of both countries, we have to know

(1) the opportunity costs of production of both countries.
(2) the terms of trade.
(3) the resources endowment of both countries.
(4) the trade volume of the goods.
questions.explanation: Total gains from trade depend on each country's opportunity costs, the agreed terms of trade and the quantity traded. Resource endowment alone does not determine the gain without its effect on opportunity costs and trade volume.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of free trade and a tariff on price, domestic output, import, consumption quantity and tariff revenue for a small open economy
questions.stem: The diagram below shows the demand for and the supply of a good in an economy. Pw is the world price of the good.

choices.text: the shortage of the good will decrease.
domestic supply of the good will increase.
domestic production of the good will increase.
consumers' total expenditure on the good will increase.

questions.explanation: The official key marks C. An effective tariff raises the domestic price, causing a movement up the domestic supply curve and hence higher domestic production. The item is ambiguous because this standard diagram also implies a smaller difference between quantity demanded and quantity supplied; choice A is therefore plausible under the usual meaning of shortage. The official answer is retained for marking-scheme fidelity.

visuals.caption: Tariff in a small open economy

Downward-sloping demand D

diagramDetails.answerFocus: Official key: domestic production increases after an effective tariff; the published option A is also diagrammatically plausible.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on imports and exports
questions.keyPoint: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on import and export prices in terms of domestic and foreign currencies, import and export volumes, and values of imports and exports in terms of domestic and foreign currencies
questions.explanation: The euro appreciates against the US dollar. Since the Hong Kong dollar is linked to the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar depreciates against the euro, so (1) is correct. Hong Kong goods become cheaper in euro terms; the official key treats this as increasing the Hong Kong-dollar value of European imports from Hong Kong, so (3) is correct. The total expenditure in euros by European tourists is not determined from the exchange-rate change alone.
questions.postVisualStem:
Under the linked exchange rate system in Hong Kong, the above change in the exchange rate will result in

(1) a drop in the exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the Euro.
(2) an increase in the total expenditure (in terms of the Euro) of European tourists in Hong Kong.
(3) an increase in the total value (in terms of Hong Kong dollar) of European imports from Hong Kong.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Current account (main components: goods, services, income and current transfers)
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of trade surplus and deficit
questions.stem: Refer to the following information of an economy in a certain year.
questions.explanation: The invisible-trade balance is $50 - $80 = -$30 billion. The visible-trade balance is $20 + $75 - X = $95 - X billion. Setting them equal gives $95 - X = -$30, so X = $125 billion.
questions.postVisualStem: The balance of visible trade and invisible trade are equal. The value of X is ________.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Types of price elasticity of demand
questions.stem: Some smokers never reduce cigarette consumption even when the tobacco duty imposed increases. Their demand for cigarettes is
questions.explanation: Their quantity demanded does not fall when the duty-induced price rises. Price elasticity of demand is therefore zero, which is perfectly inelastic demand.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: Taiwan's "gutter oil" (地溝油) scandal has caused many local bakeries to turn from imported Taiwan-made lard (豬油) to imported Dutch-made lard to make pineapple buns. Meanwhile, consumers consume fewer pineapple buns and some bakeries make fewer pineapple buns amid the scandal. Which of the following diagrams could represent the results of the above events?
questions.explanation: Bakeries switching to Dutch-made lard raise its demand, which is shown by (2). For Hong Kong pineapple buns, consumers buy less and some bakeries make less, so both demand and supply shift left, as in (3).

visuals.alt: Four demand-supply diagrams: (1) and (2) for imported Dutch-made lard, and (3) and (4) for Hong Kong pineapple buns.
visuals.caption: Market-diagram options for the gutter-oil scenario

movements: For Dutch-made lard, bakery demand increases from D1 to D2.
For pineapple buns, both demand and supply decrease from D1 to D2 and S1 to S2 respectively.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Diagram (2) shows higher demand for Dutch-made lard; diagram (3) shows lower demand and lower supply for pineapple buns.

questions.keyPoint: Explain how prices of related goods, income, price expectations, weather, number of consumers in the market, etc. affect individual demand and market demand
questions.stem:
Malaysia Airlines was hit by two incidents in 2014, first the disappearance of a flight, then a flight crash in Ukraine. Which of the following statements about the impact of the incidents is/are CORRECT?

(1) The quantity demanded of Malaysia Airlines services falls.
(2) The demand for Malaysia Airlines services becomes less elastic.
(3) The demand for the services of competitors of Malaysia Airlines rises.
questions.explanation: The incidents reduce consumers' willingness to use Malaysia Airlines, which is a decrease in demand rather than a movement along the demand curve, so statement (1) is not precise. Customers may switch to competing airlines, raising demand for competitors' services. The information does not establish that Malaysia Airlines' demand becomes less elastic.

questions.topicGroup: Money Price (Nominal Price) and Relative Price
questions.keyPoint: Explain phenomena by applying the law of demand (using relative price or full price)
questions.stem:
Suppose the price of chilled chickens increases from $60 to $65 while the price of live chickens increases from $100 to $105. Which of the following statements are CORRECT?

(1) People's expenditure on chilled and live chickens would increase.
(2) The price of chilled chickens relative to live chickens increases.
(3) The consumer surplus for people buying chilled and live chickens would decrease.
questions.explanation: The relative price of chilled chickens rises because 65/105 is greater than 60/100. Since the money price of each chicken rises, consumer surplus for buyers falls. Expenditure cannot be determined without knowing the change in quantity demanded.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: The following is the demand-supply diagram of nursing places offered by a private university. E0 is the initial equilibrium point.
questions.explanation: The subsidy lowers the university's effective cost and shifts supply right from S0 to S2. Better nursing-industry prospects increase demand from D0 to D1. Their new intersection is E4.

visuals.alt: Demand-supply diagram of nursing places with supply curves S0-S2, demand curves D0-D2 and equilibrium points E0-E4.
visuals.caption: Nursing places at a private university

movements: A subsidy shifts supply from S0 to S2.
A more favourable industry outlook shifts demand from D0 to D1.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The new intersection of S2 and D1 is E4.

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the government provided the university with a subsidy of $10,000 per nursing place, and the number of applicants for admission to the programme increased because of the prosperous prospect of nursing industry. As a result, the new market equilibrium will be at ________.

questions.topicGroup: Tax on goods and services (Sales tax)
questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of a unit tax on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc., and show the share of the tax burden between producers and consumers
questions.stem: Answer Questions 16 and 17 by referring to the demand-supply diagram of good X below. S0 and S1 are the supply curves before and after imposing a per-unit sales tax respectively.
questions.explanation: At the post-tax quantity of 5, buyers pay $6 while producers receive $4, so the tax is $2 per unit, not $1. Tax revenue is $2 x 5 = $10. Between the original and new equilibria, both demand and supply have the same proportional price and quantity changes, so their elasticities are equal.

visuals.alt: Demand-supply diagram of good X, with pre-tax supply S0, post-tax supply S1, demand D, and price and quantity axes from 0 to 10.
visuals.caption: Demand and supply of good X before and after a per-unit sales tax

curves: S0 is the supply curve before tax.
S1 is the supply curve after tax.
D is the downward-sloping demand curve.
movements: The per-unit tax shifts supply upward from S0 to S1.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Before tax, equilibrium is price $5 and quantity 6. After tax, buyers pay $6, producers receive $4 and quantity is 5; the per-unit tax is $2 and tax revenue is $10.

questions.postVisualStem:
Which of the following statements about the situation after imposing the tax is/are CORRECT?

(1) The government imposes $1 of sales tax per unit of good X.
(2) Within the price range before and after imposing the tax, the elasticity of demand for good X is equal to its elasticity of supply.
(3) Total government tax revenue is $10.

questions.topicGroup: Tax on goods and services (Sales tax)
questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of a unit tax on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc., and show the share of the tax burden between producers and consumers
questions.stem: What is the total sales revenue net of tax of producers?
questions.explanation: After tax, 5 units are sold and producers receive $4 per unit after paying the tax. Their sales revenue net of tax is therefore $4 x 5 = $20.

visuals.alt: Demand-supply diagram of good X, with pre-tax supply S0, post-tax supply S1, demand D, and price and quantity axes from 0 to 10.
visuals.caption: Demand and supply of good X before and after a per-unit sales tax

curves: S0 is the supply curve before tax.
S1 is the supply curve after tax.
D is the downward-sloping demand curve.
movements: The per-unit tax shifts supply upward from S0 to S1.
