Given that the profit-maximising output of the firm is 3 units, which of the following statements are CORRECT?

(1) The average variable cost is $14 at the profit-maximising output level.
(2) The profit is $4 at the profit-maximising output level.
(3) The market price of the good is $16.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.keyPoint: Understand the meaning and give examples of each type of internal expansion
questions.stem: MUJI, a shop selling home accessories, opens a coffee shop, Cafe&Meal MUJI. This is regarded as ______________ expansion and MUJI has the advantage of ______________.

choices.text: lateral ... extending its brand name to other industries

questions.explanation: Opening a coffee shop is conglomerate expansion because it adds an unrelated line of business to selling home accessories. The main advantage is diversification, which spreads the firm's risk across different activities.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the provision of a unit subsidy on price, quantity transacted, total revenue etc., and show the share of the subsidy between producers and consumers
questions.stem:
To cut government spending, the per-unit production subsidy on a good is cancelled. Which of the following are the results of cancelling the subsidy?

(1) an improvement in economic efficiency
(2) a reduction in the total expenditure on the good
(3) a reduction in the consumer surplus
questions.explanation: A per-unit subsidy causes overproduction and deadweight loss, so cancelling it improves efficiency. The consumer price rises and consumer surplus falls. The change in total expenditure depends on demand elasticity, so a reduction cannot be concluded.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.keyPoint: Negative externality and economic inefficiency; internalising external costs
questions.stem:
The government plans to revitalise the Tsim Sha Tsui Waterfront, renovating ageing facilities and introducing restaurants, retail and leisure facilities. Which of the following are the possible external costs/benefits brought about by the revitalisation plan?

(1) Cost of the revitalisation plan overruns due to inflation.
(2) The revitalisation plan attracts more residents and tourists to shop in Tsim Sha Tsui.
(3) Some leisure facilities block the sea view of rooms of hotels near the waterfront.
questions.explanation: Attracting more shoppers and tourists creates a benefit for nearby businesses and the area, while blocking hotel rooms' sea views imposes a cost on others. A cost overrun is a direct cost of the project rather than an external cost.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (II)
questions.keyPoint: Interpret the information delivered from the Lorenz curve
questions.stem: The diagram below shows the Lorenz curves of Country A and Country B.
questions.explanation: Country A's Lorenz curve is farther from the line of equality, so Country A has greater income inequality and a higher Gini coefficient. Country B's distribution is more even. A Lorenz curve alone does not reveal either GDP or the tax systems used by the two countries.

visuals.alt: Lorenz curves of Country A and Country B. Country A is a dashed curve farther from the line of equality, while Country B is a solid curve closer to equality.
visuals.caption: Lorenz curves of Country A and Country B

curves: Country A: dashed Lorenz curve
Country B: solid Lorenz curve
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Country A has the higher Gini coefficient; Country B has the more even income distribution. The diagram does not reveal GDP or tax structure.

questions.postVisualStem:
According to the above diagram,

(1) Country B has a higher gross domestic product than Country A.
(2) Country A's Gini coefficient is higher than that of Country B.
(3) Country B has a more even distribution of income than Country A.
(4) Country A imposes mainly regressive tax while Country B imposes mainly progressive tax.

questions.topicGroup: Relationship between GDP at factor cost and GDP at market prices
questions.keyPoint: Relationship between GDP at factor cost and GDP at market prices
questions.stem: Refer to the following table.
questions.explanation: GDP at market prices is $340m + $20m indirect taxes - $30m subsidies = $330m. By the expenditure approach, GDP is $150m + $50m - $10m + $20m + exports of goods + $120m exports of services - $40m imports of goods - $60m imports of services. Equating this to $330m gives exports of goods of $100m.
questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the GDP at factor cost is $340 million. The total exports of goods for that year is ______________.

questions.keyPoint: Gross national income (Gross national product)
questions.stem: Which of the following amounts should be added to Hong Kong's gross domestic product to calculate its gross national product?

choices.text: the salary of a foreign domestic helper from working in Hong Kong for one year
the dividends earned by a Japanese citizen on shares issued by a Hong Kong company
the interest earned by a Hong Kong resident on bonds issued by an American company
the salary of a Hong Kong resident from working in Germany for one year

questions.explanation: Gross national product equals GDP plus net factor income from abroad. Interest received by a Hong Kong resident from an American company is factor income received from abroad and is added. The foreign domestic helper's income is earned in Hong Kong, Japanese shareholders' dividends are paid to non-residents, and a person working in Germany for a year is treated as resident there for production purposes.

questions.topicGroup: Effects of fiscal policy on price and output levels
questions.keyPoint: Effects of expansionary fiscal policy
questions.stem: Which of the following will cause the price level and aggregate output of an economy to fall in the short run?

choices.text: an increase in the progressivity of the salaries tax
an increase in average labour productivity
a reduction in the required reserve ratio
a reduction in the profits tax rate

questions.explanation: A more progressive salaries tax lowers disposable income and consumption, shifting aggregate demand left. In the short run this lowers both the price level and aggregate output. Higher labour productivity shifts SRAS right, while the two monetary or profits-tax measures raise aggregate demand.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: The mechanism of moving from a short run equilibrium to a long run equilibrium
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the aggregate demand (AD) curve, the short run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve and the long run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve of an economy. The economy is initially at E0.
questions.explanation: Business optimism increases investment and shifts AD right, creating an inflationary gap. In the long run, money wages rise and SRAS shifts left until real output returns to potential. The resulting price level is higher than P0, so it does not restore to P0.

visuals.alt: AS-AD model with downward-sloping aggregate demand AD, upward-sloping short-run aggregate supply SRAS, vertical long-run aggregate supply LRAS, and initial equilibrium E0 at P0 and Y.
visuals.caption: AS-AD model at long-run equilibrium

movements: Business optimism increases investment and shifts AD right, creating an inflationary gap in the short run.
In the long run, higher money wages shift SRAS left until output returns to LRAS; the price level is above P0.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Only statement (1) is correct. SRAS shifts left, not right, in the long-run adjustment and the price level does not return to P0.

questions.postVisualStem:
Suppose firms are optimistic about their business prospect. Which of the following statements are CORRECT?

(1) There will be an inflationary gap in the short run.
(2) The short run aggregate supply curve will shift to the left in the long run.
(3) The price level will restore to P0 in the long run.

questions.topicGroup: Factors affecting short run aggregate supply
questions.keyPoint: Factors affecting short run aggregate supply
questions.stem: Which of the following can narrow a deflationary gap without putting a pressure on inflation?

choices.text: increasing the expenditure on export promotion
lowering the import surcharge on raw materials

questions.explanation: Lowering the import surcharge reduces firms' production costs and shifts SRAS right. Output rises while the price level falls, narrowing a deflationary gap without creating inflationary pressure. The other measures expand aggregate demand and can raise the price level.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Current account (main components: goods, services, income and current transfers)
questions.keyPoint: Whether and how a given transaction affects the current account
questions.stem:
In August 2015, there was a bomb attack in central Bangkok which had an impact on Thailand's tourism. Which of the following are the possible effects of such an attack?

(1) The national income of Thailand would decrease.
(2) The current account balance of Thailand would worsen.
(3) The employment level of Thailand would decrease.
questions.explanation: A fall in tourism reduces service exports and aggregate demand. It can lower national income and employment, while the lower tourism receipts worsen the current account balance. All three effects are therefore possible.

questions.keyPoint: Qualities of good money
questions.stem:
Which of the following is/are the reason(s) for diamonds being preferred to cigarettes when used as money?

(1) Diamonds are more homogeneous than cigarettes.
(2) Diamonds are more durable than cigarettes.
(3) Diamonds are scarcer than cigarettes.
questions.explanation: Good money should be durable and scarce enough to retain value. Diamonds are more durable and scarcer than cigarettes. Their varying quality means they are not necessarily more homogeneous, so statement (1) is not a reason.

questions.keyPoint: Effects of asset transfers on money supply
questions.stem: Mr. Chan withdraws HK$150,000 cash from his current account in a bank in Hong Kong. Then he remits HK$50,000 to the US and puts the rest as time deposits in a deposit-taking company. Hong Kong's money supply M2 will decrease by ______________ and M3 will decrease by ______________.
questions.explanation: The original current-account deposit is included in both M2 and M3. The $50,000 remittance leaves both measures. The remaining $100,000 time deposit with a deposit-taking company is included in M3 but not M2. Hence M2 falls by $150,000, whereas M3 falls by only $50,000.

questions.keyPoint: Understand and calculate maximum and actual changes in deposits, loans, money supply, etc. after deposit creation/contraction
questions.stem: Refer to the following balance sheet of a banking system. Suppose there is an excess reserve of $100 and the public always hold the same amount of cash.

choices.text: the amount of reserves in the banking system will be $250.
the money supply will increase by $200.
the actual banking multiplier of the banking system will decrease.
the banking system can expand its loans by $50.

questions.explanation: Initial required reserves are $200, so the required reserve ratio is 20%. After it rises to 25%, the banking system's $300 reserves can support deposits of $1,200 when no excess reserves are held. Deposits, and therefore the money supply when the public's cash holding is unchanged, rise by $200. The actual banking multiplier rises and loans can ultimately expand by $200, not $50.

visuals.caption: Balance sheet of a banking system

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the central bank increases the required reserve ratio by 5%. If the banks no longer hold any excess reserves,

questions.keyPoint: Analyse changes in money demand, money supply and nominal interest rate
questions.stem:
Which of the following will lead to an increase in the interest rate?

(1) The central bank sells government bonds to the public.
(2) The liquidity of other interest-bearing assets increases.
(3) The government lowers the salaries tax rate.
questions.explanation: Selling government bonds reduces the monetary base and money supply, which raises the interest rate. A salaries-tax cut raises disposable income and transaction demand for money, also raising the interest rate. Greater liquidity of other interest-bearing assets reduces money demand, tending to lower the interest rate.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Relationship between nominal and real interest rates
questions.keyPoint: Understand the equation: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation rate
questions.stem: Suppose the nominal interest rate on a one-year bond is 8% and the expected deflation rate is 2%. If the general price level eventually increases by 2%, the expected real interest rate is ______________ and the real rate of return on holding money is ______________.
questions.explanation: Expected inflation is -2% because deflation of 2% is expected. Therefore the expected real interest rate is 8% - (-2%) = 10%. Money earns no nominal interest; with an actual 2% rise in the price level, its real rate of return is -2%.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Inflation and quantity theory of money
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of quantity theory of money
questions.stem:
According to the classical quantity theory of money, which of the following is/are the result(s) of an increase in money supply?

(1) There will be inflation.
(2) The real GDP will increase.
(3) The nominal GDP will increase.
questions.explanation: In the classical quantity theory, real output is determined by real factors and is unchanged by a once-and-for-all increase in the money stock. With velocity unchanged, a higher money supply raises nominal GDP. The statement that there will be inflation is not implied by a single increase in the money stock, because inflation refers to a continuing rise in the general price level.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Losses to society caused by unemployment
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a cost of unemployment?

choices.text: a rise in government expenditure on social welfare
a rise in the risk of social unrest
a fall in potential output level
a fall in direct tax revenue

questions.explanation: Unemployment means actual output is below potential output; it does not reduce the economy's potential output itself. Higher welfare spending, a greater risk of social unrest and lower direct-tax revenue are all possible costs of unemployment.

questions.keyPoint: Progressive tax, proportional tax and regressive tax
questions.stem: The table below shows the change in the salaries tax system of an economy.
questions.explanation: Under the old system, the average tax rate falls as income rises, so it is regressive. Under the new system, the average tax rate is 2% at every income level, so it is proportional. Replacing a regressive system with a proportional one improves income inequality. The old system, not the new one, conflicts with the equity principle.

visuals.caption: Change in the salaries tax system

questions.postVisualStem:
According to the above data,

(1) income inequality will be improved after changing the tax system.
(2) the old tax system is in line with the equity principle of taxation put forward by Adman Smith while the new one does not.
(3) the old tax system is a regressive tax while the new one is a proportional tax.

questions.keyPoint: Expansionary and contractionary monetary policy, including changes in required reserve ratio and discount rate
questions.stem: Suppose an economy attains full employment. An open market purchase will lead to an increase in

choices.text: the aggregate output in the long run.
the aggregate output in the short run.

questions.explanation: An open-market purchase increases the money supply and lowers the interest rate, raising aggregate demand. At full employment, real output rises only in the short run; in the long run it returns to potential output while the price level rises. The policy does not directly raise money demand.

questions.keyPoint: Expansionary and contractionary monetary policy, including changes in required reserve ratio and discount rate
questions.stem: Initially an economy operates at the full-employment equilibrium. Suppose there is an economic recession in the economy's major trading partner. The government can stabilise the price and employment levels by

choices.text: raising the subsidy on the production of small and medium enterprises.
reducing its spending on transfer payments.

questions.explanation: A recession in a major trading partner lowers exports and shifts aggregate demand left. Lowering the discount rate is expansionary monetary policy: it encourages bank lending, raises the money supply and helps restore aggregate demand. The other measures either shift SRAS or further reduce aggregate demand.

questions.topicGroup: Understand the condition(s) under which mutually beneficial trade is possible
questions.keyPoint: Understand the condition(s) under which mutually beneficial trade is possible
questions.stem:
For mutually beneficial trade to be possible between two countries, the two countries must have

(1) different productivity in production.
(2) different opportunity costs in production.
(3) different absolute advantages in production.
questions.explanation: Mutually beneficial trade requires different opportunity costs, so that each country has a comparative advantage in at least one good. Different productivity or different absolute advantages are not necessary for comparative advantage and gains from trade.

questions.keyPoint: Calculate the gains from trade
questions.stem: Each unit of resources can be used to produce the following amount of goods in Country A and Country B:

choices.text: Country B has absolute advantages in producing both good X and good Y.
Country B will export good Y.
The total gain of the two countries from trading 1 unit of good Y is 0.25 units of good X.

questions.explanation: Country B can produce more of both goods from each unit of resources, so it has absolute advantages in both. The opportunity cost of one unit of Y is 0.75 units of X in Country A but 0.5 units of X in Country B; Country B has comparative advantage in Y and exports it. The difference in opportunity cost is 0.25 units of X, the total gain from trading one unit of Y.

visuals.caption: Output from each unit of resources

questions.postVisualStem: Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of a quota on domestic price, domestic consumption, domestic production and import quantity for a small open economy
questions.stem: The supply curve of a good is upward-sloping in a small open economy. If the government reduces the effective import quota on the good,

choices.text: the value of quota will increase.
local producers will increase their production.
the trade balance of the economy will worsen.
the world price of the good will increase.

questions.explanation: A tighter effective import quota raises the domestic price. Local producers move up their upward-sloping supply curve and increase domestic production. The world price is unchanged in a small open economy, and the stated effects on quota value and trade balance do not follow.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Current account (main components: goods, services, income and current transfers)
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of trade surplus and deficit
questions.stem: Suppose the trade balance of an economy improves. This implies that

choices.text: the current account is in surplus.
the value of exports of goods is larger than the value of imports of goods.
the increase in the value of exports of goods is larger than the increase in the value of imports of goods.

questions.explanation: An improvement in the trade balance means that the change in exports of goods exceeds the change in imports of goods. It does not require trade in goods to be in surplus, and it does not determine the balance of the full current account, which also includes services, income and transfers.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Balance of payments and balance of the BOP account
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of balance of payment surplus and deficit
questions.stem: The table below shows the items of the balance of payments of a country in a certain year.
questions.explanation: The current account is $100m credits less $60m debits, a $40m surplus. Excluding foreign reserves, the capital and financial account has $30m inflow and $40m outflow, a $10m deficit. Together they create a $30m BOP surplus, matched by a $30m increase in foreign reserve assets so that the accounting total balances.
questions.postVisualStem:
According to the above data, which of the following statements are CORRECT?

(1) There is a balance of payments surplus of $30 million.
(2) There is a surplus of $40 million in the current account.
(3) There is a deficit of $10 million in the capital and financial account (excluding changes in foreign exchange reserves).

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on imports and exports
questions.keyPoint: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on import and export prices in terms of domestic and foreign currencies, import and export volumes, and values of imports and exports in terms of domestic and foreign currencies
questions.stem: The table below shows the change in the exchange rate between the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) and the Australian dollar (AUD).

choices.text: Hong Kong's total import value of Australian's goods (in terms of the Hong Kong dollar).
the number of Australian tourists to Hong Kong.
the volume of Hong Kong goods exported to Australia.
Australian's export revenue from exporting goods to Hong Kong (in terms of the Australian dollar).

questions.explanation: The Hong Kong dollar appreciates against the Australian dollar because one HKD buys more AUD. Australian goods become cheaper in Hong Kong dollars, raising their quantity demanded and Australian exporters' revenue in AUD. Australian visitors find Hong Kong more expensive, while Hong Kong exports become more expensive to Australians; the total import value in HKD is indeterminate because price and quantity move in opposite directions.
questions.postVisualStem: The above change in the exchange rate between the Hong Kong dollar and the Australian dollar would lead to an increase in

questions.topicGroup: Determination of equilibrium price and output
questions.keyPoint: Market disequilibrium: excess demand and excess supply
questions.stem:
During peak hours, buses running through Kwun Tong industrial district are always found full and some people need to queue for a long time to get on a bus. This implies that

(1) passengers have to engage in non-price competition when they take buses running through Kwun Tong industrial district during peak hours.
(2) the fares of buses running through Kwun Tong industrial district during peak hours are below the equilibrium level.
(3) there is an excess supply of bus service in Kwun Tong industrial district during peak hours.
questions.explanation: Long queues and full buses show excess demand at the prevailing fare. Queuing is non-price competition, and excess demand means the fare is below equilibrium. Statement (3) is false because there is excess demand, not excess supply.

questions.topicGroup: Money Price (Nominal Price) and Relative Price
questions.keyPoint: Explain phenomena by applying the law of demand (using relative price or full price)
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the law of demand?

choices.text: The sale of high-quality wine increases as people's income increases.
After imposing a lump-sum tax on automobiles, the ratio of the sale of luxury cars to ordinary cars decreases.
After the depreciation of the Renmenbi against the Hong Kong dollar, the number of Mainland tourists visiting Hong Kong decreases.
If the interest rate decreases, people will increase their present consumption.

questions.explanation: A lump-sum tax adds the same monetary amount to each car. It reduces the relative price of luxury cars compared with ordinary cars, so the law of demand predicts a higher, not lower, luxury-to-ordinary sales ratio. The other statements can be explained by changes in income or full/relative prices.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: The following is a demand-supply diagram of the bottled water market. E0 is the original equilibrium point.
questions.explanation: Lead in tap water increases demand for bottled water, shifting demand from D0 to D2. More foreign brands raise supply, shifting supply from S0 to S2. The new equilibrium is E3.

visuals.alt: Demand-supply diagram of the bottled-water market, with supply curves S0 to S2, demand curves D0 to D2 and equilibria E0 to E4.
visuals.caption: Bottled-water market

movements: Lead found in tap water raises demand for bottled water, shifting demand from D0 to D2.
More foreign bottled-water brands increase market supply, shifting supply from S0 to S2.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The new equilibrium is E3, where D2 intersects S2.

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose more people buy bottled water because lead (鉛) is found in the tap water of some residential blocks and at the same time more foreign brands of bottled water are introduced to the market. The new equilibrium point in the diagram will be ________.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Factors affecting price elasticity of supply
questions.stem: Kims' Store is a book store mainly selling Korean popular books. Under which of the following situations would the elasticity of supply of books from Kims' Store likely be higher?

choices.text: More publishers supplies books for Kims' Store.
A book store selling similar books opens next to Kims' Store.
The prices of books sold at Kims' Store are cheaper than other book stores.

questions.explanation: More available publishers give Kims' Store more sources from which it can obtain books when price changes, making supply more responsive. The other situations affect demand or competition rather than the ability to expand supply.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Relationship between price elasticity of demand and total revenue
questions.stem: The table below shows the relationship between the price of good A and its sales revenue.

choices.text: the demand for good A is inelastic ... supply
the demand for good A is elastic ... supply
the supply of good A is inelastic ... demand
the supply of good A is elastic ... demand

questions.explanation: When price rises from $20 to $30, sales revenue falls from $800 to $750. Demand is therefore elastic in this range. A decrease in supply raises price and lowers quantity; with elastic demand, that combination reduces sales revenue.

visuals.caption: Price and sales revenue of good A

questions.postVisualStem: Within the above price range, ___________________ and a decrease in sales revenue may be caused by a decrease in ____________.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) quota on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, product quality, etc.
questions.stem:
After the imposition of a quota on good X, the total expenditure spent by consumers on good X remains unchanged. Which of the following can be CORRECT?

(1) The quota is effective while the demand is unitarily elastic.
(2) The quota is effective while the demand is perfectly elastic.
(3) The quota is effective while the supply is perfectly inelastic.
(4) The quota is ineffective.
questions.explanation: With an effective quota and unitary-elastic demand, the percentage rise in price equals the percentage fall in quantity, so total expenditure can remain unchanged. An ineffective quota also changes neither price nor quantity. A binding quota with perfectly elastic demand lowers quantity at an unchanged price, while perfectly inelastic supply prevents the quota from restricting the supplied quantity in this way.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) price ceiling on (money) price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc.
questions.stem: The following is the demand-supply diagram of good X.

choices.text: The price control imposed is ineffective.
The quantity demanded of good X will decrease.
Consumers' total expenditure spent on good X will remain unchanged.

questions.explanation: P1 is below the equilibrium price, so it is an effective price ceiling. The lower price raises quantity demanded and reduces the price received by sellers, so producer surplus decreases. Total consumer expenditure is not known to remain unchanged.

visuals.alt: Demand-supply diagram for good X, with price ceiling P1 below the equilibrium price.
visuals.caption: Market with a price ceiling

movements: P1 is below the equilibrium price, so the price ceiling is effective and creates a shortage.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: An effective price ceiling lowers the price received by sellers and reduces producer surplus.

questions.postVisualStem:
Suppose the government sets a price control on good X that it cannot be sold higher than P1. Which of the

following statements is CORRECT?

questions.keyPoint: Understand how price elasticities of demand and supply affect the share of the subsidy
questions.stem: Suppose the government lowers the per-unit subsidy on good X by $30. As a result, its market price increases from $30 to $40 and the quantity transacted changes by 10%. We can conclude that

choices.text: the demand for good X is elastic.
total revenue (excluding subsidy) of the producers of good X will decrease.
the decrease in consumers' share of subsidy is smaller than that of producers' share of subsidy.
the supply of good X is more elastic than its demand.

questions.explanation: Consumers pay $10 more after a $30 subsidy cut, so producers' net receipt falls by $20. The fall in consumers' subsidy share is therefore smaller than the fall in producers' share. The 10% quantity change is smaller than the 33.3% consumer-price rise, so demand is inelastic and producers' revenue excluding subsidy need not fall.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) price floor on (money) price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc.
questions.stem: The table below shows the demand and supply schedules for good X without any market intervention.
questions.explanation: The free-market equilibrium is $120 with 30 units transacted. The $130 floor is effective: quantity demanded, and hence quantity transacted, falls to 20 units. The lost mutually beneficial trades reduce total social surplus and economic efficiency.

visuals.caption: Demand and supply schedules for good X without market intervention

questions.postVisualStem:
Suppose the government imposes a price floor of $130 on good X. As a result,

(1) total social surplus will decrease.
(2) quantity transacted will decrease.
(3) economic efficiency will decrease.

questions.keyPoint: Identify the type of market structure
questions.stem: The market structure of real estate agency in Hong Kong is

choices.text: a perfect competition as price competition does not exist in the market.
a monopolistic competition as real estate agencies provide heterogeneous services.
an oligopoly as several large real estate agencies dominate the market.
a monopoly as the properties the agencies sell are the same.

questions.explanation: The market is dominated by several large real estate agencies, which is the defining feature of an oligopoly. The absence of price competition is not a condition for perfect competition, differentiated services alone do not establish monopolistic competition, and identical properties do not make agencies a single seller.

questions.keyPoint: Identify and calculate the cost (explicit cost and implicit cost) involved in choosing an option
questions.stem: Mr. Leung paid $50 to buy a raffle ticket. He won a foldable bike which cost $1,500. Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

choices.text: If Mr. Leung finds that the bike functions well, the cost of using the bike is $1,550.
If Mr. Leung does not want to keep the bike, the cost of using the bike will decrease.
If the bike can be resold in the market, Mr. Leung's cost of using the bike is the resale value of the bike.
Mr. Leung's explicit cost of using the bike is $1,500.

questions.explanation: The raffle-ticket payment is past and irrecoverable, so it is not a cost of using the bike. If the bike can be sold, using it means forgoing its resale value; that is the opportunity cost. The $1,500 is neither paid by Mr. Leung nor necessarily the market resale value.

questions.topicGroup: Interest as the cost of earlier availability of resources
questions.keyPoint: Explain why interest can be regarded as an opportunity cost
questions.stem:
Which of the following statements about interest is/are CORRECT?

(1) Interest would not exist without money.
(2) Even if someone does not borrow money, interest is still the cost of his/her present consumption.
(3) The existence of interest implies scarcity.
questions.explanation: Interest is the opportunity cost of using resources now rather than later. It can exist without money, for example in an exchange involving present and future goods. Present consumption gives up future consumption even without borrowing, and positive interest reflects scarce resources over time.

questions.chapterTitle: The Three Basic Economic Problems and Private Property Rights
questions.keyPoint: Ways of tackling the three basic economic problems by different societies
questions.stem: Compared to a market economy, in a planned economy,

choices.text: there is no market price for goods.
less production is guided by price signals.
there is keener price competition for goods.
the income distribution is more uneven.

questions.explanation: A planned economy relies more on central direction and less on price signals to allocate resources. Market prices may still exist, price competition is weaker rather than keener, and income distribution is not necessarily more uneven.

questions.keyPoint: Classification of private firms: sole proprietorship, partnership, private limited company and public limited company
questions.stem: Study the following information about a firm in Hong Kong.
questions.explanation: A sole proprietorship is not a separate legal entity, and a partnership requires more than one owner. Both a private limited company and a public limited company have separate legal status and can have one owner or shareholder.

visuals.caption: Information about a firm in Hong Kong

questions.postVisualStem:
According to the above information, the firm can be a ______________.
(1) sole proprietorship
(2) partnership
(3) private limited company
(4) public limited company

questions.topicGroup: Types of goods and services produced
questions.keyPoint: Producer goods and consumer goods
questions.stem: Which of the following is a consumer good?

choices.text: popcorns that customers bought in a cinema
blankets for customers to use in a cinema

questions.explanation: Popcorn bought by customers is used for direct consumption. The audio system, seats and blankets are used by the cinema in providing its service, so they are producer goods for the firm.

questions.keyPoint: Mobility of labour
questions.stem:
Suppose more retraining programmes are available for eligible people to attend. Which of the following would increase?

(1) occupational mobility of labour
(2) unemployment rate
(3) labour productivity
questions.explanation: Retraining equips workers with new skills, raising occupational mobility and productivity. It does not itself increase the unemployment rate, and may instead help workers move into available jobs.

questions.topicGroup: Input-output relationship in the short run
questions.keyPoint: Law of diminishing marginal returns
questions.stem: The table below shows the production of a farm. The only inputs required for production are machines and land.
questions.explanation: Marginal product is 20 for the sixth machine. For diminishing marginal returns to begin with the eighth machine, the seventh machine's marginal product must exceed the eighth's. With X = 124, the seventh machine adds 24 units and the eighth adds 23 units; the ninth then adds 18 units. The other values make the eighth machine's marginal product larger than the seventh's.
questions.postVisualStem: Diminishing marginal returns sets in when the 8th unit of machines is employed. Which of the following is a possible value for X?

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.topicGroup: The basic objective of firms: profit maximisation
questions.keyPoint: Profit-maximising choice of output for a competitive firm
questions.stem: Firm A is operating in a perfectly competitive market and its marginal cost increases with output. Suppose some firms leave the market. Which of the following statements would be CORRECT?

choices.text: Firm A will decrease its output because market supply will decrease.
Firm A will increase its output because the market price will increase.
Firm A will keep its output unchanged because the market price will remain unchanged.
Firm A will keep its output unchanged because the marginal cost of firm A will remain unchanged.

questions.explanation: When firms leave, market supply decreases and market price rises. A competitive firm maximises profit where price equals marginal cost; with an upward-sloping marginal-cost curve, the higher price leads Firm A to increase its output.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.keyPoint: Give possible motives behind each type of integration
questions.stem: Suppose a property management company takes over an insurance company. Which of the following is LEAST likely the advantage to the property management company?
questions.explanation: Taking over an unrelated insurance company is conglomerate integration. It can diversify risk, may offer scale economies and may strengthen goodwill, but it does not enlarge the firm's market share in its original property-management market.

questions.keyPoint: Explain how prices of related goods, cost of production, technology, price expectations, weather, number of sellers in the market, etc. affect individual supply and market supply
questions.stem: Lithium (鋰) is a major material for producing mobile phone batteries. Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?

choices.text: When the demand for mobile phone batteries increases, the demand for lithium will also increase.
When the supply of mobile phone batteries increases, the supply of lithium will also increase.
When the supply of lithium decreases, the supply of mobile phone batteries will also decrease.
When the price of lithium decreases, the price of mobile phone batteries will also decrease.

questions.explanation: Lithium is an input in battery production. Higher battery demand raises derived demand for lithium, a fall in lithium supply raises battery production cost and reduces battery supply, and cheaper lithium lowers production cost and battery price. A rise in the supply of batteries does not itself imply a rise in the supply of lithium.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.keyPoint: Negative externality and economic inefficiency; internalising external costs
questions.stem: There is a problem of divergence between private and social costs in the tobacco market so the government suggests imposing a duty on tobacco. Which of the following statements about the suggestion is INCORRECT?

choices.text: Imposing a tobacco duty will cause the consumption of cigarettes to be closer to the socially optimal quantity.
Imposing a tobacco duty will eliminate the external cost of smoking.
Imposing a tobacco duty will increase the private cost of smoking.
Imposing a tobacco duty will encourage people to reduce their smoking.

questions.explanation: A tobacco duty can internalise part of the external cost by raising smokers' private cost and reducing consumption towards the socially optimal quantity. It does not eliminate the health and other external costs of smoking altogether.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.keyPoint: Negative externality and economic inefficiency; internalising external costs
questions.stem: Tseung Kwan O residents often complain that the landfill nearby creates serious air pollution problems. Suppose the government is planning to increase the charge for disposing of waste into the landfill. If the plan is carried out,

choices.text: the landfill will no longer cause external cost to Tseung Kwan O residents.
the external benefit brought by the landfill to Tseung Kwan O residents will be greater than the external cost.
the divergence between private cost and social cost will be narrowed.

questions.explanation: A higher disposal charge makes users bear more of the social cost caused by landfill pollution, narrowing the gap between private and social cost. It does not guarantee that the external cost disappears or becomes smaller than an external benefit.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (II)
questions.keyPoint: Equalising opportunities
questions.stem: Which of the following is in line with the principle of equalising opportunities?

choices.text: The government exempts rates for a year.
The government grants land at a very low price to build a private hospital.
Applicants with relatives as teaching staff will be given priority in admission in some primary schools.
The government provides local non-profit-making kindergartens with a basic subsidy to offer a three-year half-day service for all eligible children.

questions.explanation: Equalising opportunities aims to give eligible people fair access to essential opportunities, such as early education. The kindergarten subsidy directly widens that access; the other measures do not do so or give advantage based on family connections.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (II)
questions.keyPoint: Interpret the information delivered from the Gini coefficient
questions.stem: If two countries have the same Gini coefficient,

choices.text: the shapes of the Lorenz curves of the two countries are the same.
the living standards of the two countries are the same.
the income distribution of the two countries are the same.

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient summarises the area between a Lorenz curve and the equality line. Different Lorenz-curve shapes can produce the same coefficient, and the coefficient says neither how high average incomes are nor that every part of the income distribution is identical.

questions.topicGroup: Relationship between GDP at factor cost and GDP at market prices
questions.keyPoint: Relationship between GDP at factor cost and GDP at market prices
questions.stem: Refer to the following table.
questions.explanation: GDP at market price is $1,700 million + $10 million of indirect taxes - $5 million of subsidies = $1,705 million. Using the expenditure approach, GDP at market price is $560 + ($400 + $60 + X) + $800 + ($200 - $300) + ($150 - $120) = $1,750 + X million. Hence X = -$45 million. Net factor income from abroad is not part of GDP.
questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the GDP at factor cost is $1,700 million. The value of X is ___________________.

questions.topicGroup: Meanings of GDP and resident producing units; items included/excluded in calculating GDP
questions.keyPoint: Meanings of GDP and resident producing units; items included/excluded in calculating GDP
questions.stem:
Mr. Cheung is a Hong Kong resident. In 2015, he worked in New Zealand for half a year through the Working Holiday Scheme and earned an income of HK$50,000. The income he earned

(1) will be included in the calculation of Hong Kong's GDP.
(2) will be included in the calculation of New Zealand's GDP.
(3) will be included in the calculation of Hong Kong's GNP.
questions.explanation: The work is performed in New Zealand, so the income is included in New Zealand's GDP rather than Hong Kong's GDP. Mr. Cheung is a Hong Kong resident, so the income is included in Hong Kong's GNP.

questions.topicGroup: Deviations of short run equilibrium from long run equilibrium
questions.keyPoint: Deflationary gap
questions.stem: There is a deflationary gap in economy A. If the government _________ the income tax rate, __________ will shift to the right and the deflationary gap can be narrowed.

choices.text: increases ... the short run aggregate supply curve
decreases ... the short run aggregate supply curve

questions.explanation: Cutting income tax increases households' disposable income and consumption expenditure. Aggregate demand shifts right, raising output and helping to narrow a deflationary gap.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: Explain how a given event leads to changes in AD, SRAS and/or LRAS by specifying the component(s) of AD affected and/or factor(s) affecting SRAS and/or LRAS, leading to a shift of the AD curve, the SRAS curve and/or the LRAS curve
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the aggregate demand (AD) curve, the short run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve and the long run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve of an economy. The economy is initially at E0.
questions.explanation: A higher profits-tax rate discourages investment and shifts AD left, so it does not create an inflationary gap. Subsidising university research raises long-run productive capacity, shifting LRAS right. With higher potential output, the long-run price level is below P0.

visuals.alt: AD-AS diagram with downward-sloping AD, upward-sloping SRAS, vertical LRAS and initial equilibrium E0 at price level P0 and real output Y.
visuals.caption: Initial AD-AS equilibrium

curves: AD slopes downward, SRAS slopes upward and LRAS is vertical through initial output Y.
movements: A higher profits-tax rate lowers investment and shifts AD left in the short run.
A subsidy for university information-technology research raises productive capacity and shifts LRAS right in the long run.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: There is no short-run inflationary gap from the higher profits tax. The long-run price level is below P0 after LRAS shifts right.

questions.postVisualStem:
Suppose the government increases the profits tax rate and increases the subsidy on the universities' research of information technology. Which of the following statements are CORRECT?

(1) There will be an inflationary gap in the short run.
(2) The long run aggregate supply curve will shift to the right in the long run.
(3) The price level will be lower than P0 in the long run.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: Explain how a given event leads to changes in AD, SRAS and/or LRAS by specifying the component(s) of AD affected and/or factor(s) affecting SRAS and/or LRAS, leading to a shift of the AD curve, the SRAS curve and/or the LRAS curve
questions.stem: Suppose the price level increases due to an increase in the cost of production. Which of the following can help stabilise the price level in the short run?

choices.text: reducing the spending on promoting exports

questions.explanation: Higher production costs shift SRAS left and raise the price level. Reducing government spending on export promotion lowers aggregate demand, which can offset the upward pressure on the price level. The other policies either raise cost or increase aggregate demand.

questions.topicGroup: Effects of fiscal policy on price and output levels
questions.keyPoint: Effects of expansionary fiscal policy
questions.stem:
To ease the burden on enterprises, the government announced in the Budget to reduce profits tax for 2015-16 by 75%, subject to a ceiling of $20,000.

Which of the following are the possible effects resulted by the measure?

(1) Government tax revenue of Hong Kong will decrease.
(2) The long run aggregate supply of Hong Kong will decrease.
(3) The GDP of Hong Kong will increase.
questions.explanation: A profits-tax cut lowers government tax revenue. It raises firms' retained profits and investment incentives, increasing aggregate demand and GDP in the short run. It does not decrease long-run aggregate supply.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse changes in money demand, money supply and nominal interest rate
questions.stem: Suppose the central bank raised the discount rate. Which of the following events can keep the nominal interest rate unchanged?

choices.text: The central bank raises the required reserve ratio.
The central bank sells government bonds to the public.
The liquidity of other interest-bearing assets decreases.
Many employers change the wage payment for their employees from a monthly payment to a weekly payment.

questions.explanation: A higher discount rate reduces money supply and raises the nominal interest rate. Paying wages weekly lets workers hold smaller average transaction balances, reducing money demand and putting downward pressure on the rate. The other changes either reduce money supply further or raise money demand.

questions.keyPoint: Barter and its limitations
questions.stem: When compared with an economy where goods are traded in exchange for money, in a barter economy,

choices.text: it is more difficult to store wealth.
the cost of transactions is higher.
the time needed for transactions to take place is shorter.
the exchange ratios are easier to determine.

questions.explanation: Barter requires a double coincidence of wants and many separate exchange ratios, so finding suitable trading partners and completing trades takes more resources. Hence transaction costs are higher, not lower.

questions.keyPoint: Effects of asset transfers on money supply
questions.stem: Mr. Wong withdraws HK$50,000 cash from his savings account in a bank in Hong Kong. Then he remits half of the amount overseas and puts the rest as demand deposits in the same bank. Hong Kong's money supply _________ will increase by HK$25,000 and _________ will decrease by HK$25,000.
questions.explanation: Moving HK$25,000 from savings deposits to demand deposits raises M1, because demand deposits are included in M1 while savings deposits are not. Remitting the other HK$25,000 overseas removes it from Hong Kong's M3, so M3 falls by that amount.

questions.keyPoint: Understand and calculate maximum and actual changes in deposits, loans, money supply, etc. after deposit creation/contraction
questions.stem: Refer to the following balance sheet of a banking system. Suppose there is an excess reserve of $100 and the public do not hold cash.

choices.text: the amount of deposits in the banking system
the actual banking multiplier of the banking system

questions.explanation: Required reserves are initially $400, so the required reserve ratio is 25%. After the public withdraw $200, reserves are $300 and deposits contract to $1,200 when excess reserves become zero. Money supply falls from $1,600 to $1,400 and the actual banking multiplier changes, but the monetary base remains $500: $300 bank reserves plus $200 cash held by the public.

visuals.caption: Balance sheet of a banking system

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the public withdraw $200 from the banking system and hold it in cash, and the banks no longer hold any excess reserves. Which of the following will remain unchanged?

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Relationship between nominal and real interest rates
questions.keyPoint: Understand the equation: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation rate
questions.stem: Suppose the nominal interest rate of the economy is 6% and the expected inflation rate is -2%. However, the general price level eventually increases by 1%. The expected real interest rate is _________ and the opportunity cost of holding money is _________.
questions.explanation: Expected real interest rate equals nominal interest rate minus expected inflation: 6% - (-2%) = 8%. The opportunity cost of holding money is the nominal interest rate, 6%. The eventual inflation rate does not change the expected calculation stated in the question.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Inflation and quantity theory of money
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of quantity theory of money
questions.stem: According to the classical quantity theory of money,

choices.text: real output increases when the percentage increase in money supply is larger than the percentage increase in the price level.
the price level increases when the percentage increase in money supply is smaller than the percentage decrease in the real output.
the extent of change in money supply is the same as the extent of change in the price level.
the change in money supply does not have any effect on the price level.

questions.explanation: In the classical quantity theory, velocity and real output are treated as given. From MV = PY, a proportional change in money supply produces the same proportional change in the price level. It does not imply that higher money supply directly raises real output.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Explain why debtors will gain (lose) and creditors will lose (gain) under unanticipated inflation (deflation)
questions.stem: Which of the following parties will lose during unanticipated inflation?

choices.text: the businessmen who have borrowed money from banks at a fixed interest rate for investment
the insurance companies who have signed insurance policies with customers which guarantee a fixed amount of compensation
the tenants who have signed rental contracts with the owners
the elderly who have received Old Age Living Allowance of a fixed amount

questions.explanation: Unexpected inflation reduces the purchasing power of a fixed nominal allowance, so elderly recipients of a fixed Old Age Living Allowance lose. Fixed-rate borrowers and tenants repay or pay with money of lower real value, while an insurer's fixed compensation payment has a lower real value.

questions.keyPoint: Progressive tax, proportional tax and regressive tax
questions.stem: The table below shows the changes in the salaries tax system of an economy.

choices.text: The government will face a fiscal deficit.
The tax base will be narrowed.
The basic tax allowance will be reduced.

questions.explanation: The new system cuts the marginal rates for lower and middle incomes but raises the rate on the remainder from 15% to 30%. This makes the tax system more progressive and is likely to reduce after-tax income inequality. The other outcomes do not necessarily follow from the rate table.

visuals.caption: Changes in the salaries tax system
columns: Marginal tax rate under the old tax system
Marginal tax rate under the new tax system

questions.postVisualStem: Which of the following is MOST likely to be a result of the above changes in the tax system?

questions.keyPoint: Analyse changes in money demand, money supply and nominal interest rate
questions.stem: Suppose people sell their shares for money due to some bad news in the market. The government is planning to take a measure to relieve the effect of this move on the interest rate. Which of the following is a possible measure?

choices.text: increasing its spending on transfer payments
encouraging banks to lend out excess reserves

questions.explanation: Selling shares for money raises the demand to hold money and tends to raise the nominal interest rate. Encouraging banks to lend excess reserves expands money supply, offsetting this interest-rate pressure. The other measures do not provide the needed expansion of money supply.

questions.topicGroup: Factors affecting long run aggregate supply
questions.keyPoint: Factors affecting long run aggregate supply
questions.stem: The Financial Secretary forecasts the growth rate of real GDP is 1-2% in 2016, which is lower than that in 2015. Which of the following policies would stimulate the economic output in the long run?

choices.text: strengthening professional training for construction industries
increasing the spending on promoting Hong Kong's tourism

questions.explanation: Professional training raises workers' skills and labour productivity, increasing productive capacity and long-run aggregate supply. The other policies primarily affect aggregate demand, saving choices or tourism promotion rather than long-run capacity.

questions.topicGroup: Understand the condition(s) under which mutually beneficial trade is possible
questions.keyPoint: Understand the condition(s) under which mutually beneficial trade is possible
questions.stem: Each unit of resources can be used to produce the following amount of goods in Country A and Country B.
questions.explanation: Country A gives up 2Y to produce 1X, while Country B gives up 8/6Y, or about 1.33Y, to produce 1X. Country B exports X and Country A imports it. At 1X = 1.4Y, B receives more than 1.33Y and A pays 1.4Y plus 0.5Y transport cost, or 1.9Y, less than its own 2Y opportunity cost. Both gain.

visuals.caption: Production possibilities per unit of resources

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose Country A and Country B engage in trade and the importing country has to pay 0.5 units of good Y as transport cost for each unit of good X imported. Which of the following is a possible mutually beneficial terms of trade?

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of free trade and a tariff on price, domestic output, import, consumption quantity and tariff revenue for a small open economy
questions.stem: Suppose a small open economy raised the per-unit tariff on imported computers. Which of the following is MOST likely the result of the increase in tariff?

choices.text: The quality of locally produced computers will improve.
The total revenue of the local producers of computers will decrease.
The expenditure on computers (including the tariff) will increase if the demand for computers is inelastic.
The international price of imported computers will increase after the increase in tariff.

questions.explanation: A tariff raises the domestic price of imported computers while the world price is unchanged in a small open economy. If demand is inelastic, the percentage fall in quantity demanded is smaller than the price rise, so total expenditure including tariff increases. Domestic producers' revenue is more likely to rise, not fall.

questions.keyPoint: Comparison between tariff and quota
questions.stem:
When the government of a small open economy introduces a new policy on imported bananas, the price of bananas decreases. Which of the following may be the new policy?

(1) lowering the tariff
(2) abolishing the import quota
(3) embargo on imported bananas
questions.explanation: Lowering a tariff reduces the domestic price paid for imports. Abolishing a binding import quota increases import supply and can also lower price. An embargo restricts imports and raises, rather than lowers, the domestic price.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Current account (main components: goods, services, income and current transfers)
questions.keyPoint: Whether and how a given transaction affects the current account
questions.stem: Which of the following would increase Hong Kong's current account surplus?

choices.text: An investor remits the dividends earned from the shares in Hong Kong to Australia.
A cosmetic shop reduces its purchases from overseas because of poor business.
A property developer buys a piece of residential land from the government.
The number of tourists visiting Hong Kong decreases.

questions.explanation: Reducing purchases from overseas lowers imports of goods, improving the current account balance. Remitting dividends abroad is an income outflow, buying local land is not a current-account transaction, and fewer tourists reduce exports of services.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Brief introduction to the linked exchange rate system in
questions.keyPoint: Brief introduction to the linked exchange rate system in
questions.stem: Suppose there is a depreciation of the US dollar against most other currencies. Under the linked exchange rate system,

choices.text: Hong Kong's exports will become more competitive.
Hong Kong's current account will be in surplus.
deflation will occur in Hong Kong.
prices of imported goods (in terms of HKD) will decrease.

questions.explanation: The Hong Kong dollar is linked to the US dollar, so it depreciates alongside the US dollar against most other currencies. Hong Kong exports become cheaper in those currencies and more competitive. Imported goods from those economies become more expensive in HKD; a current-account surplus or deflation does not necessarily follow.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.topicGroup: The basic objective of firms: profit maximisation
questions.keyPoint: Profit-maximising choice of output for a competitive firm
questions.stem: The following table shows the cost schedule of a price-taking firm.
questions.explanation: Marginal costs are $50, $60, $75, $95 and $100. The price-taking firm produces 3 units, where price equals marginal cost and the next unit's marginal cost exceeds price. Profit is $225 - $195 = $30. Producer surplus is total revenue minus variable cost: $225 - ($195 - $10) = $40.

visuals.caption: Cost schedule of a price-taking firm

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the market price is $75. At the profit-maximising output level, the profit and total producer surplus of the firm are __________ and __________ respectively.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.keyPoint: Give possible motives behind each type of integration
questions.stem: In 2014, the world largest social network “Facebook” acquired the instant messaging application “WhatsApp” with US$19 billion. Which of the following is LEAST likely the motive behind the expansion?

choices.text: to ensure a higher profit for the company
to spread risk by business diversification
to extend its brand name to other products

questions.explanation: An expansion cannot ensure a higher profit, even though higher profit may be an intended outcome. Economies of scale, business diversification and brand extension can each be a direct motive behind acquiring another business, so statement (A) is least likely.

questions.topicGroup: Money Price (Nominal Price) and Relative Price
questions.keyPoint: Explain phenomena by applying the law of demand (using relative price or full price)
questions.stem: Which of the following is INCONSISTENT with the law of demand?

choices.text: When the average rent of car parks increases, the number of private cars on the roads will decrease.
When the government increases the quota on imported meat, the average quality of meat will decrease.
When the government increases the lump-sum air passenger departure tax, the percentage of economy class to first class passengers will decrease.
When the government increases the lump-sum fee on accident & emergency services, the average time patients need to queue for such services will increase.

questions.explanation: A higher lump-sum fee raises the full price of accident and emergency services. The law of demand predicts lower quantity demanded, so queues and the average waiting time should fall rather than increase. The other statements can be explained by changes in full or relative prices.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: The following is a demand-supply diagram of the express delivery services market. E0 is the original equilibrium point.
questions.explanation: More online shopping increases demand for express delivery services, shifting demand from D0 to D2. More logistics companies increase supply, shifting supply from S0 to S2. The new equilibrium is E3.

visuals.alt: Demand-supply diagram of express delivery services, with supply curves S0 to S2, demand curves D0 to D2 and equilibria E0 to E4.
visuals.caption: Express delivery services market

movements: Online shopping becoming more popular raises demand, shifting the demand curve from D0 to D2.
More logistics companies raise supply, shifting the supply curve from S0 to S2.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The new equilibrium is E3, where D2 intersects S2.

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose online shopping is getting more popular and at the same time more logistics companies enter the express delivery services market. The new equilibrium point in the diagram will be _________.

questions.keyPoint: Understand the meanings of complements, substitutes, normal and inferior goods
questions.stem: Holding other factors constant, under which of the following situations will an increase in the price of good X lead to an increase in the total revenue of good Y?

choices.text: Good X and good Y are in competitive supply.
Good X and good Y are in joint supply.
Good Y is a complement for good X.
Good Y is a substitute for good X.

questions.explanation: If Y is a substitute for X, a rise in the price of X increases demand for Y. The resulting rise in both equilibrium price and quantity of Y increases Y's total revenue. A complement would face lower demand, while joint and competitive supply do not produce this result.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: Some samples of domestic seasonings were found to contain a substance that can cause cancer. Suppose some of the suppliers decided to recall the products and some consumers turned to imported seasonings instead. Which of the following diagrams could represent the results of the above event?
questions.explanation: Recalling domestic products reduces the supply of domestic seasonings. Consumers switching to imported seasonings reduces demand for domestic seasonings. Option C shows both domestic supply and domestic demand shifting left.

visuals.alt: Four demand-supply diagram options for domestic and imported seasonings, with shifts labelled S1/S2 and D1/D2.
visuals.caption: Possible seasoning-market shifts

movements: A product recall reduces the supply of domestic seasonings.
Consumers turning to imports reduces demand for domestic seasonings.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Option C shows both the domestic-seasoning supply curve and demand curve shifting left.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Factors affecting price elasticity of supply
questions.stem:
A scientific study found that eating almonds benefits our health. A week later, the price of almonds changed by 30% and the quantity transacted increased from 500 units to 600 units.

Which of the following best explains the extent of the above change in price and quantity transacted?

choices.text: There is no substitute for almonds.
Consumers are used to eating almonds.
Firms producing almonds have excess capacity in production.
Almonds cannot be produced within a short period.

questions.explanation: The health finding raises demand. Price rises by 30% while quantity rises by 20%, indicating supply is relatively inelastic in the short run. Almonds cannot be produced quickly, which limits producers' ability to increase supply and produces a larger price response.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) quota on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, product quality, etc.
questions.stem: The table below shows the demand and supply schedules for good X without any market intervention.

choices.text: the quantity transacted of good X will be lower than 30 units.
there will be an excess supply of good X.
the consumer surplus will decrease and the consumers’ expenditure on good X will increase.
marginal benefit will be higher than marginal cost and the market is inefficient.

questions.explanation: The free-market equilibrium is 35 units at $130. An effective quota of 30 units restricts output below equilibrium. At 30 units, marginal benefit is $140 while marginal cost is $120, so beneficial trades are prevented and the market is inefficient. Quantity transacted is 30, and consumer expenditure falls from $4,550 to $4,200.

visuals.caption: Demand and supply schedules for good X without market intervention

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose a quota of 30 units is imposed on the good. As a result,

questions.keyPoint: Identify the type of market structure
questions.stem: Which of the following is the reason why the market for property agency in Hong Kong is NOT perfectly competitive?

choices.text: Different property agents sell the same properties.
Property agents charge the same percentage of commission.
The services of property agencies have no substitutes.
The market is dominated by several property agencies.

questions.explanation: A market dominated by several large property agencies is an oligopoly, so it is not perfectly competitive. Identical properties and similar commission rates do not establish perfect competition, while the services do have substitutes from other agencies.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the provision of a unit subsidy on price, quantity transacted, total revenue etc., and show the share of the subsidy between producers and consumers
questions.stem: Study the following diagram about good X. Suppose S0 and S1 are the supply curves before and after the provision of a unit subsidy respectively.
questions.explanation: The subsidy shifts supply from S0 to S1, lowers the consumer price from P0 to P1 and increases quantity from Q1 to Q2. Consumers gain K on original units and P + O on additional units, so consumer surplus rises by K + P + O. N is the deadweight loss from overproduction.

visuals.alt: Demand-supply diagram for good X with supply curves S0 and S1, demand D, prices P0 to P2, quantities Q1 and Q2, and areas J to P.
visuals.caption: Consumer surplus and deadweight loss after a subsidy

movements: A unit subsidy shifts supply from S0 to S1.
The price paid by consumers falls from P0 to P1 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The increase in consumer surplus is K + P + O, while the deadweight loss is N.

questions.postVisualStem: After the provision of the subsidy, the change in consumer surplus is represented by ___________ while the deadweight loss is represented by ___________.

questions.keyPoint: Explain whether and how cost changes under different circumstances
questions.stem: Mr. Lee spent $2,000 on buying a fitness bicycle in a second-hand store. The original price of the fitness bicycle was $5,500. Later, he found that the fitness bicycle could not function properly due to mechanical problems and it cost $500 for him to have it repaired. Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

choices.text: Mr. Lee’s full cost of buying the fitness bicycle is $5,500.
If Mr. Lee did not repair the fitness bicycle, his cost of buying the fitness bicycle is lower than $2,000.
If the fitness bicycle can be resold again, Mr. Lee’s cost of keeping the fitness bicycle is its resale value.
If Mr. Lee repaired the fitness bicycle, the repair cost of $500 is not included in the GDP of the current year.

questions.explanation: The relevant cost of keeping the bicycle is the alternative forgone: its resale value. The original price is not Mr. Lee’s purchase cost, the $2,000 paid is unchanged by a decision not to repair, and the repair service is included in current-year GDP.

questions.keyPoint: Explain whether and how cost changes under different circumstances
questions.stem: If the government raises the stamp duty rates on property transactions,

choices.text: the cost of renting out a property decreases.
the number of property transactions in the market increases.
the cost of living in a owner-occupied flat increases.
the cost of buying a property increases.

questions.explanation: Stamp duty is a transaction cost paid when buying property. A higher rate therefore raises the cost of buying. It does not directly lower the cost of renting out a property or raise the cost of living in an owner-occupied flat, and higher transaction costs do not increase the number of transactions.

questions.topicGroup: Types of goods and services produced
questions.keyPoint: Producer goods and consumer goods
questions.stem:
A restaurant chain cooperates with a mobile game developer on a game in which players can get specific props for the game inside the restaurants.

The game props customers get in the restaurants are an example of __________________.

(1) a free good
(2) an economic good
(3) a producer good
(4) a consumer good
questions.explanation: The game props are scarce, so they are economic goods. In the restaurant chain's joint promotional activity, the props are used as an input in providing and promoting its service, so they are producer goods rather than consumer goods.

questions.chapterTitle: The Three Basic Economic Problems and Private Property Rights
questions.keyPoint: The meaning of private property rights and its importance in a market economy
questions.stem: Private property rights

choices.text: do not exist in a command economy.
are always well-protected in a market economy.

questions.explanation: Private property rights can exist in a traditional economy. They are not necessarily absent in every command economy, do not rule out competition, and may be poorly protected even in an economy that is otherwise market-based.

questions.topicGroup: Shares and bonds as sources of capital
questions.keyPoint: Advantages and disadvantages of buying shares and bonds from small investors’ point of view
questions.stem:
From the point of view of investors in general, which of the following are the reasons for buying ordinary shares instead of bonds?

(1) If the company earns huge profits, the rate of dividend of shares may be higher than the interest rate of bonds.
(2) Shareholders have voting rights in an annual general meeting while bondholders do not have.
(3) If the company liquidates, shareholders can claim repayment before bondholders.
questions.explanation: Shares may provide a higher dividend when a company earns high profits, and shareholders usually have voting rights. In liquidation, bondholders have priority over shareholders in claims for repayment, so statement (3) is false.

questions.topicGroup: Types of goods and services produced
questions.keyPoint: Private goods and public goods
questions.stem: The traffic signs on roads are ____________ because ________________.

choices.text: capital goods … cost is involved in the production of the traffic signs
free goods … the users do not need to pay for the services
public goods … the traffic signs can be concurrently used by many people
private goods … people prefer to have more traffic signs

questions.explanation: Traffic signs are public goods because many people can use the same signs concurrently. A production cost and users paying no direct price do not define capital or free goods, and wanting more signs does not make them private goods.

questions.keyPoint: Different methods of wage payment
questions.stem:
Domestic helpers in Hong Kong are usually paid by time rate. This wage payment method is chosen because

(1) their work is varied and non-standardised.
(2) the cost of measuring their output is high.
(3) their work incentive is usually high.
questions.explanation: Time rate suits varied, non-standardised work where output is difficult or costly to measure. A high work incentive is not a reason to choose time rate; piece rate is normally used to strengthen an incentive tied to measurable output.

questions.keyPoint: Mobility of labour
questions.stem: If the government imposes a stricter policy on immigration and emigration,

choices.text: labour geographical mobility of labour will decrease.
labour occupational mobility of labour will decrease.

questions.explanation: Immigration and emigration concern workers moving between places, so stricter rules reduce geographical mobility of labour. They do not directly determine average productivity, unemployment or workers’ ability to move between occupations.

questions.keyPoint: Internal economies/diseconomies of scale
questions.stem: A juice manufacturer cut its output by half by reducing all its inputs. Its profit has increased consequently. The following table shows the change in average cost of production after the decrease in output.

choices.text: diminishing marginal returns set in before the manufacturer reduced its output.
the manufacturer did not aim at profit maximisation before reducing output.
the manufacturer enjoyed economies of scale before reducing output.
the manufacturer was not producing at the optimal scale before reducing output.

questions.explanation: Average cost falls from $800 at 2,000 units to $600 at 1,000 units when all inputs are reduced. The larger output was therefore subject to internal diseconomies of scale, so the manufacturer was not producing at its optimal scale before the reduction. This does not establish diminishing marginal returns or the firm’s objective.

visuals.caption: Change in average cost of production after the decrease in output

questions.postVisualStem: Based on the above information, we can conclude that

questions.topicGroup: Input-output relationship in the short run
questions.keyPoint: Law of diminishing marginal returns
questions.stem: The law of diminishing marginal returns implies that

choices.text: the marginal product of a variable factor can be negative.
the average product of a variable factor can be negative.
the total variable cost of production in the short run will diminish.
the average cost of production in the long run will increase.

questions.explanation: As additional units of a variable factor are added to fixed factors in the short run, marginal product eventually falls and can become negative. Average product need not become negative, total variable cost does not diminish, and the law does not determine long-run average cost.

questions.topicGroup: Tax on goods and services (Sales tax)
