questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of a unit tax on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc., and show the share of the tax burden between producers and consumers
questions.stem:
Suppose the government imposed a unit tax of $10 on a plastic product. As a result, the market price of the product increased by $3. Which of the following statements about the market of such a product are CORRECT?

(1) The market demand is more elastic than the market supply.
(2) Consumer surplus will increase after imposing the tax.
(3) Total sales revenue (excluding tax) will decrease.
(4) There will be a deadweight loss after imposing the tax.
questions.explanation: Consumers bear $3 of the $10 tax, while producers bear $7. The side bearing the smaller share is more elastic, so demand is more elastic than supply. A unit tax lowers consumer surplus and seller revenue excluding tax, and it restricts mutually beneficial transactions, creating deadweight loss.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.keyPoint: Negative externality and economic inefficiency; internalising external costs
questions.stem: Many shopping malls in Hong Kong hold exhibitions of cartoon characters during holidays. In which of the following situations will there be NO divergence between private and social costs/benefits?

choices.text: People can take photographs with the cartoon characters and they need to pay for the service.
The amount of rubbish collected in the shopping malls greatly increases and blocks some walkways. The cost of handling the rubbish collected is borne by the shopping malls.
The revenue of shops in the shopping malls increases but no payment is needed for holding the exhibitions.
The parking spaces in the shopping malls are fully occupied, leading to a long queue of cars waiting outside the shopping malls and causing traffic congestion.

questions.explanation: In (A), users pay for the photography service, so the private benefit and cost are reflected in the transaction. The other cases involve spillover effects: blocked walkways and congestion impose external costs, while higher shop revenue without payment is an external benefit.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (II)
questions.keyPoint: Interpret the information delivered from the Gini coefficient
questions.stem: Suppose the post-tax post-social transfer Gini coefficient of an economy is lower than its pre-tax pre-social transfer Gini coefficient. Which of the following descriptions is CORRECT?

choices.text: The tax system of the economy is regressive.
The income distribution reflected by the post-tax post-social transfer Gini coefficient is more even.
The people in the economy received a large amount of transfer payments.
The living standard of the people in the economy is lower after paying tax and receiving transfer payments.

questions.explanation: A lower Gini coefficient indicates a more even income distribution. The comparison alone does not reveal whether taxes are regressive, how large transfer payments are, or whether living standards have fallen.

questions.topicGroup: Relationship between GDP at factor cost and GDP at market prices
questions.keyPoint: Relationship between GDP at factor cost and GDP at market prices
questions.stem: Refer to the following table.
questions.explanation: Gross domestic investment is $300 million net fixed capital formation plus $10 million depreciation, minus the $50 million inventory change: $260 million. GDP at market prices is $700 + $260 + $500 + (80 - 40) + (150 - 120) = $1,530 million. Thus GDP at factor cost is $1,530 - X + $50 = $1,450 million, so X is $130 million.
questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the GDP at factor cost is $1,450 million. The value of X is __________.

questions.keyPoint: Growth rate of GDP
questions.stem: The following table shows the information of an economy.
questions.explanation: Nominal GDP changes with real GDP and the general price level. A 2.7% fall in real GDP is more than offset by a 3% rise in the price level, so nominal GDP rises. Real GDP per capita falls by more than real GDP, so population must have increased.

visuals.caption: Percentage change relative to the previous year
columns: Percentage change (relative to the previous year) (%)

questions.postVisualStem: We can conclude from the above data that the nominal GDP has ___________ and the population size has ___________ in the above period.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Calculate the unemployment rate and identify the labour force
questions.stem: The following table shows the statistics about the labour market of an economy.
questions.explanation: Five per cent of 8,000 graduates is 400, so unemployment becomes 55,400. All 8,000 graduates join the labour force, giving a new labour force of 800,000 + 55,000 + 8,000 = 863,000. The unemployment rate is 55,400 / 863,000 x 100% = 6.42%.
questions.postVisualStem: Suppose 8,000 fresh university graduates enter the labour market, and 5% of them cannot find a job. If the graduates do not replace any of the job holders exiting the job market, the new unemployment rate of the economy will be ___________.

questions.keyPoint: Factors that cause a shift of an AD curve
questions.stem: Which of the following can neutralise the impact of an economic recession experienced by the economy A’s trading partner on economy A’s aggregate demand?

choices.text: a decrease in the household’s desire to save in economy A
a decrease in the price level in economy A
an increase in the rate of the progressive salaries tax in economy A
an increase in the desire to import in economy A

questions.explanation: A recession in a trading partner lowers economy A's exports and aggregate demand. A decrease in households' desire to save raises consumption, increasing aggregate demand and offsetting the export decline. The other changes either move along AD or reduce net exports or consumption.

questions.topicGroup: Factors affecting short run aggregate supply
questions.keyPoint: Factors affecting short run aggregate supply
questions.stem: Which of the following events will lead to a decrease in the price level and an increase in the aggregate output in the short run?

choices.text: a provision of professional training for financial industries
a decrease in the married person’s tax allowance
damage to electrical generators due to a natural disaster
an increase in the cost of production

questions.explanation: Professional training raises labour productivity and shifts short-run aggregate supply rightward, reducing the price level while increasing output. A lower tax allowance reduces AD, while generator damage and higher production cost shift SRAS left and raise the price level.

questions.topicGroup: Deviations of short run equilibrium from long run equilibrium
questions.keyPoint: Inflationary gap
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the aggregate demand (AD) curve, the short run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve and the long run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve of an economy. The economy is initially at E0.

choices.text: raises the basic tax allowance … inflationary gap
raises the profits tax rate … inflationary gap
provides an extra allowance to recipients of the Old Age Allowance … deflationary gap
lessens the restrictions on importing labour … deflationary gap

questions.explanation: At E0, output is to the right of Yf, so there is an inflationary gap. A higher profits tax reduces investment and aggregate demand, shifting AD leftward and narrowing that gap. The other measures are expansionary or supply-side measures that do not narrow the stated gap.

visuals.alt: Aggregate demand and supply diagram with AD, SRAS, LRAS, full-employment output Yf and initial equilibrium E0 to the right of Yf.
visuals.caption: AS-AD model with an inflationary gap

movements: E0 lies to the right of full-employment output Yf, so the economy has an inflationary gap.
Raising the profits tax rate reduces investment and shifts AD leftward.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: A contractionary profit-tax change can narrow the inflationary gap.

questions.postVisualStem: If the government ____________________, the ____________________ of the economy can be narrowed.

questions.keyPoint: Functions of money
questions.stem: In recent years, many shops refuse to accept HK$1,000 banknotes in transactions for fear of receiving counterfeit notes. Which of the following statements about the situation is CORRECT?

choices.text: HK$1,000 banknotes are not legal tender in Hong Kong.
HK$1,000 banknotes do not perform the function of money as a medium of exchange effectively.
HK$1,000 banknotes are not included in the money supply of Hong Kong.

questions.explanation: When many shops refuse the notes, they cannot be used readily to buy goods and services, so they perform the medium-of-exchange function less effectively. The notes remain legal tender, retain value and remain part of the money supply.

questions.keyPoint: Effects of asset transfers on money supply
questions.stem: Mrs. Cheng receives a HK$150,000 overseas remittance from her nephew. She puts 1/3 of the amount in a safe deposit box at a licensed bank and the remainder in her time deposit account with a deposit-taking company in Hong Kong. Which of the following is the immediate effect of the above actions on Hong Kong’s money supply?

choices.text: M1 increases by HK$50,000; M2 and M3 increase by HK$100,000.
M1 increases by HK$50,000; M2 remains changed; M3 increases by HK$150,000.
M1 and M2 increase by HK$50,000; M3 increases by HK$150,000.
M1, M2 and M3 increase by HK$150,000.

questions.explanation: The $50,000 kept as currency is included in M1 and M2. The $100,000 time deposit with a deposit-taking company is included in M3 but not M2. Therefore M1 and M2 rise by $50,000, while M3 rises by the full $150,000.

questions.keyPoint: Understand and calculate maximum and actual changes in deposits, loans, money supply, etc. after deposit creation/contraction
questions.stem: Refer to the following balance sheet of a banking system. Suppose the banking system does not hold any excess reserves.
questions.explanation: The required reserve ratio is $2,500 / $12,500 = 20%. After the $200 withdrawal, deposits are $12,300 and reserves are $2,300. Required reserves are $2,460, so the immediate reserve shortfall is $160; banks must call back $160 of loans to meet the requirement.

visuals.caption: Balance sheet of a banking system

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the public withdraw $200 from the banking system and hold it in cash. What is the amount of loans banks will have to call back to meet the reserve requirement?

questions.keyPoint: Analyse changes in money demand, money supply and nominal interest rate
questions.stem: Refer to the following diagram. Suppose the initial equilibrium point of the money market is at point E.
questions.explanation: More liquid non-monetary assets reduce the demand for money, shifting Md0 to Md1. A lower required reserve ratio increases money supply, shifting MS0 to MS2. The new equilibrium is point B.

visuals.alt: Money-market diagram with money supply lines MS1, MS0 and MS2, money demand lines Md1, Md0 and Md2, and points A to E.
visuals.caption: Money-market shifts

movements: Higher liquidity of non-monetary assets lowers money demand, shifting Md0 to Md1.
A lower required reserve ratio raises money supply, shifting MS0 to MS2.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The two shifts meet at point B.

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the liquidity of non-monetary assets increases, and at the same time, the required reserve ratio decreases. The new equilibrium point in the diagram will be _________.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Relationship between nominal and real interest rates
questions.keyPoint: Nominal interest rate as the (opportunity) cost of holding money
questions.stem: Assume that the real interest rate is constant. If the expected inflation rate decreases, the nominal rate of return of holding money will ______________, while the cost of holding money will ______________.
questions.explanation: Money itself has no nominal interest return, so that return remains unchanged. With a constant real interest rate, lower expected inflation lowers the nominal interest rate; the nominal interest rate is the opportunity cost of holding money, so that cost decreases.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Relationship between nominal and real interest rates
questions.keyPoint: Understand the equation: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation rate
questions.stem:
The government issued the first Silver Bond (銀色債券) for subscription by Hong Kong residents aged 65 or above on August 2016. The bond will have a tender of three years and the interest rate is linked to the inflation of Hong Kong, subject to a minimum rate of 2%.

Under which of the following situations persons will people who subscripted to the Silver Bond gain?

choices.text: The inflation rate is higher than 2%.
The inflation rate is equal to 2%.
The inflation rate is lower than 2%.

questions.explanation: When inflation is below 2%, the bond still pays the 2% minimum rate. Its real return is therefore positive, so subscribers gain. When inflation is at or above 2%, the inflation-linked rate only preserves the real value of the return.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Inflation and quantity theory of money
questions.keyPoint: Meaning of quantity theory of money
questions.stem: The classical quantity theory of money predicts that

choices.text: the velocity of circulation of money is constant.
money supply is negatively related to the nominal interest rate.
money supply is positively related to the price level.
real output of an economy is always at the full-employment output level.

questions.explanation: Under the classical quantity theory, with velocity and real output treated as given, a higher money supply causes a proportional rise in the price level. Thus money supply and the price level are positively related.

questions.keyPoint: Progressive tax, proportional tax and regressive tax
questions.stem: The table below shows the change in the tax system of an economy.
questions.explanation: The old tax system is proportional at 2%. Under the new system, the tax rate rises from 1.6% for $50,000 income to about 2.13% for $150,000 income, making the system more progressive and helping equalise income. The information does not establish total revenue or the tax base.

visuals.caption: Change in the tax system
columns: Tax payment under the old tax system ($)
Tax payment under the new tax system ($)

questions.postVisualStem: From the above information, we can conclude that the change in the tax system can

questions.keyPoint: Expansionary and contractionary monetary policy, including changes in required reserve ratio and discount rate
questions.stem: Suppose there is an inflationary gap due to an increase in the basic allowance of the salaries tax. Which of the following can help narrow the inflationary gap without causing an increase in the price level?

choices.text: raising the investment in human capital

questions.explanation: Raising the required reserve ratio is contractionary monetary policy: it reduces money supply, interest-sensitive spending and aggregate demand, narrowing the inflationary gap without increasing the price level. Reducing the discount rate is expansionary, while reducing an import quota can raise prices.

questions.topicGroup: Effects of fiscal policy on price and output levels
questions.keyPoint: Effects of expansionary fiscal policy
questions.stem:
The government will provide a one-off extra allowance to social security recipients. The amount is equal to one month of the Comprehensive Social Security Assistance standard rates, Old Age Allowance, Old Age Living Allowance or Disability Allowance payments.

Which of the following are the possible effects of providing the extra allowance?

(1) The government consumption expenditure in the component of Hong Kong’s GDP will increase.
(2) Hong Kong’s aggregate demand will increase.
(3) Hong Kong’s short run aggregate supply will increase.
(4) The GDP of Hong Kong will increase.
questions.explanation: The extra allowance is a transfer payment, not government consumption expenditure in GDP. Recipients can raise consumption, increasing aggregate demand and GDP, but the payment does not directly increase short-run aggregate supply.

questions.keyPoint: Surplus budget, deficit budget and balanced budget
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about a balanced budget is CORRECT?

choices.text: A balanced budget implies neither a fiscal deficit nor a fiscal surplus.
A balanced budget means that the government’s actual tax revenue is equal to its actual expenditure.
The government cannot impose an expansionary fiscal policy under a balanced budget.
If both the government expenditure and tax revenue in a balanced budget decrease by the same amount, the effect on aggregate output is contractionary.

questions.explanation: A fall in government expenditure has a full negative multiplier, while an equal tax cut has a smaller positive multiplier because part of the tax cut is saved. The combined effect is contractionary. A balanced budget concerns planned revenue and expenditure and can accompany an expansionary change in both.

questions.keyPoint: Understand the meaning of comparative advantage
questions.stem: Suppose both Country A and Country B produce good X and good Y. Country B has absolute advantage over Country A in producing good X and good Y. Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

choices.text: Country A’s costs of producing both good X and good Y are higher than Country B.
Country A has a comparative advantage in producing either good.
Country A will gain less from trade than Country B.
The two countries will not engage in trade.

questions.explanation: Absolute advantage does not determine opportunity costs, the size of gains from trade, or whether trade occurs. With two countries and two goods, comparative advantage is based on relative opportunity cost, so Country A can have a comparative advantage in one of the goods even when Country B has absolute advantage in both.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of a quota on domestic price, domestic consumption, domestic production and import quantity for a small open economy
questions.stem: The diagram below shows the supply of and the demand for good X in a small country. PW is the world price of good X.

choices.text: The quantity of good X produced domestically is Q4.
The extent of the increase in import volume of good X is (Q4 − Q3).
The international price of good X is P2.
The excess demand for good X is (Q5 − Q2).

questions.explanation: The change in the kinked supply curve represents a relaxation of the import quota. The diagram shows the quota, and hence import volume, increasing by Q4 - Q3. The world price remains PW and domestic production is determined by domestic supply at PW.

visuals.alt: Small-country supply-demand diagram with world price Pw, prices P1 and P2, supply curves S0 to S2, demand D and quantity labels Q1 to Q6.
visuals.caption: Import-quota change

movements: The kinked supply curve moves from S1 to S2 after the import quota changes.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The diagram shows that the increase in import volume is Q4 - Q3.

questions.postVisualStem:
Suppose that after the change of the import quota, the kinked supply curve of good X changes from S1 to S2.

Which of the following is the effect of such a change on the country?

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.keyPoint: Whether and how a given transaction affects the capital and financial account
questions.stem: Mr. Wong is a foreign businessman. In 2015, he bought a tablet computer and also a premise in a shopping mall for his company during his business trip in Hong Kong. The above transactions

choices.text: will improve both Hong Kong’s visible trade balance and capital and financial account balance.
will improve Hong Kong’s invisible trade balance but will not affect its capital and financial account balance.
will not affect Hong Kong’s invisible trade balance but will improve its capital and financial account balance.
will not affect Hong Kong’s visible trade balance but will improve its capital and financial account balance.

questions.explanation: Buying the premises is a capital and financial account inflow because a non-resident acquires a Hong Kong real asset. The local tablet purchase does not by itself represent an export of goods, so it does not affect the visible trade balance.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on imports and exports
questions.keyPoint: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on import and export prices in terms of domestic and foreign currencies, import and export volumes, and values of imports and exports in terms of domestic and foreign currencies
questions.stem: In 2016, the British pound depreciated sharply against the US dollar following Britain’s vote to leave the European Union (EU). Which of the following is the possible effect of the depreciation of the British pound on Hong Kong under the linked exchange rate system?

choices.text: The value of goods exported from Britain to Hong Kong (in terms of the British pound) increases.
The value of British’s assets held by Hong Kong people (in terms of the Hong Kong dollar) increases.
The cost of travelling in Hong Kong (in terms of the British pound) for citizens of Britain decreases.
The number of Hong Kong students studying in Britain decreases.

questions.explanation: Since the Hong Kong dollar is linked to the US dollar, a depreciation of the pound makes British exports cheaper in Hong Kong dollars. Hong Kong demand for British goods can rise, increasing their value in pounds. British assets lose Hong Kong-dollar value, Hong Kong travel becomes more expensive in pounds, and studying in Britain becomes cheaper for Hong Kong students.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Brief introduction to the linked exchange rate system in
questions.keyPoint: Brief introduction to the linked exchange rate system in
questions.stem: Under the linked exchange rate system in Hong Kong,

choices.text: Hong Kong banknotes have to be fully backed by foreign exchange reserves.
the exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar between banks and the Exchange Fund is fixed.
the market exchange rate of Hong Kong dollars relative to the US dollar is fixed.
the three note-issuing banks have to provide the service of exchanging Hong Kong dollars for US dollars at the linked rate.

questions.explanation: Hong Kong banknotes are fully backed by foreign exchange reserves through the currency-board arrangement. The market exchange rate can move within the convertibility zone, and it is the Exchange Fund rather than note-issuing banks that provides convertibility at the linked rate.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.keyPoint: Understand the meaning and give examples of each type of integration
questions.stem:
Suppose firm A takes over firm B, and its aim is to ensure a stable supply of raw materials required in production.

Firm A is most likely _____________ and firm B is most likely _____________.

choices.text: a Korean restaurant ... a Japanese restaurant
a cafe ... a coffee bean farm
an airline company ... a travel agency
a design company ... an advertising company

questions.explanation: To secure an input, a firm takes over a supplier in a backward vertical integration. A cafe taking over a coffee-bean farm best matches this objective; the other pairs are competitors, downstream businesses or related service firms rather than a raw-material supplier.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.topicGroup: The basic objective of firms: profit maximisation
questions.keyPoint: Profit-maximising choice of output for a competitive firm
questions.stem: Refer to the following table showing the production costs of a price-taking firm.

choices.text: the maximum profit the firm can make is $36.
the firm will produce 7 units of output to maximise its profit.
the total cost is $202 at the profit maximising output level.
the total variable cost is $84 at the profit maximising output level.

questions.explanation: A price-taking firm produces 8 units, where price equals marginal cost ($30) and the next unit's marginal cost is higher. At 8 units, average variable cost is $14 and average fixed cost is $11.25, so total cost is (14 + 11.25) x 8 = $202. Total variable cost is $112 and profit is $38.

visuals.caption: Production costs of a price-taking firm

questions.postVisualStem: If the product price is $30,

questions.keyPoint: Understand the meanings of complements, substitutes, normal and inferior goods
questions.stem: Which of the following is LEAST likely an example of joint demand?
questions.explanation: Jointly demanded goods are used or consumed together. A computer monitor and keyboard, a washing machine and water, and bread and butter are complementary pairs. A hair stylist provides the hair-cutting service rather than being a separate good jointly demanded with it.

questions.topicGroup: Money Price (Nominal Price) and Relative Price
questions.keyPoint: Explain phenomena by applying the law of demand (using relative price or full price)
questions.stem: Which of the following is INCONSISTENT with the law of demand?

choices.text: When the banks raise the service fee of safe deposit boxes sharply, the waiting time for applying a safe deposit box reduces.
When the government reduces the quota on imported wine, a lower proportion of high quality wine is imported.
When the government increases the penalty on illegal parking, parking fees in private car parks increase.
People who live further away from a supermarket spend more in the supermarket per visit than those who live nearer to the supermarket.

questions.explanation: The official answer key marks B. A quota reduction is a supply restriction, but the stated change in the quality composition of imports does not follow from the law of demand. The other cases can be explained through changes in full price, including monetary, time and penalty costs.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: Suppose public housing is an inferior good. People’s income decreased due to economic recession and at the same time the government built less public housing. Which of the following diagrams could represent a result of the above events?
questions.explanation: With public housing as an inferior good, lower income raises its demand. Building fewer public flats lowers supply. Option B is the public-housing diagram with demand shifting right and supply shifting left.

visuals.alt: Four demand-supply diagram options for public and private housing, with supply and demand shifts labelled S1/S2 and D1/D2.
visuals.caption: Possible housing-market shifts

movements: When income falls, demand for inferior public housing rises, shifting demand from D1 to D2.
Building less public housing reduces supply, shifting supply from S1 to S2.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Option B is the public-housing diagram showing supply shifting left and demand shifting right.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Relationship between price elasticity of demand and total revenue
questions.stem: Suppose people regard peanut oil and corn oil are substitutes to each other and both of them have a price elasticity of demand smaller than 1 at their prevailing prices. If the price of peanut oil increases, the total expenditure spent on peanut oil will ____________ and that on corn oil will ____________.
questions.explanation: Demand for peanut oil is inelastic, so its price rise increases expenditure on it. Corn oil is a substitute, so demand for corn oil rises; its equilibrium price and quantity both rise, increasing total expenditure on corn oil.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the labour market of railway maintenance staff. E0 is the original equilibrium point.
questions.explanation: The railway expansions raise firms' demand for maintenance staff, while training programmes increase the supply of qualified staff. The new intersection of D2 and S2 in the diagram is E3.

visuals.alt: Labour-market demand and supply diagram for railway maintenance staff, with D0 to D2, S0 to S2 and equilibrium points E0 to E4.
visuals.caption: Railway maintenance labour market

movements: Opening the railway lines increases employers' demand for maintenance staff, shifting demand from D0 to D2.
More related training programmes increase the supply of qualified staff, shifting supply from S0 to S2.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The new equilibrium is E3, the intersection of D2 and S2.

questions.postVisualStem: With the opening of the Kwun Tong Line Extension and the South Island Line, MTRC plans to employ more railway maintenance staff. At the same time, to attract young people to enter the industry, the government put in more resources on related training programmes. The new equilibrium point will be at ___________.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) quota on price, quantity transacted, total revenue, product quality, etc.
questions.stem: Refer to the following demand and supply schedules for good A.

choices.text: within the range of the original and the new market prices, demand for good A is inelastic.
the unit price of good A will increase by $50.
the quantity transacted of good A will be lower than 75 units.
the unit price of good A’s substitutes will decrease.

questions.explanation: The original equilibrium is 85 units at $30. A binding quota of 75 units raises the price to $50, so the price rises by $20 and 75 units are transacted. Between the two equilibria, price rises by 66.7% while quantity demanded falls by 11.8%, so demand is inelastic.

visuals.caption: Demand and supply schedules for good A

questions.postVisualStem: When a quota of 75 units is imposed on good A,

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) price floor on (money) price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc.
questions.stem: Which of the following is LEAST likely the result of raising the statutory minimum wage by the government?

choices.text: The total wage earnings of the employed low-income workers increase.
The demand for low-skilled workers increases.
The wage of high-skilled workers increases.

questions.explanation: An effective statutory minimum wage raises employers' labour cost and reduces the quantity of low-skilled labour demanded. It can increase unemployment, may raise the earnings of those who remain employed, and can raise the wage of high-skilled workers if they are substitutes for low-skilled workers.

questions.keyPoint: State the general features of different market structures
questions.stem: When a market changes from an oligopoly to a monopoly,

choices.text: the seller does not need to face competition anymore.
the seller changes from a price taker to a price searcher.
the seller completely controls the quantity supplied of the good in the market.
the market only provides one product.

questions.explanation: A monopoly has one seller, so that seller controls the market supply of the good. Oligopolists are already price searchers, and a monopoly can still face potential competition or substitutes; it also need not provide only one product.

questions.keyPoint: Definition of free goods and economic goods
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about free goods is CORRECT?

choices.text: Free goods are not necessities in daily life.
The supply of free goods is unlimited.

questions.explanation: Free goods are available in amounts sufficient to satisfy wants and therefore are not scarce. People may want them, and their physical supply need not be unlimited in every sense.

questions.topicGroup: Distinction between positive statements and normative statements
questions.keyPoint: Distinction between positive statements and normative statements
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the difference between a positive statement and a normative statement is CORRECT?

choices.text: A positive statement is always true while a normative statement is not.
A positive statement involves value judgement while a normative statement does not.
A normative statement cannot be tested by facts while a positive statement can.
A normative statement is an objective description while a positive statement is not.

questions.explanation: Positive statements make claims that can be tested against facts. Normative statements contain value judgements, so facts alone cannot establish whether they are correct.

questions.keyPoint: Explain whether and how cost changes under different circumstances
questions.stem:
Kelly is considering attending university in Australia. If ________________________, her cost of studying in Australia will increase.

(1) the lodging fee for residential halls in Australia increases
(2) the study life in Australia is easier than she expected
(3) Australian dollar appreciates against other currencies
questions.explanation: A higher lodging fee raises the monetary cost of studying in Australia. An appreciation of the Australian dollar also makes Australian expenses more costly in other currencies. An easier-than-expected study life does not raise the cost.

questions.chapterTitle: The Three Basic Economic Problems and Private Property Rights
questions.keyPoint: The meanings of the three basic economic problems and examples of the problems
questions.stem:
In 2016, the Hong Kong Housing Authority launched the Green Form Subsidised Home Ownership Pilot Scheme (「綠置居」) to sell flats to eligible applicants at a relatively low price. The current tenants of public rental housing are eligible to apply. Which of the following statements about the scheme is/are CORRECT?

(1) The scheme involves non-price competition.
(2) The scheme will widen the income gap in society.
(3) The scheme is about the “for whom to produce” question in Economics.
questions.explanation: Selling scarce subsidised flats below the market price creates competition by eligibility rather than by price. Deciding that public-rental tenants may buy the flats concerns for whom the flats are produced. The scheme does not widen the income gap as stated.

questions.chapterTitle: The Three Basic Economic Problems and Private Property Rights
questions.keyPoint: Ways of tackling the three basic economic problems by different societies
questions.stem: If an economy changes from a market economy to a command economy,

choices.text: all privately owned resources will be owned by the government.
private property rights will not exist.

questions.explanation: A command economy involves greater government direction of resource allocation, but it does not necessarily mean that all resources become government-owned, that private property rights wholly disappear, or that living standards must fall.

questions.topicGroup: Types of goods and services produced
questions.keyPoint: Producer goods and consumer goods
questions.stem:
Seasonings (調味料) provided in fast food shops for free are regarded as ________________.

(1) public goods
(2) economic goods
(3) producer goods
(4) normal goods
questions.explanation: The seasonings use scarce resources, so they are economic goods even when customers are not separately charged. The fast-food shop uses them as an input in providing its food service, so they are producer goods. Free provision does not make them public goods or normal goods.

questions.keyPoint: Comparison of features, advantages and disadvantages of different forms of ownership
questions.stem: If a partnership is converted into a public limited company,

choices.text: the risk of being taken over will be reduced.
the existing shareholders’ power of control over the company will be diluted.
the company will shut down when the existing owners quit.
the government will have a greater degree of control on the management of the company.

questions.explanation: A public limited company can issue shares to the public. Bringing in more shareholders dilutes the existing owners’ control. Its continuity is not tied to the existing owners, and public ownership is not created by this conversion.

questions.keyPoint: Productivity of labour
questions.stem: The following table shows the production information of a factory in 20X5 and 20X6.
questions.explanation: Labour productivity rises from 55,000 / (220 x 50) = 5 to 80,000 / (250 x 40) = 8 units per worker-hour. More intensive use of capital goods and a move from time rate to piece rate may raise productivity; a poorer working environment would not.

visuals.caption: Production information of a factory
rows: Number of working hours per worker per week

questions.postVisualStem:
The change in the labour productivity during the above period may be due to

(1) a poorer working environment.
(2) a more intensive use of capital goods.
(3) a change in the wage payment method from time rate to piece rate.

questions.keyPoint: Different methods of wage payment
questions.stem: Which of the following is LEAST likely to be paid on a time rate basis?
questions.explanation: A property agent is commonly paid by commission, with pay linked to completed property transactions. The output of cleaners, waiters and kindergarten teachers is less readily measured and their work is more typically paid by time rate.

questions.topicGroup: Input-output relationship in the short run
questions.keyPoint: Law of diminishing marginal returns
questions.stem: The law of diminishing marginal returns implies that

choices.text: the marginal product of a variable factor can be negative.
the average product of a variable factor can be negative.
the total variable cost of production in the short run will diminish.
the average cost of production in the long run will increase.

questions.explanation: As more units of a variable factor are combined with fixed factors, marginal product eventually falls and can become negative. The law does not require average product to be negative, total variable cost to fall, or long-run average cost to rise.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.keyPoint: Negative externality and economic inefficiency; internalising external costs
questions.stem: External cost exists when

choices.text: income in society is unevenly distributed.
private benefit is not equal to social benefit.
there is a divergence between private cost and social cost.

questions.explanation: An external cost is a cost imposed on third parties, so social cost exceeds private cost. Uneven income distribution, a private-social benefit gap, or inefficiency may occur in other contexts but do not define an external cost.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.topicGroup: With the aid of a demand-supply diagram, analyse the effects of market interventions on consumer surplus, producer surplus and efficiency
questions.keyPoint: Price floor
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the supply and demand curves of a good without any market intervention.
questions.explanation: A price floor at P2 and a quota at Q1 both yield a market price of P2 and quantity Q1. Consumer surplus is then area I and producer surplus is J + K + L. A price ceiling or per-unit tax produces a different allocation of surplus.

visuals.alt: Demand-supply diagram with prices P0 to P2, quantities Q0 and Q1, curves S and D, and areas I to N.
visuals.caption: Market intervention and surplus

movements: An effective price floor at P2 restricts the quantity transacted to Q1.
A binding quota at Q1 produces the same price-quantity outcome, with price P2.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Both a price floor and a quota can give consumer surplus I and producer surplus J + K + L.

questions.postVisualStem:
Suppose that after imposing a market intervention on the good, the consumer surplus is equal to area I and the producer surplus is equal to area (J + K + L). Which of the following are likely the market interventions?

(1) price ceiling
(2) price floor
(3) quota
(4) per unit tax

questions.topicGroup: Meanings of GDP and resident producing units; items included/excluded in calculating GDP
questions.keyPoint: Meanings of GDP and resident producing units; items included/excluded in calculating GDP
questions.stem:
Which of the following are included in the calculation of gross domestic product of an economy?

(1) the salary paid to a foreign consultant who is employed by the Ocean Park for 1 month
(2) the advertising cost paid by the Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong) Limited for organising a local marathon race
(3) the salary paid by the Shanghai Disneyland to a Hong Kong resident who works in the park for 3 months
questions.explanation: GDP includes production within the economy regardless of the worker's nationality. The Ocean Park salary and local advertising service are part of Hong Kong production. Work performed in Shanghai is included in Shanghai's GDP, not Hong Kong's GDP.

questions.keyPoint: Meanings of nominal GDP and real GDP
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about real GDP and nominal GDP is CORRECT?

choices.text: During inflation, real GDP and nominal GDP will increase at the same time.
During deflation, the growth rate of real GDP will be higher than that of nominal GDP.
When the growth rate of nominal GDP is lower than the inflation rate, real GDP will increase.
When the growth rates of both real GDP and nominal GDP are negative, the inflation rate will be negative.

questions.explanation: Nominal GDP changes with both real output and the general price level. During deflation, the falling price level makes nominal-GDP growth lower than real-GDP growth. The other statements need not follow from inflation or the stated growth rates.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Relationship between nominal and real interest rates
questions.keyPoint: Understand the equation: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation rate
questions.stem: Suppose the nominal interest rate is 5%. When the realised inflation rate is higher than expected, which of the following statements is CORRECT?

choices.text: The realised real interest rate will be lower than the expected real interest rate.
The cost of holding money will be lower than 5%.
The nominal rate of return on holding money will increase.
The real rate of return on holding money will be 5%.

questions.explanation: With the nominal rate fixed at 5%, higher-than-expected inflation reduces the realised real interest rate below the expected real interest rate. The opportunity cost of holding money remains the nominal interest rate, while its real rate of return is reduced by inflation.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Measurements of the general price level
questions.keyPoint: Calculate/Determine the rate of change in the general price level (inflation/ deflation rate) by using the CPI and the implicit price deflator of GDP
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the trend of GDP deflator of an economy.
questions.explanation: A rising GDP deflator shows that the general price level rises and the purchasing power of money falls. The curve becomes steeper, so inflation is not slowing down. Real output is unknown, so nominal GDP cannot be determined from the deflator alone.

visuals.alt: Upward-curving GDP-deflator trend over time.
visuals.caption: GDP deflator trend

trends: The GDP deflator rises throughout the period and rises at an increasing rate.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The general price level rises and purchasing power of money falls; the graph alone does not determine nominal GDP growth.

questions.postVisualStem:
According to the above diagram, we can conclude that during the above period,

(1) the price level has been increasing.
(2) the nominal GDP has been increasing.
(3) the purchasing power of money has been decreasing.
(4) the inflation rate has been slowing down.

questions.keyPoint: Factors that cause a shift of an AD curve
questions.stem: Which of the following can offset the effect of an increase in the basic allowance of the salaries tax on aggregate demand?

choices.text: The central bank purchases government bonds in the open market.
The actual reserve ratio in the banking system increases.

questions.explanation: A higher basic allowance raises disposable income and shifts aggregate demand right. A higher actual reserve ratio reduces deposit creation and money supply, raising interest rates and offsetting the increase in aggregate demand. The other changes are expansionary or movements along the AD curve.

questions.topicGroup: Deviations of short run equilibrium from long run equilibrium
questions.keyPoint: Inflationary gap
questions.stem:
Suppose there is an inflationary gap in an economy. Which of the following can help the economy restore the long run equilibrium?

(1) developing the infrastructure
(2) raising the discount rate
(3) tightening the arrangement on importing labour
(4) lowering the sales tax rate
questions.explanation: Developing infrastructure raises productive capacity, while raising the discount rate is contractionary monetary policy that reduces aggregate demand. Both can help remove an inflationary gap. Tightening imported labour reduces capacity and lowering sales tax expands demand, so both work in the wrong direction.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: Explain how a given event leads to changes in AD, SRAS and/or LRAS by specifying the component(s) of AD affected and/or factor(s) affecting SRAS and/or LRAS, leading to a shift of the AD curve, the SRAS curve and/or the LRAS curve
questions.stem: The diagram below shows the aggregate demand (AD) curves, short run aggregate supply (SRAS) curves and the long run aggregate supply (LRAS) curves of an economy. The economy is initially at E0.
questions.explanation: A lower oil price lowers firms' production costs and shifts SRAS right from SRAS0 to SRAS2, moving the short-run equilibrium to E3. Oil-price changes do not change productive capacity, so the economy returns to long-run equilibrium E0 at the original LRAS0.

visuals.alt: AD-AS-LRAS diagram with AD0 to AD2, SRAS0 to SRAS2, LRAS0 and LRAS1, and equilibria E0 to E4.
visuals.caption: Oil price and AD-AS equilibrium

movements: A fall in oil price lowers production cost and shifts short-run aggregate supply from SRAS0 to SRAS2.
In the long run, output returns to the original potential output at LRAS0.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: The short-run equilibrium is E3 and the long-run equilibrium is E0.

questions.postVisualStem: If the oil price decreases, the short-run economic equilibrium will be at point ____________ while the long-run economic equilibrium will be at point ____________.

questions.keyPoint: Barter and its limitations
questions.stem: Suppose the problem of counterfeit banknotes in Country A is so serious that people in the country tend to trade by barter. Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?

choices.text: The storing of wealth will become more difficult compared with using money.
The cost of transaction will increase compared with using money.
Exchange may not take place even when the condition of double coincidence of wants is fulfilled.
If money can no longer be used in transaction, price will not exist.

questions.explanation: Barter makes wealth storage and transactions more difficult. Even with double coincidence of wants, a proposed exchange may still fail for other practical reasons. In a barter economy, however, goods still have relative prices expressed as exchange ratios, so statement D is incorrect.

questions.keyPoint: Understand and calculate excess reserves, required and actual reserve ratios
questions.stem: Refer to the following balance sheet of a banking system. Its excess reserve is $200 million.

choices.text: the maximum possible amount of deposits will be $5,000 million.
the public will hold $200 million cash.
the monetary base will increase by $200 million.
the money supply will increase by $1,200 million.

questions.explanation: Required reserves are $800 million, so the required reserve ratio is 20%. Lending the $200 million excess reserve permits a maximum deposit increase of $1,000 million, raising deposits from $4,000 million to $5,000 million.

visuals.caption: Balance sheet of a banking system

questions.postVisualStem: If the banks no longer keep the excess reserves,

questions.keyPoint: Effects of asset transfers on money supply
questions.stem:
Karmen withdraws HK$200,000 from her time deposit account in a licensed bank. She remits 10% of the amount overseas. She then puts half of the remaining amount into her savings account in the same bank and the other half into the safe deposit box of the bank.

What will be the immediate effect of the above actions on the money supply of Hong Kong?

choices.text: M1 and M3 will both decrease by $20,000.

questions.explanation: After the $20,000 overseas remittance, $90,000 is transferred to savings and $90,000 is held as cash in the safe-deposit box. The cash and savings are both in M1, so M1 increases by $90,000 relative to the original time deposit component.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse changes in money demand, money supply and nominal interest rate
questions.stem: Suppose the risk of holding bonds decreases and at the same time the central bank lowers the required reserve ratio. Which of the following is MOST likely the result caused by the two events?
questions.explanation: A lower bond risk reduces money demand as people prefer bonds, while a lower required reserve ratio raises money supply. Both changes put downward pressure on the interest rate.

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.topicGroup: Inflation and quantity theory of money
questions.keyPoint: Transaction equation and velocity of circulation (V)
questions.stem: Refer to the following diagram.

choices.text: The growth rate of real output is decreasing.
The real value of money is increasing.
The purchasing power of money is increasing.

questions.explanation: With constant velocity, money-growth rate equals inflation plus real-output growth. The graph shows constant money growth but rising price-level growth, so real-output growth must decrease.

visuals.alt: Growth-rate chart with a rising price-level line and a constant money-supply line.
visuals.caption: Quantity theory of money

trends: Money-supply growth is constant while price-level growth rises.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: With constant velocity, real-output growth decreases as inflation rises.

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the velocity of circulation of money remains unchanged. According to the quantity theory of money, which of the following statements is CORRECT?

questions.chapterTitle: Business Cycle, Changes in the General Price Level and Unemployment
questions.keyPoint: Features of the four phases of a business cycle
questions.stem: It is observed that economy A’s deflation rate is increasing sharply, and the growth rate of real GDP is decreasing. We can conclude that the economy is at the stage of
questions.explanation: A worsening deflation rate and slowing real-GDP growth are features of recession, when economic activity is contracting toward a trough.

questions.keyPoint: Four basic principles of taxation
questions.stem: The following table shows the three tax systems on salaries in three economies.
questions.explanation: Economy A has a proportional salaries tax and is least effective in reducing income inequality. Salaries taxes are direct taxes and cannot be shifted. More than economy B can satisfy the equity principle, so statement (1) is false.
questions.postVisualStem:
According to the above table,

(1) only economy B’s tax system is in line with the equity principle of taxation put forward by Adam Smith.
(2) economy A’s tax system is least effective in improving income inequality.
(3) taxpayers in all three economies cannot shift the tax burden to other parties.

questions.keyPoint: Progressive tax, proportional tax and regressive tax
questions.stem: Economy A adopts a proportional tax system. If nominal income in the economy increases at a higher rate than the inflation rate, this implies that

choices.text: the amount of tax that taxpayers pay will remain unchanged.
the tax rate that taxpayers pay will increase.
the amount of tax that taxpayers pay in terms of purchasing power will increase.
the post-tax Gini coefficient of economy A will decrease.

questions.explanation: Nominal income rises faster than prices, so real income rises. With a constant proportional tax rate, nominal and real tax payments both rise; the tax rate and income inequality need not change.

questions.topicGroup: Changes in the equilibrium level of output and price level caused by change(s) in AD and/or AS
questions.keyPoint: Explain how a given event leads to changes in AD, SRAS and/or LRAS by specifying the component(s) of AD affected and/or factor(s) affecting SRAS and/or LRAS, leading to a shift of the AD curve, the SRAS curve and/or the LRAS curve
questions.stem:
Recently, a political party has asked the government to increase the subsidy of “Work Incentive Transport Subsidy Scheme” and to raise the income and asset limits so that more people can participate in the scheme.

Which of the following are the possible effects of the above suggestions?

(1) Hong Kong’s aggregate demand will increase.
(2) Hong Kong’s short run aggregate supply will increase.
(3) Hong Kong’s long run aggregate supply will increase.
(4) The GDP of Hong Kong will increase.

choices.text: All of the above are correct.

questions.explanation: The subsidy raises recipients' disposable income and work incentive. It can raise aggregate demand, labour participation and productive capacity, shifting both SRAS and LRAS right and increasing GDP.

questions.topicGroup: Deviations of short run equilibrium from long run equilibrium
questions.keyPoint: Inflationary gap
questions.stem: Suppose an inflationary gap and a fiscal deficit exist in an economy. Which of the following measures can narrow the inflationary gap and improve the fiscal balance at the same time?

choices.text: buying government bonds from the public
reducing the basic allowance of the salaries tax

questions.explanation: Reducing the basic allowance raises tax revenue and lowers households' disposable income, improving the fiscal balance and reducing aggregate demand. The other measures are expansionary or reduce revenue.

questions.keyPoint: Calculate the gains from trade
questions.stem: The following table shows the output per unit of resources in Country A and Country B.
questions.explanation: Country B gives up 4 oranges to produce one corn, so importing 10 corn would cost 40 oranges domestically. Trade costs 20 oranges plus 10 oranges transport cost, giving a gain of 10 oranges.
questions.postVisualStem: Suppose 2 units of oranges can be exchanged for 1 unit of corn and the country importing corn has to pay a transport cost of 1 unit of oranges for each unit of imports. If the country importing corn imports 10 units of corn, its gain from trade will be __________.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of free trade and a tariff on price, domestic output, import, consumption quantity and tariff revenue for a small open economy
questions.stem: The following is the demand-supply diagram of good X in a small country. Pw is the world price of the good.

choices.text: Good X’s quantity of imports will increase to Q4.
Consumers’ total expenditure spent on good X will increase.
The government’s loss of tariff revenue will equal (P1 − Pw) x Q3.
The domestic production of good X will decrease by (Q2 − Q1).

questions.explanation: Removing the tariff lowers price to Pw. Domestic production falls from Q2 to Q1, while imports rise from Q3 − Q2 to Q4 − Q1. The tariff-revenue expression and consumer expenditure claim are not generally correct.

visuals.alt: Small-country tariff diagram with demand D, supply S, prices P1 and Pw, and quantities Q1 to Q4.
visuals.caption: Tariff removal in a small country

movements: Abolishing the tariff lowers domestic price from P1 to Pw.
Domestic production falls from Q2 to Q1 while consumption rises from Q3 to Q4.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Domestic production decreases by Q2 - Q1.

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the country abolishes the tariff imposed on good X, causing the domestic price of the good to decrease from P1 to Pw. Which of the following statements about the situation after abolishing the tariff is CORRECT?

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of a quota on domestic price, domestic consumption, domestic production and import quantity for a small open economy
questions.stem:
A country’s demand curve for and the supply curve of good X are downward and upward sloping respectively under autarky.

Suppose the country opens to trade and imposes an import quota on good X. Compared to the situation under autarky,

(1) the quantity sold of good X in the country will increase.
(2) the international price of good X in the country will increase.
(3) the revenue of domestic producers in the country from selling good X will increase.
questions.explanation: With imports, the domestic price is below the autarky price and total quantity sold rises. The international price is unchanged for a small country, and domestic-producer revenue does not rise when the domestic price and output fall.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Current account (main components: goods, services, income and current transfers)
questions.keyPoint: Whether and how a given transaction affects the current account
questions.stem: Which of the following should be included in the calculation of invisible imports in the current account of Hong Kong?

choices.text: A Hong Kong retailer purchases clothing from a retailer in the Mainland.
An American billionaire donates money to the faculty of medicine of a university in Hong Kong.
A Hong Kong resident receives treatment in a clinic in Japan.
A Japanese tourist buys souvenirs at Hong Kong Disneyland.

questions.explanation: Medical treatment bought in Japan is an import of services, or an invisible import. The other transactions are goods trade, a transfer, or Hong Kong's service export.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Balance of payments and balance of the BOP account
questions.keyPoint: The balance of payments is always balanced in the accounting sense
questions.stem: If the capital and financial account of a country is in deficit,

choices.text: its net exports of goods and services must be positive.
its current account must be in surplus.
its reserve assets must be positive.
the country must be running a balance of payment deficit.

questions.explanation: In balance-of-payments accounting, a deficit in the capital and financial account is offset by a current-account surplus when reserve changes are not stated. A country's BOP is always balanced in the accounting sense.

questions.chapterTitle: Balance of Payments Account and Exchange Rate
questions.topicGroup: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on imports and exports
questions.keyPoint: Effects of a change in the exchange rate on import and export prices in terms of domestic and foreign currencies, import and export volumes, and values of imports and exports in terms of domestic and foreign currencies
questions.stem: A change in the exchange rate between the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) and the Renminbi (RMB) is shown below.

choices.text: an increase in Mainland students’ cost of attending university in Hong Kong (in terms of RMB).
an increase in the number of Mainland tourist visiting Hong Kong.
an increase in the competitiveness of Chinese exports to Hong Kong.
an increase in the value of goods exported from the Mainland to Hong Kong (in terms of HKD).

questions.explanation: HKD 1 buying fewer RMB means the RMB appreciates against the HKD. Hong Kong becomes cheaper for Mainland visitors, increasing tourism to Hong Kong; Mainland goods become more expensive in HKD.
questions.postVisualStem: Under the linked exchange rate system in Hong Kong, the above change in the exchange rate would lead to

questions.topicGroup: Shares and bonds as sources of capital
questions.keyPoint: Advantages and disadvantages of buying shares and bonds from small investors’ point of view
questions.stem: Susan bought the shares of Cathay Pacific Airways Limited from the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

choices.text: Susan can receive interest from Cathay Pacific Airways Limited.
Susan may not receive any return from Cathay Pacific Airways Limited if it records a loss.
Susan can participate in the routine operation of Cathay Pacific Airways Limited.
Susan can participate in the Board of Directors' meetings.

questions.explanation: A shareholder may receive no dividend when a company records a loss. Shareholders receive dividends rather than interest, and an ordinary shareholder does not automatically take part in routine management or board meetings.

questions.keyPoint: State the general features of different market structures
questions.stem: A market can be regarded as monopolistic competition when __________ and __________.

choices.text: there are only several dominant sellers ... market information is not perfect
there are many sellers ... different sellers sell differentiated products
market information is perfect ... there is free entry into the market
all sellers sell homogeneous products ... there is free entry into the market

questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition has many sellers and differentiated products. Several dominant sellers describe oligopoly, while perfect information or homogeneous products are not defining features of monopolistic competition.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Relationship between price elasticity of demand and total revenue
questions.stem: A rise in the price of good X will lead to an increase in the total revenue of good Y if _____________ and the demand for good Y is _________.

choices.text: good X and good Y are complements ... elastic
good X and good Y are complements ... inelastic
good X and good Y are in competitive supply ... elastic
good X and good Y are in joint supply ... elastic

questions.explanation: Jointly supplied goods are produced together. A higher price of X encourages more joint production, increasing the supply of Y and lowering its price. With elastic demand for Y, the percentage increase in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage fall in price, so Y's total revenue rises.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Factors affecting price elasticity of supply
questions.stem: Which of the following would increase the elasticity of supply of medical services provided by private hospitals?

choices.text: The hiring requirements for doctors from other regions to practice in Hong Kong are relaxed.
The government builds more public hospitals.
The number of local medical graduates decreases.

questions.explanation: Relaxing entry requirements makes additional doctors available more easily, allowing private hospitals to expand service output more readily when price changes. This makes supply more elastic; the other changes do not increase the responsiveness of private-hospital supply.

questions.chapterTitle: Price Elasticity of Demand and Supply
questions.keyPoint: Types of price elasticity of supply
questions.explanation: As price rises from $10 to $30, quantity supplied rises from 50 to 80. The percentage rise in quantity supplied is smaller than the percentage rise in price, so price elasticity of supply is less than one and supply is inelastic.

visuals.alt: Supply curve SS for good X, with point A at price $10 and quantity 50 and point B at price $30 and quantity 80.
visuals.caption: Supply curve for good X

curves: SS is an upward-sloping supply curve.
movements: Along SS, price rises from $10 to $30 while quantity supplied rises from 50 to 80 units.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Quantity supplied rises by a smaller percentage than price, so supply is inelastic over this range.

questions.postVisualStem: SS is the supply curve for good X. In the price range $10 to $30, good X has

questions.topicGroup: Money Price (Nominal Price) and Relative Price
questions.keyPoint: Explain phenomena by applying the law of demand (using relative price or full price)
questions.stem:
Hong Kong Disneyland Hotel provides different types of room: standard room and deluxe room. Which of the following statements are CORRECT?

(1) The relative price of deluxe rooms (in terms of standard rooms) decreases when the rate of standard rooms rises.
(2) The occupancy rate of deluxe rooms increases when the rate of standard rooms rises.
(3) There would be a higher proportion of tourists from other countries staying in deluxe rooms than local visitors.
questions.explanation: When the standard-room rate rises, a deluxe room becomes cheaper in relative-price terms and standard and deluxe rooms are substitutes, so demand for deluxe rooms rises. Overseas tourists are more likely than local visitors to stay in deluxe hotel rooms, so all three statements are correct.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.keyPoint: Give possible motives behind each type of internal expansion
questions.stem: The core business of Link REIT was to renovate shopping malls and wet markets and earn rental income. It expanded its business to property development and is going to build several office premises. Which of the following is the LEAST likely motive behind the expansion?

choices.text: to achieve a higher growth of profit
to extend its brand name to other markets
to diversify the risk of retail market downturn

questions.explanation: Expanding into property development can seek higher profit growth, extend a brand into another market and diversify risk away from retail rentals. Reducing competition is most closely associated with taking over a competitor in the same market, not this expansion into a different activity.

questions.topicGroup: Tax on goods and services (Sales tax)
questions.keyPoint: Understand how price elasticities of demand and supply affect the share of the tax burden
questions.stem:
The market price of good X increases by $3 after a $5 per-unit tax is imposed. Which of the following are CORRECT?

(1) The total sales revenue (net of tax) will decrease.
(2) The price elasticity of demand for good X is smaller than its price elasticity of supply.
(3) The total expenditure of consumer will increase if the supply of good X is elastic.
questions.explanation: The producer's net price falls by $2 and the quantity transacted falls, so sales revenue net of tax falls. Consumers bear $3 of the $5 tax while producers bear $2, so demand is less elastic than supply. An elastic supply alone does not establish that consumers' total expenditure rises.

questions.keyPoint: Analyse the effects of the imposition of (effective) price ceiling on (money) price, quantity transacted, total revenue, etc.
questions.stem: Refer to the following demand and supply schedules for good X.

choices.text: There would be a surplus of 16 units.
The black market price could be as high as $50.
It is easier for low income group to obtain good X.
The total expenditure will increase by $80.

questions.explanation: Initial equilibrium is $30 and 24 units. A ceiling that leaves 16 units transacted is $10, creating a shortage of 16 units. A black-market price can rise to $50, where quantity demanded is 16. The ceiling makes rationing by non-price means more likely and reduces total expenditure from $720 to $160.

visuals.caption: Demand and supply schedules for good X

questions.postVisualStem: Suppose the market of good X is initially in equilibrium. After the government imposes an effective price ceiling, the quantity transacted of good X is 16 units. Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

questions.topicGroup: Changes in both demand and supply
questions.keyPoint: Explain the effects of a change in demand and a change in supply on equilibrium price and quantity
questions.stem: The equilibrium price of good X will increase and the change in equilibrium quantity is uncertain when the demand for good X __________ and the supply of good X __________.
questions.explanation: An increase in demand and a decrease in supply both raise equilibrium price. The demand increase raises equilibrium quantity while the supply decrease lowers it, so the net change in quantity is uncertain.

questions.keyPoint: Explain whether and how cost changes under different circumstances
questions.stem: John plans to go to a job interview by either driving himself or taking the MTR. Both options normally require the same travel time and expenses. Which of the following will increase John's opportunity cost of going to the interview by driving himself?

choices.text: John feels sick during his driving.
John's performance is poor in the job interview.
There is a delay for MTR services.
A traffic jam causes John's travel time to increase by 10 minutes.

questions.explanation: The traffic jam makes driving use an additional 10 minutes of scarce time, so the cost of travelling by car increases. Feeling sick or performing poorly at the interview does not change the travel cost, and an MTR delay does not add to the time used in driving.

questions.keyPoint: Distinguishing between free goods and economic goods
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about economic goods is CORRECT?

choices.text: An economic good must be a private good.
An economic good cannot be free of charge.
A good must be an economic good if people are willing to pay for it.
There is no opportunity cost in obtaining economic goods in a barter economy.

questions.explanation: A willingness to pay shows that the good is scarce relative to wants and therefore has an opportunity cost. Economic goods can be public goods and can be supplied free of direct charge. Barter exchanges still involve giving up resources or goods with alternative uses.

questions.topicGroup: Distinction between positive statements and normative statements
questions.keyPoint: Distinction between positive statements and normative statements
questions.stem:
Which of the following are positive statements?

(1) The average waiting time for public housing would decrease if country park land is used to build public housing.
(2) Building public housing on country park land would damage the ecological environment of Hong Kong.
(3) Developing country park land is the best way to solve the housing problem in Hong Kong.
(4) Developing country park land is a faster way to provide land for building public housing than land reclamation.
questions.explanation: Statements (1), (2) and (4) make claims that can be tested with evidence. Statement (3) uses the value judgement 'best', so it is normative rather than positive.

questions.chapterTitle: The Three Basic Economic Problems and Private Property Rights
questions.keyPoint: The meanings of the three basic economic problems and examples of the problems
questions.stem: Foxconn, a supplier of Apple Inc., announced it is to open its new factory in the United States. This is related to the __________ question(s) in economics.
questions.explanation: Choosing where to locate a factory is a decision about the method and location of production. It therefore concerns how to produce, rather than the type of output or who receives it.

questions.keyPoint: Meaning and examples of the three types of production; identify the type of production
questions.stem: Samuel works for a newspaper as a social media editor, responsible for attracting more readers by engaging in social media platforms. In economics, he provides the service of ___________ and he engages in __________ production.
questions.explanation: Samuel supplies labour because he contributes human effort to the newspaper. Managing social-media engagement is a service activity, so it is tertiary production rather than secondary production.

questions.keyPoint: Different methods of wage payment
questions.stem: Instead of calculating wages based on the quantity of food they produced, cooks in restaurants are usually paid by time rate because

choices.text: it is costly to measure their outputs.
they have no tendency to shirk.

questions.explanation: A cook's output is not easily measured by quantity alone because food quality and different tasks matter. When output measurement is costly, time-rate pay is more suitable; occupational mobility, an absence of shirking, and workers' preference do not explain the payment method.

questions.topicGroup: Input-output relationship in the short run
questions.keyPoint: Law of diminishing marginal returns
questions.stem: The following table shows a production plan of a firm which employs two factors only, namely labour and machinery.
questions.explanation: Total product is 120, 165, 220, 250 and 270 units as labour rises from two to six units. The corresponding marginal products after the second unit are 45, 55, 30 and 20. Marginal product first falls when the fifth unit is employed.
questions.postVisualStem: The marginal product of labour starts diminishing when the _______ unit of labour is put to work.

questions.keyPoint: External economies/diseconomies of scale
questions.stem: More and more technology companies have increased their investment on developing artificial intelligence (AI) in recent years. This has lead to a surge in the price of graphics processing units (GPU), which are a crucial part of developing artificial intelligence. In this case, the technology companies

choices.text: suffer from internal diseconomies of scale.
suffer from external diseconomies of scale.

questions.explanation: The increased demand for GPUs comes from expansion across the technology industry and raises an input price for all AI developers. This is an external diseconomy of scale, rather than a cost change caused solely by one individual firm's expansion.

questions.keyPoint: Comparison of features, advantages and disadvantages of different forms of ownership
questions.stem: Which of the following is the feature of a partnership in Hong Kong?

choices.text: It pays a lower profits tax rate than a private limited company.
All owners share the liability of the firm equally when it liquidates.
It earns a higher profit than a private limited company.
There is an upper limit on the number of owners.

questions.explanation: A partnership is an unincorporated business, so its profits are taxed at the lower unincorporated-business rate than a private limited company. Partners have unlimited liability but do not necessarily share it equally, profit is not guaranteed to be higher, and the stated upper-limit claim is not a general partnership feature in this comparison.

questions.chapterTitle: The Objectives and Expansion of Firms
questions.topicGroup: The basic objective of firms: profit maximisation
questions.keyPoint: Profit-maximising choice of output for a competitive firm
questions.stem: The schedule below shows the average cost of a firm in a perfectly competitive market.
questions.explanation: At two units, total cost is 2 x $20 = $40 and marginal cost is $25. The original competitive price is therefore $25. After a $10 price rise, the price is $35 and the firm produces three units, where marginal cost is $35. Revenue is then $105 and total cost is 3 x $25 = $75, giving a profit of $30.

visuals.caption: Average cost of a perfectly competitive firm

questions.postVisualStem: Given that the profit-maximising output of the firm is 2 units. If the market price increases by $10, the profit of the firm will be __________.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (II)
questions.keyPoint: Equalising opportunities
questions.stem: Which of the following policies does not involve a trade-off between equity and efficiency?

choices.text: The government lowers the statutory minimum wage rate.
The government provides more scholarships for needy students to pursue tertiary education.
The government introduces an effective rent control on residential units.

questions.explanation: More scholarships for needy students can equalise opportunities while improving human capital and productive capacity, so it need not sacrifice efficiency. The other policies can improve one objective only at the expense of the other.

questions.chapterTitle: Efficiency, Equity and the Role of Government (I)
questions.topicGroup: With the aid of a demand-supply diagram, analyse the effects of market interventions on consumer surplus, producer surplus and efficiency
questions.keyPoint: Price ceiling
questions.stem: The following diagram shows the supply and demand curves for good X.
questions.explanation: Supply is fixed at Q0, so lowering the ceiling from P0 to P1 leaves the quantity transacted unchanged. Consumers gain area J, producers receive a surplus equal to K at P1, and total social surplus stays unchanged because the output level does not change.

visuals.alt: Demand-supply diagram with a vertical supply curve S at Q0, downward demand D, price ceilings P0 and P1, and areas I, J and K.
visuals.caption: Effects of lowering a price ceiling

curves: Supply is vertical at Q0.
Demand slopes downward.
movements: The effective price ceiling falls from P0 to P1 while the quantity transacted remains Q0.
diagramDetails.answerFocus: Consumer surplus rises by J, producer surplus at P1 is K, and total social surplus is unchanged because quantity stays at Q0.

questions.postVisualStem:
Suppose the price ceiling of good X decreased from P0 to P1. Which of the following statements are CORRECT?

(

1) The increase in consumer surplus is equal to area J.
(2) The producer surplus is equal to area K.
(3) The total social surplus remains unchanged.

questions.keyPoint: Gross national income (Gross national product)
questions.stem: In order to calculate the gross national product of Hong Kong, which of the following items should be deducted from Hong Kong's gross domestic product (GDP) figure?
